Do not give the tool the title, abstract, results, or discussion; the exercise depends on neither of you knowing where the paper lands.

Working the question by hand before seeing the machine’s versions is what makes the comparison legible in both directions, since the analysis targets biases in the AI’s outputs and the ones you brought to the prompting. Setting the variants beside one another shows what the model fills in when the only thing that has changed is a city, and the critical analysis that follows asks what those assumptions imply for audiences and stakeholders in technical communication. The engineered prompt is the instrument here and the completions are the data; reading them as evidence of social bias, rather than as answers, is the work the use-case idea exists for.

acts.sum: You freewrite answers to a set of biographical questions — the setting of a favorite childhood memory, your talents, how you unwind, favorite food, how you dress, where you vacation — while deliberately not giving your identity away directly, then hand those answers to GPT-3 and ask it to infer aspects of your social identity. The reflection asks which information “exposed” your identities and why, and what might have “misled” the model; you go on to propose questions that would improve or impair its guesses and explain how the output would change. Running alongside literary texts on race and gender performance, the survey ends in discussion of the ethical implications for societal understandings of identity. Because personal information goes into the tool, privacy guidance is a live consideration.

acts.sum: The workshop is built on Hosseini’s blog experiment from July 2023, which you read before delivering it and share again afterward as follow-up reading. At its center sits a set of DALL·E images generated from one prompt varied only in the grandmother’s national origin — “a sweet, old [Polish / Russian / American / Black American] grandmother making pancakes” — four images per variant, sixteen in all. Discussion, case studies, and hands-on activities work outward from what those images reveal about how algorithms produce their outputs, and then toward strategies for recognizing and addressing bias and making ethical choices, supported by the authors’ slide deck and worksheets, with a survey collecting feedback. Concrete outputs from a single controlled prompt are what turn claims about the race and gender biases GenAI reproduces into something examinable.

acts.sum: Writing the prompts is itself part of the analysis: you compose text and image prompts designed to surface gender bias, generate the outputs with ChatGPT, DALL·E, or other AI tools, and bring what returns to a group that works out where exactly the bias appears. Discussion then turns to how it could be mitigated, with the ORF commentary on gender bias and the Berkeley Haas playbook on mitigating AI bias suggested alongside. The outputs function as evidence rather than illustration, collected and argued over. What gives the exercise its stakes is that AI already figures in automated decisions such as medical treatment and hiring, so discriminatory data producing gender-biased systems is a question about who those decisions fall on, and about the risk of machines widening gender gaps.

acts.sum: Three routes lead into the same question, framed through Michael McKenna’s distinction between useful and harmful bias. One has you analyze AI text and image outputs for gender or other biases directly. Another sends you into case studies of law enforcement case-management systems, hiring algorithms, or facial recognition, with COMPAS and OASys among the materials. The third is a jigsaw, where each group takes one type of AI bias, works out its implications and how to spot it, and then teaches the class what it found. Whichever route, what comes out is an analysis or a presentation rather than a summary, and the spread across gender, racial, socioeconomic, and disability-related bias is deliberate: the awareness being raised concerns real-world effects, not a defect in a tool.
acts.t: Exploring AI Bias: Output Analysis, Case Studies, and Jigsaw

acts.sum: Choose a model to audit, image or text, and give it a task, prompting repeatedly and systematically with the same input until you hold a small dataset of outputs rather than a single specimen. Reading each output on its own and then the collection as a whole, you draw inferences about how the system “thinks” about the task and record them in a 200-word reflection, working from the Mini Audit form. Adapted from Metaxa and Buolamwini’s audit methods, the exercise concluded an AI and Writing module in Fall 2024 over one week with more than 70 students, and the audit target can be narrowed to a discipline, with readings on algorithmic auditing to support it. Patterns tracked across a dataset are what make AI defaults readable, and reading them is also how you evaluate a model as a collaborator.
acts.t: Mini Audits of GenAI Outputs

acts.sum: When no tutor is present to nudge the conversation along, the nudges can come from elsewhere: you enter a case study presented in class into ChatGPT and ask it for a list of topics the discussion should consider — ethics, boundaries, relationships, techniques — then use that list to guide the discussion your group actually has. The AI supplies the agenda, not the analysis, which stays with you. Repeated across case study discussion workshops built on real-world cases, the list gradually becomes unnecessary as the key topics get internalized. For counseling students in the early, formative stages, that is what the nudge list is for: learning which considerations belong in a case discussion by having them named until you name them yourself.

acts.sum: Once you can write prompts that generate clinical case studies — and training in writing them is part of the use-case idea — the supply of cases stops being a constraint. You generate novel cases aimed at the topics or issues you find difficult, and discuss them independently or in small groups, inside class and outside it. Because the cases are made rather than collected, they tilt toward your own gaps while still integrating ethics, boundaries, relationships, and techniques, and they form a safe exploratory environment for practicing the discussion of real-world cases. Building a case bank takes time in counseling education; regular practice with diverse cases tailored to where your knowledge thins is what this puts in its place.
acts.t: Endless Case Studies for Counseling Practice

acts.sum: Working inside an extracurricular, online, open, and synchronous module that complements Clinical Psychology at UNAM and lives in the course LMS, you meet a clinical case presented by the instructor and propose a solution grounded in the literature before anything is put to a model. You and the instructor then query ChatGPT-3.5 with predefined clinical cases, and you analyze what comes back against research articles and clinical guidelines, tracking where the model’s answers diverge from what the literature actually supports. That analysis becomes an individual final clinical case report, and the module closes with a collaborative debate and feedback, an instructor supervising throughout. The specialist literature resolves the case; the model supplies a response to be tested, not an authority. The point is to see the gap between an AI answer and the evidence, and to close it yourself.

acts.sum: One course session is devoted to ChatGPT, and after the instructor’s demonstration, you work in a group of four to six to invent an imaginary culture and craft scenarios in which cultural differences produce subtle communication barriers rather than obvious clashes. Your group identifies the values and norms shaping those dynamics and proposes ways of overcoming them that are both feasible and empathetic, then presents the scenarios to the class. acts.sum: Writing out the parameters of the scenario you want, along with the challenges and complexity it should contain, is what determines everything downstream: ChatGPT generates the problem-based learning scenario from that specification, and it goes to individuals or small groups who identify the problem inside it and resolve it through inquiry. The source shows sample prompts and a sample scenario from 5 February 2023. Students can also write the prompts themselves, which makes the generation a shared exercise in co-creation rather than leaving the scenario authored entirely elsewhere; the source asks, as an open question, whether coming together to identify and solve problems could help develop collaborative capacity. What the use-case idea aims at is scenarios that trigger curiosity and inquiry, with the difficulty built in deliberately at the prompt stage.

acts.sum: The use-case idea takes key AI concepts and ethical dilemmas from the curriculum — machine learning, algorithmic bias, data privacy, societal impacts — and stages them. Around a fictional scenario, the authors’ working example being an AI system that optimizes a city’s energy use to cut carbon emissions, you develop scripts or improvise scenes peopled by engineers facing technical and ethical challenges, citizens experiencing the benefits and the drawbacks, and policymakers balancing advancement against equity. acts.sum: You work under a set of AI Standards of Conduct that names both sides of the line: brainstorming, exploring topics and counterarguments, and revisiting drafts using AI suggestions are acceptable, while offloading most of the writing or research, generating large chunks with little input, trusting output at face value, or substituting AI for research and thinking are not. In the Brainstorming Counterarguments assignment you write a thesis answering the prompt question, or develop one with the AI assistant, then use the assistant to explore counterarguments and rebuttals before writing with substantial original contribution; a second assignment puts an AI-powered assistant to work exploring research. Anything worth keeping has to be saved, since the assistant does not retain it, and everything it returns is reviewed for bias, falsehood, or harm. Over one or two class sessions, the standards are what let you tell AI-assisted writing from AI-generated writing.

The policy is not written once and filed: it comes back into view as each new assignment is introduced, or an AI Use Scale level is set per assignment instead. Drafting works from the institutional policy and the assignment descriptions and stays inside what the institution requires and what consistency across sections demands. Instructors who have run it report that students sometimes settle on stricter rules than they would have set, alongside more dialogue about AI and less AI-based plagiarism — expectations end up clear because they are shared rather than announced.

acts.sum: Across an eight-hour unit in Design and Assessment of Digital Resources, two hours introduce AI in education and two more are a hands-on introduction to ChatGPT before the design work begins. In teams of three, each taking a scenario no other team has — a hands-on story for primary pupils, an educational problem approached from three roles, a didactic unit, an AI-assisted essay with summary and presentation, a full assessment approach, gamified units, math exercise sets, gamified English activities, or a free theme — you spend two and a half hours developing and documenting it with free ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing. For every stage you ask Microsoft Copilot, on a mobile phone, to “create a drawing,” adjusting or replacing images that miss and writing prompts that specify diversity, disability, or gender where relevant so the storyboard does not inherit the model’s representational defaults. Anatomical errors turn up and are tolerable here, because storyboarding is a fault-tolerant stage rather than a finished artifact. Over about four weeks in an intermediate digital writing course, the log of that conversation becomes your evidence: you analyze the writing and thinking patterns in its output, set them against the selected readings, write an analytical report, and then present your findings and your experience orally. acts.sum: Two game-like, paper-based activities carry this, and neither needs a computer. In the first you add probability weightings to a network of word-type nodes until the chain generates grammatical phrases; in the second you build a chain out of an existing text extract, drawing a [Start] box linked to the first word and then, for each “current word,” counting its occurrences and drawing weighted arrows to the words that follow, closing with a [Stop] box after the last word. Running the finished chain generates text probabilistically, and you can see exactly why it produced what it did, because you drew every weight yourself. The discussion afterward asks what these word-to-word preferences reveal about how language models work and what they imply for linguistics.
acts.t: Understanding Markov Chains by Hand

acts.sum: The framing question — what it would actually mean for AI to “replace” humans in language work — is what you design against. You build your own Turing Test-inspired experiment to get an LLM to perform some language task, crafting and iterating the prompts and then testing the outputs with human readers to see whether they hold up. Documentation takes the form of a “slidedoc,” slides written in full sentences so they read like a report, a format that keeps the write-up from swallowing the experiment it describes. Presenting the findings, you weigh the advantages and drawbacks of handing that task to a machine. What this interdisciplinary elective develops is the ability to pose a research question about an LLM’s capabilities and build a method that can answer it.

Using a premade module, you train your own text generator on that dataset, then examine the output for patterns and emergent meanings rather than for correctness. The closing reflective essay takes up the affordances, challenges, and generative potential of LLMs through a neuroqueer lens, treating the direction you gave the machine as a writing practice being renegotiated rather than handed off. As the final project of the six-week summer course Hypermedia and Digital Rhetorics, it runs about two weeks, though more time is advised for trial and error; no computer science background is needed, only patience for troubleshooting. An artist statement sets the project against combinatory writing, procedural generation, novelty and repetition, authorship and creativity. acts.sum: Repetition is the subject before it is the technique: you read and discuss poems and digital works built on it, among them Poe’s “The Bells,” Emmett Williams’ “Soldier,” Saroyan’s “Crickets,” Durand’s “Pastoral,” Bertram’s “Incident,” and digital pieces by Flores, Strand, and Whalen, and then write a p5.js sketch that loops 50,000 times, appending a word to a “book” string and printing the result to the console. Changing the repeated word or phrase and rerunning shows how much a single term alters, and from there you develop the repetition into a book of at least 50,000 words, ideally formatted as a printable, book-like PDF. Framed by NaNoGenMo, National Novel Generation Month, the work uses a generation method small enough to read line by line, so what the machine is doing stays fully transparent, a contrast with LLMs that Whalen draws in the source.
acts.t: Repetition: Programming a 50,000-Word Book

acts.sum: Three parts carry this one. In the first, found poems, you study Tzara, Oulipo, and Padgett, collect found text, scan or photograph it, and cut it up and collage it into 2–3 pages, alongside Eunsong Kim’s “FOUND, FOUND, FOUND; LIVED, LIVED, LIVED.” The second part, Markov memory, moves the same impulse into code: your own text is loaded into RiTa.markov(4) in RiTa.js, and lines are generated out into an HTML page. A 200-word reflection, framed with a quote from Kim, accounts for your formal choices, for the slippage and limits you ran into in the generation, and for authorship and erased voices, which is where the Dada and Oulipo lineage stops being history and becomes a question about whose words you are working with.

Assignment “Translating a Policy Document into Plain English,” sections as headed on the page
acts.rf: Comparison questions.
acts.sum: You take a complex policy document and render it into plain English at a reading level accessible to most Americans, which means deciding line by line what can go and what cannot. The same document then goes to an LLM with the same task, and the two translations are set against each other around three questions: what meaning did you sacrifice, what did the machine sacrifice, and did it make serious errors? The comparison is the analysis, not a verdict on the tool in the abstract but a record of what each of you chose to lose. The use-case idea adapts to most disciplines and levels, since what changes is only which policy document you take on. acts.sum: Run a series of prompts in a single chat, ending with one that relates back to your first but has been colored by everything in between, and paste that output into a discussion post. Then open a fresh chat, enter that same final prompt with no conversation behind it, and paste the second output directly below the first so the two sit together. Analyzing what separates them is the work: what the accumulated context added, what it distorted, what it quietly carried forward. Saving, renaming, and sharing chats belongs to the use-case idea as well, since comparison depends on being able to keep a thread. The post that results makes visible something otherwise easy to miss — that an answer depends on the conversation around it, and that starting over is sometimes the correction.

The more demanding move comes after you have written your own analysis, when you hand it over with something like “Analyze my analysis of this poem… play devil’s advocate” and ask for an alternative reading of the same lines. An optional extension turns the tool the other way, asking it to build a figurative-language game for a science concept such as intermolecular forces. Annotated analyses are what you keep, and what the sequence builds is comprehension of the poem and of figurative language, with your own reading tested against a competing one rather than replaced by it.

Credibility and relevance are then evaluated laterally rather than from inside any single platform, and a comparative analysis of the three is what you produce. The comparison builds a working sense of how research platforms, traditional and AI alike, mediate what reaches you.
acts.t: Lateral Approaches to AI-Supported Research

That second move matters most on fictional projects, where the generated persona is the only learner available to consult. The use-case idea shows where AI might improve an instructional design while leaving the question of the persona’s fidelity open rather than settled.
acts.t: Interviewing Learner Personas

Specialized tools are named for several of these tasks, among them PCS patient avatars, Quizlet Q-Chat, SkillCat, Rongo, and Shark Tank AI, and a general chatbot can often do similar work in a less immersive visual environment. You ask ChatGPT for a definition and multiple example sentences for each, put as plainly as “Define the word systematic and use it in five different sentences,” and read what comes back for grammar, collocations, and context rather than meaning alone. acts.sum: A quiz show format the group already knows is the frame — Who Wants to Be a Millionaire or Kaun Banega Crorepati, Family Feud or 100 Mexicanos Dijeron. You prompt ChatGPT or a similar chatbot to host that format on a specific topic for a small group, specifying the number of players and the mode: scored questions, round elimination, first to answer. Where the format is unfamiliar to the chatbot, its rules go into the prompt, and where its knowledge of the topic is thin, you paste the content in and ask it to use that as its source, which keeps questions relevant and reduces accuracy problems. Answers arrive by text while the chatbot tracks scores and eliminations, with private answer cards, buzzers, or timers added where the format needs them and a team-based run as an option. acts.sum: Revision is the moment for this one. With a draft already written, you read Craig A. Meyer’s “The Evolution of Imitation” and use its imitation activities to rewrite a paragraph of that draft in a different style; class discussion of the rewrites brings in Aull and Lancaster’s framework of style as stance. You then summarize your own work and run it through a text generator, ChatGPT or Lex, to produce versions in different styles, analyze the stance markers in each, and enact a chosen style in your revision. acts.sum: Pick a reading from class and try to get an LLM to recreate it as closely as it can. The use-case idea runs two ways: unscaffolded, where you prompt freely and often do little more than name the text, or scaffolded, where the class first learns prompt engineering and builds a prompt together. Either way, what comes back is set against the original and discussed, and length, depth, and the handling of abstract concepts are where the gaps tend to open. The LLM does the imitating; naming what it missed is the work. Because the shortfall shows up fast, the exercise reveals the model’s limits quickly while pushing you back into the reading itself, since describing what is absent from the recreation means articulating the original’s voice, style, tone, and message.

Alongside poetry resources and poems such as Danez Smith’s “dear white america,” Ariana Brown’s “For everyone who tried on the slipper before Cinderella,” and Amiri Baraka’s “Babylon Revisited,” you compose two spells of your own, one centered on a personal “wish,” and then prompt ChatGPT to write its own, iterating the prompts as you go. acts.sum: Feed an LLM the prompt you already have for your writing assignment and read what comes back as a specimen rather than a model. In small groups you discuss the text’s strengths and weaknesses on two counts, plausibility and quality; as a class, over 5–10 minutes, the weaknesses several groups noticed are highlighted and framed as missing “moves” tied to genre, purpose, and audience. You then tweak the prompt iteratively to fix the most salient of those weaknesses, adding as few words as possible each time, and carry the moves you identified into your own composing. Run before anyone writes in the target genre, with an LLM (GPT-3/ChatGPT, a dollar or two of credits if paid) and a projector, it builds metacognitive awareness of the textual moves, in Swales’ sense, that make examples of a genre succeed.

acts.rf: In-class critical analysis.
acts.sum: When you ask ChatGPT to write about VARK learning styles, the answer that comes back is wholly positive and treats learning styles as accepted, though they lack scientific foundation. Against that you gather as many varied resources on the topic as you can find, then sort them: those that still spread the myth on one side, those that critique it on the other, with a discussion of what separates the two. Digging deeper means asking what the critiques actually say, who authored each viewpoint, and where the ideas come from. The AI-created resource is the object of analysis here, not the source of the answer. Sorting a real body of sources around a claim the AI stated confidently and wrongly is what makes the quality of an AI-created resource something you can critically analyze.
acts.t: Debunking the Learning Styles Myth with ChatGPT

acts.sum: Set a human-written article beside one ChatGPT produced on the same topic, and annotate the first against the second using the PROMPT framework, which covers provenance, relevance, objectivity, method, presentation, and timeliness. Your critique of the ChatGPT output hunts for sentences that sound plausible but are wrong or do not quite make sense, checks the sources and references it offers, notes anything it missed, and comments on its language. Discussion then asks what lessons you draw, and whether the human article would look different had its author started from a ChatGPT answer and revised it. Evaluating AI output exactly as you would any other web resource is the move: it keeps the assessment on familiar critical ground while making the particular shortcomings of generated text visible.

For each entry you upload a screenshot from your institution’s library database showing what you found, or failed to find. Extensions push further: evaluate a real scholar’s credibility and summarize their work, build a bibliography of sources that do exist, or test AI quotations in a search engine using quotation marks and replace the fake ones. acts.sum: Deepfake videos and images produced by AI are the material here, examined closely enough that the common hallmarks of faked imagery start to become recognizable. Alongside that examination you explore the online sources available for fact-checking viral disinformation and then practice on potential fakes, working out whether a given item is authentic. No AI tool is needed to run this; what it takes is examples of AI-produced deepfake video and images and the fact-checking resources to test them against. Relevance is checked alongside existence, since a reference whose subject does not match the text it supposedly supports can itself be the signal of a hallucination. You then put the question back to the AI, asking it to verify its own references, and compare its account against what your searching turned up, with a verification log recording the results; later parts of the source move on to avoidance strategies. Working through it as co-researchers makes visible how readily fabricated references appear.

acts.sum: A polished infographic circulates among colleagues along with its reference list, and the questions put to the room are deliberately plain: where did this information come from, and how would you know it is correct? Once the answers have run their course, you reveal that the references are fabricated — correctly formatted, attributed to real journals and real authors, plausible on their face, and produced by ChatGPT. The debate that follows takes up accuracy, truth, trust, and accountability, and what it means for claims about developing critical thinkers that fake information can be packaged this well. The same infographic, made with ChatGPT, QuillBot, and Canva, is all the exercise needs, and it suits educational development work or any meeting on AI accuracy and sourcing. The discussion is about how far AI output can be relied on.

The source’s sample prompts concern a nuclear physicist explaining MRI, a Florida manatee statute, social workers’ obligations around elder abuse, and FERPA and discussing grades with parents. acts.rf: Class discussion and revision.
acts.sum: Deciding what images to use in a multimodal memoir, you write a brief, effective summary of your own writing for DALL·E 2 or another image generator, built to give a command, a desired output, and context rather than everything at once — an early trial that pasted an entire essay as the prompt produced irrelevant images. What comes back is held against the memoir’s intended message, and where the images miss the point, the question turns back on the writing: does the essay convey what you meant? Revision follows from that mismatch, and class discussion traces how refining the prompt changes the relevance of the images. Refined prompts, the AI images, and a revised memoir are what you end with. The gap between image and intent is the instrument, showing you what your prose actually says.
acts.t: Rewriting with AI Image Generators

acts.sum: If appearing on camera is the obstacle, you record your presentation as audio and hand it to Adobe’s Animate from Audio feature in Adobe Express, which animates a 2D character and lip-syncs it to what you said, using AI to detect tone and add motion. The animated presentation is then what you share in place of on-camera video, so your voice and your understanding of the material do the presenting while your face stays out of it. Offered across all levels of education as an accessibility and confidence option for camera-averse students, it leaves you with a finished presentation in your own voice. What it works on is confidence in presenting, without making visibility the price of taking part.
acts.t: Animated Avatars to Enable Student Voices

acts.sum: Roughly five minutes of close observation comes before any typing: you look at an open-access artwork — Vermeer’s The Milkmaid, in the source’s example — and only then translate what you have noticed into a prompt specific enough to recreate the painting. Any text-to-image generator serves, DALL·E, Midjourney, or Adobe Firefly among them, and the images that return are analyzed and discussed for how closely they match the artist’s style and technique. Informed by the contributor’s work in the Rijksmuseum education department, the use-case idea runs in class or in a museum, and the goal is observation rather than recreation, with prompt writing practiced along the way. Prompting is used here as a reason to keep looking, long and attentively, at the work itself.

acts.sum: Playing with image-generation prompts in DALL·E 2, Midjourney, or something similar yields a spread of outcomes, which are then arranged on the axes and intersections of a morphological matrix — symbolism and color among them — to analyze elements, composition, and style. How the matrix fills is itself readable: clusters indicate that the variables need finer delineation or that prompts are too open or too closed, while sparse areas mark plausible ideas that neither students nor the AI typically generate. Genre space and topology from multimodal linguistics supply the theory for what you are looking at, after which you test again, critiquing combinations and reevaluating AI’s potential for communicative visuals. A formative workshop that also suits assessment, it develops Idea 83 from the 2023 collection and keeps critique from settling on aesthetics or treating outputs as solutions.
acts.t: Structured Critique of AI Images Through a Morphological Matrix

acts.sum: Take a piece of academic content you are working with — a journal article, a research book — and redesign it as a comic strip, generating the frames with DALL·E 2, Midjourney, or another text-to-image tool. The redesign is a matter of deciding which parts of the source carry the story and how they distribute across frames, and the finished strip is what presents the content. Addressed to higher education students and educators alike, the exercise converts text-heavy academic material into visual storytelling, on the premise that content seen in frames is more engaging, and easier to remember, than the same content in continuous prose.

acts.sum: The invitation is deliberately open — invent a creature, a plant, a piece of furniture, or a building that does not exist yet — and whatever you come up with you realize as an image in DALL·E 2. Sharing the results in a group is where the warm-up does most of its work: you talk through each other’s creations and then extend the possibilities by combining ideas, so that one person’s invention feeds into the next thing generated. The AI-generated images and the combined ideas are what the session leaves with. Torrance and Guilford’s tests of creative thinking are the inspiration, used here to draw creativity out rather than to measure it, and the exercise fits any educational setting, group settings especially.
acts.t: Creative Warm-Ups: Dream Up a New Creation

acts.sum: You describe an emotion, or a pair of them, along with a real or fictional context in which someone might feel it, and that description becomes the image prompt — “Happiness and safety, forest, birds, clouds, flowers, digital art” is the source’s example — put to DALL·E 2 or something similar. Play follows the pattern of Dixit, the board game that inspired the use-case idea, with players guessing each other’s emotional representations from the cards. acts.rf: Reflective five-minute essay.
acts.sum: Choose a term or concept you want to represent visually, assemble descriptive words for it, and feed those words to DALL·E 2. With the first image in front of you, write a five-minute essay describing what you see and linking it back to the term, working out as you write where the picture falls short of your understanding and what would have to change. That diagnosis feeds the second attempt: you adapt your wording and generate a revised image that better reflects the concept, leaving two images and the essay that connects them. The writing carries the conceptual work while the generator renders only what your words specify, so the gap between the two is where the reflection sits, and working that gap closed is also your first-hand experience of working with AI.
acts.t: Visualizing Terms and Concepts with DALL·E

Editing follows with Track Changes on, applying the comprehensive editing principles from class, which means working above the sentence level rather than hunting typos. Because everyone has already worked with AI writing tools before the paper and blue books come out, the unplugged stretch registers as a comparison rather than a deprivation, and the final unit becomes a decision made from experience on both sides. The course work closes by comparing what writing was like across the three units. Reversing the more common unplugged-first sequence is what makes that comparison possible, since a shared baseline of AI familiarity exists before the unit that withholds it.

acts.sum: Working in a group of three or four, you build prompts on topics of interest relevant to the class, then collect consecutive responses inside a single ChatGPT chat, since staying in one chat is what keeps the responses from replicating each other, and save them. From there you analyze the genre and the content of what the machine produced critically. Those three moves are the required core of the use-case idea. Beyond them it extends optionally into editing the machine-generated writing, summarizing individual responses and synthesizing across them, and writing an original paper on the same topic built on rigorous library research and current references. Understanding how the text was produced, and watching where its strategies run thin, is what the original writing is meant to rest on.

Readings on the extended mind (Clark) and posthumanism (Hayles) supply the terms for that mapping. What you produce is a personal posthuman research protocol stating where human judgment is non-negotiable and how AI collaboration will be documented and disclosed. acts.sum: Peer review here begins in conversation, with you and your peer talking through the goals and concerns they have for their draft of the Investigative Field Essay before you read a word of it. You then read it yourself and write comments against the rubric on Canvas, and the same draft also goes to a generative AI tool for its feedback. The writer now holds two bodies of response, human and machine, and weighs them to decide which to act on, revising and then reflecting on those choices. Putting the two kinds of feedback side by side makes revision a rhetorical judgment about whose reading of the draft is worth taking up, rather than a checklist of corrections to apply.

acts.sum: As you work on components of a final project, the Three-Stage AI Engagement Reflection Chart catches your thinking at three moments. Before turning to a tool, you set down what you are trying to do, why you want AI for it, what support you actually need, and what you intend to do yourself. While working, you take stock of your own judgment and strategies and of how the AI is supporting or challenging them. Afterward, you evaluate the AI’s performance, its effect on your writerly identity, and the areas where you have grown. Your answers are recorded in the chart, which is what the use-case idea leaves behind. Writing the plan before the prompt and the assessment after it is what keeps a writer in control of the AI use across an extended piece of work.

Holding a table of lexical and grammatical techniques, you paraphrase a short journal abstract of about 100 words using them. Students work through introductory Python and data-processing notebooks, interpolate and normalize spectra, and inspect the 630–880 cm−1 region with PCA. acts.sum: In this optional third-year chemistry practical, small groups of students learn data processing and machine-learning evaluation by identifying ortho, meta, and para substitution patterns of benzene derivatives from infrared spectra. Working through introductory Python and Jupyter notebooks, students interpolate and normalize a labeled library of spectra, inspect the diagnostic region with principal component analysis, and evaluate a k-nearest-neighbors classifier over repeated training and test splits. They then measure two unknown samples on an ATR infrared spectrometer and classify them against the full-spectrum library. The classifier supplies predicted labels; students judge its performance from held-out results, with demonstrators supporting interpretation. The outcome is a set of predicted assignments, visualized spectral structure, and model-performance results.

The LED/sensor apparatus is assembled and calibrated in a light-tight enclosure, and voltage–spectrum data are collected. acts.sum: Physics educators describe how to build an affordable self-driving optical laboratory in which a machine-learning controller tries to reproduce a target light spectrum through repeated measurement. acts.sum: A DeepXDE tutorial shows how to estimate an unknown coefficient in a partial differential equation with a physics-informed neural network while also approximating the equation’s solution. The analyst specifies a one-dimensional diffusion equation with the coefficient declared as a trainable unknown, adds the domain, boundary and initial conditions, and supplies ten observations of the solution at the final time. The network and the coefficient are trained together so that both the physics residual and the mismatch with observations are minimized, and coefficient estimates are logged during training. Because the tutorial uses a synthetic problem with a known solution, the analyst can inspect loss and error against that solution. The output is an estimated coefficient, an approximate solution, and training diagnostics.

acts.sum: An analyst who needs to find records referring to the same person or entity across files without a shared unique identifier uses Splink, an open-source probabilistic record-linkage library. The analyst defines blocking rules that limit which pairs are compared and specifies how fields such as names and dates are compared; the software estimates prior and non-match parameters and uses expectation maximization to learn match parameters without labeled training data, then predicts a match probability for each candidate pair. The analyst chooses a threshold, clusters records above it into linked groups, and inspects the diagnostics to judge whether the links and their uncertainty are acceptable. The repository’s worked example uses synthetic data; linking real personal records raises data-protection questions that the software license does not settle.
acts.t: Link uncertain duplicate records with probabilistic matching

acts.sum: Before retraining a classifier, an analyst uses cleanlab to find training examples whose labels are probably wrong. The analyst generates out-of-sample predicted class probabilities through cross-validation, runs cleanlab’s data and label issue detection to rank suspect examples by estimated label quality, and then inspects and corrects the flagged labels or compares a workflow that prunes them. The corrected or pruned data are used to retrain the model, and performance is compared on separately evaluated data. A model’s disagreement with a label is a reason to look rather than proof of an annotation error, so the analyst’s review of flagged examples against independent evidence is the step that decides. The tutorial uses a small synthetic four-class dataset and can simulate perfect human correction, which a real review does not guarantee.
acts.t: Audit noisy labels using out-of-sample predictions and human review

acts.sum: Researchers use anchored topic modeling to examine how risk, protective, systemic, and procedural factors interact across the case histories of families in a family-preservation program. Case notes are arranged chronologically, cleaned, and anonymized; researchers read sample histories and use a socioecological framework to choose anchor words that steer Anchored CorEx toward domain-relevant topics. They fit and compare models; then several authors interpret topics independently before reconciling labels and using axial coding to relate them, and they compare topic patterns across normalized segments of each history. The authors caution against using the case notes for downstream tasks in language-processing systems, such as predicting the risk of child maltreatment, citing the limitations and biases embedded in them. The output is interpreted topics, relationships, and temporal patterns.
acts.t: Analyze how child-welfare case narratives change over time with anchored topic models

acts.sum: Before using AI images in Bible teaching, you select scenes deeply rooted in Christian iconography; the source used the Baptism of Jesus and the Last Supper. For each, you issue a deliberately vague prompt first, to see which iconographic patterns the image system produces by default, and then a targeted prompt that adds explicit references to Catholic symbolism and states the religious-education purpose. You keep the first image returned for each prompt, with no refinement, and compare the pair for narrative or interpretive character, theological depth, symbolic coherence, and Western cultural stereotyping, and against selected works of sacred art. The teacher must judge whether either image is theologically adequate for teaching and turn the comparison into didactic recommendations. In the source, both tiers showed shallow theology, symbolic oversimplification, and Western stereotypes.

Students identify the inconsistencies in the image, say how each should be corrected, and place each element accurately within the biblical passage. The student must judge each element against the biblical text and its historical setting. The exercise ends in reflection on how generative AI handles biblical interpretation. The source calls this visual debugging and frames it as turning students from observers into interpreters.
acts.t: Visual debugging: students correct symbolic dispersion in AI biblical images

srp: To use ChatGPT as a virtual peer in flipped anatomy instruction, supporting content review, group learning, and reflective thinking while building critical evaluation and digital literacy.

After pre-class H5P videos, groups of about six use ChatGPT in class only, prompting in Spanish or English, through three phases: evaluate accuracy of responses (vomeronasal organ), critique flawed explanations (ductus and truncus arteriosus), and apply comparative anatomy to a problem (aortic arch). Experiences are polled with Wooclap, and cognitive-level questions are embedded in formal assessments.
Group evaluations and critiques of chatbot output, proposed alternative names for vascular variations, a worked aortic arch solution, and assessment performance.
Students evaluate the anatomical accuracy of chatbot responses in Phase I and critique flawed explanations in Phase II.
acts.sum: In a first-year veterinary anatomy course taught as a flipped classroom, students prepare with interactive videos and then work in class in groups of about six, with ChatGPT as a virtual group member used only during those sessions. Each group puts a set question to it in Spanish or English, and students are also encouraged to write their own. In the first phase, on the vomeronasal organ, they pick out the relevant anatomical data and judge whether the chatbot’s answers are accurate. In the second, on congenital heart anomalies, they critique flawed AI explanations and sharpen their own understanding. In the third, on the aortic arch, they apply comparative anatomy to a complex problem. Students judge the chatbot’s answers against real anatomical specimens. In the source, every group at first accepted an incorrect ChatGPT answer, although 85% of students had answered correctly beforehand. Understanding is assessed through leveled questions, including one specific to the ChatGPT-supported sessions, embedded in the formal exams.
acts.t: ChatGPT as a virtual group member across three Bloom-aligned phases in flipped veterinary anatomy

You generate three to five photographic portraits per label with a text-to-image platform of your choice, vary the prompts by age, gender, or race, and document how small changes alter the images. You then gather existing portraits of the same categories from art history, social media, popular culture, and news media, and identify visual patterns, typologies, and prejudices across both sets. acts.sum: In a mathematics teaching-methods module, preservice teachers receive two contextualized, curriculum-based word problems of a kind chatbots tend to handle poorly. No prompts are supplied: each student writes their own, obtains a step-by-step solution from ChatGPT, and pastes screenshots of the output into the assignment. The task is not to solve the problems but to judge whether each generated solution is accurate, justify that judgment from their own mathematical reasoning, correct the solution where it is wrong, and reflect on the accuracy of the work. Students complete it individually within a set time. The instructor reads the submissions for generic language and for signs of uncertainty, monitoring, and error recognition. Because prompting is self-directed, students meet different outputs, including both correct and incorrect solutions.

acts.sum: This participatory workshop for journalism students builds skill in recognizing automated social media accounts in political disinformation. In the first phase the instructor explains political communication online and the manipulation of the electoral public sphere, then gives a pretest in which students judge ten Twitter accounts as automated or not. In the second phase the class sees the pretest results, the instructor formalizes the intuitive knowledge students already showed and teaches the metadata features that mark bots, students try detection tools on the accounts they judged, and they take a comparable self-assessment test with items isolating single profile features in screenshots, plus open comments on how they identified accounts. In the third phase, results are presented collectively, and the class debates reporting mechanisms, publicizing these techniques, and cases where user action led to suspensions. With 55 students, the authors report average scores on the account identification questions of 6 out of 10 before the training and 5.7 out of 10 after it, while their abstract describes a slight increase in identification ability and a more conscious process of identification.

acts.sum: After each major project milestone in an entrepreneurship course, such as customer discovery, problem-solution validation, or a pivot decision, students write a reflection journal entry with a generative AI tool as a questioning partner. Following a prompting protocol built on the six stages of Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, students direct the tool not to write the reflection but to pose probing questions at each stage about their own experience, for example what they assumed going into a customer interview or what evidence supports an interpretation. Students answer in their own words, and the model generates increasingly specific follow-up questions. Each student then revises the material into a final reflection and submits both the dialogue draft and the revised entry. Any freely available tool may be used. With 25 undergraduates in Vietnam, the authors report deeper reflection alongside concerns about generic feedback and over-reliance.

acts.sum: When you review a manuscript or grant proposal, you first check the reviewer AI policy of the journal, publisher, or funder and follow the most restrictive rule that applies; if AI is prohibited, you do not use it. Where it is permitted, you use only a system that preserves confidentiality, such as one hosted locally or by a trustworthy institution, and never upload the manuscript, any part of it, or your review comments to a cloud tool, even for language editing. The permitted system may summarize the manuscript and improve the wording of your review, on the assumption that it will make mistakes. You watch for hidden prompts planted by authors, check every AI-generated passage for accuracy, currency, and bias, disclose the use and its purposes, and keep full responsibility for the review’s judgments.

srp: To make AI-assisted scholarly workflows transparent, traceable, and accountable by replacing generic disclosure with proportionate documentation.

Classify the AI use by tier; record tool, date, purpose, input, prompt, output use, verification, modifications, privacy safeguards, manuscript relevance, and disclosure location at the tier’s depth; apply redaction principles where material is sensitive; check against the framework’s checklists and current journal, publisher, institution, funder, and ethics policies.

acts.sum: A researcher, reviewer, or editor documents how AI was used in a piece of scholarly work, not merely whether it was used. They first decide the tier: minimal for low-risk language support, extended where AI touched substance, method, evidence, or interpretation, and restricted or redacted where full disclosure would expose confidential, identifiable, proprietary, peer-review, or clinically sensitive material. They then complete the applicable fields at that depth: tool and version, date, the specific purpose, input and its sensitivity, the prompt or prompt category, what output was accepted, modified, or rejected, verification steps, manual changes, privacy safeguards, relevance to the manuscript, and where the disclosure will appear. Finally they check the record against the framework’s checklists and the target journal’s and institution’s current policies.
acts.t: Documenting your own AI-assisted scholarly workflow at one of three proportionate tiers across eleven named fields

Section 2.2 “Message generation protocol,” subsections 2.2.1 “Step 1: collecting retweeted human-generated tweets” through 2.2.4 “Step 4: selecting AI-generated messages for evaluation”; the Google Colab timing is in the Discussion paragraph on usability
acts.rf: Human rater evaluation of quality and clarity against human-written messages; computational analysis of sentiment, readability, and semantic content.
srp: To generate health awareness messages with an LLM and prompt engineering and establish how they compare with the best-performing human-written messages in quality and clarity.

Scrape posts carrying the topic hashtags and keep the thirty most shared human messages; craft prompts from their opening phrases under stated selection and discard rules; generate 600 messages with BLOOM at fixed, stated parameters; select at random per prompt and apply four exclusion criteria plus light cleaning; evaluate with human raters and computational text analysis.
A screened set of machine-generated awareness messages traceable to named prompts and fixed parameters, with quality and clarity ratings against human-written messages.
Exclusion of messages with clearly false information, out-of-jurisdiction organizations, unverifiable sources, or off-topic content; blind human ratings against the human baseline.
acts.sum: This research protocol produces public awareness messages on a health topic, folic acid in the source, with an openly available language model. You scrape posts on the topic, keep the thirty most shared human-written messages, and turn their opening phrases into prompts, discarding any prompt that yields near-identical messages, many organization or country names, or clearly false claims. The prompts go to the model with every generation parameter fixed and recorded, producing a large pool of candidate messages. You then draw candidates at random and exclude any with false information, organizations outside the target jurisdiction, sources that cannot be verified, or off-topic content, before light cleaning. The researcher must defend each prompt and every exclusion. In the source the surviving messages were rated by human samples against the human-written originals and analyzed for sentiment, readability, and content.
acts.t: Generate public health awareness messages from prompts mined from high-performing human messages, at fixed parameters, with rule-based screening
acts.tool: BLOOM (7B1); Hugging Face transformers; snscrape; Google Colab; Qualtrics

acts.sum: Because most publishers do not accept AI-generated images and treat AI-invented or manipulated images as misconduct, this five-minute workshop exercise has you ask a code-generation tool for Python or R code that plots your intended figure from your data, rather than asking for an image. You run the code, produce the figure, and share the code and data source alongside it so anyone can regenerate it; the deck marks its own charts this way, with the dataset URL on the slide. You check that no data or image was invented or falsified, and then produce a disclosure of the delegated task with a declaration generator. Photographs are not enhanced with AI at all, since they serve as evidence of the research. The researcher must read and understand the code well enough to vouch for the figure.
acts.t: Replace AI-generated images with AI-generated plotting code, so every figure is reproducible and disclosable

srp: To ensure progressive, consistent development of students’ AI skills across a program by finding where the four AI literacy dimensions are not covered and closing those gaps deliberately.

The program director reviews the whole program with the framework, looks for gaps where students’ AI skills are not present, works with module organizers to integrate AI to close each gap, provides extracurricular activities where curricular integration is difficult, and checks that all four dimensions are covered progressively.

acts.sum: A program director reviews the whole degree program against a framework of four AI literacy dimensions: know and understand AI, use and apply AI, evaluate and create with AI, and AI ethics. Each dimension comes with a learning objective, a checklist of teaching activities, and candidate tools. The director marks where a dimension is developed nowhere in the program, approaches the organizers of modules best placed to carry each missing dimension, and works with them to integrate it rather than imposing it. Where a dimension cannot be fitted into the curriculum, the director arranges workshops, clubs, or special project groups instead. The audit ends with a check that all four dimensions are covered and build progressively, so students are competent in each by graduation. The director must judge which modules can credibly carry which dimension.
acts.t: Audit a degree program against four AI literacy dimensions, find the gaps, and close them module by module or extracurricularly

The module organizer chooses the dimensions to develop, works down each dimension’s tick-box use-case idea list and candidate tool list, adapts them to the discipline, pairs AI-output use-case ideas with in-class reflection and critical evaluation, and, where ethics is included, sets AI assessment policy, acknowledgment rules, and co-created guidelines.

acts.sum: A module organizer decides which of four AI literacy dimensions the module should develop, rather than attempting all four, and reads each chosen dimension’s learning objective. You then work down that dimension’s checklist of teaching use-case ideas, ticking those that fit the module’s content and level, and choose tools from its candidate list. Use-case ideas range from formulating queries and comparing responses, AI-assisted note-taking with later reflection, and summarizing readings, through literature and systematic review support and data analysis, to evaluating a dataset and reporting the strengths and weaknesses of both data and tool. Where students will rely on AI output, the design pairs the use-case idea with in-class reflection and critical evaluation, as the framework does for AI-assisted information search. If ethics is in scope, you set the module’s AI assessment policy and acknowledgment rules and teach limitations such as paywalled sources and non-existent references.
acts.t: Design a module’s AI integration by choosing target AI literacy dimensions and selecting use-case ideas and tools from a per-dimension checklist

acts.sum: A teacher educator or program designer takes one competency block from the UNESCO AI competency framework for teachers, for example “Human agency” at the entry progression level, and adapts its learning objectives to the prior knowledge and responsibilities of the teachers being assessed. They then design assessment methods and items matched to that competency and mastery level, and specify grading criteria for performance and underlying competence. The framework’s worked example sets four sample items beside its four objectives: an essay on the benefits, limits, and risks of a common AI function in education such as facial recognition or auto-correct; a poster or presentation on how AI creators’ decisions affect teacher and student agency; naming a tool that should be banned under the EU AI Act and explaining why; and a list of daily tips for autonomous AI use. No AI tool is used in designing the items.

acts.sum: In a teacher training or support program, participating teachers first revisit pedagogical methods for their subject and basic instructional design, and are shown locally accessible, validated AI tools, including institutionally deployed systems. They analyze exemplar lessons and judge whether AI is appropriate for their subject and level, starting from the teaching need, then decide whether to use AI at all and, if so, which tool. They design and teach an AI-assisted lesson covering materials, delivery, assessment, or support for students with special needs, reflect on the design and its implementation, and evaluate its effectiveness against the need that motivated it, alongside selected evidence on the advantages and disadvantages of AI-assisted teaching. The output is an implemented lesson plan and a reflective evaluation.

srp: To let teachers produce curriculum-aligned, culturally relevant resources faster with generative AI while remaining the final judges of quality and keeping the license chain intact.

Teachers upload curriculum documents and Creative Commons-licensed OER (for example CC BY or CC BY-SA) to an offline or repository-restricted model, prompt it to adapt content, edit the output, check references and copyright, submit to mentor review and community-of-practice peer review, and publish under a compatible open license.

acts.sum: A teacher or TVET trainer gathers the ministry curriculum documents and existing subject resources under a Creative Commons license such as CC BY or CC BY-SA and loads them as source documents into an offline language model, or into an online model configured to search only selected OER repositories and return links so licenses can be identified. The teacher prompts the model to identify and adapt relevant content, for example a 45-minute lesson plan aligned with a named curriculum standard, then edits the output into a new resource and checks that every source is referenced and nothing infringes copyright. A mentor reviews the content and licenses, peers in a community of practice check it against agreed evaluation criteria, and the new resource is published under an open license compatible with its sources. Field examples include a Grade 9 mathematics pilot in India and TVET work in several countries.
acts.t: Six-step teacher-in-the-loop cycle for adapting openly licensed materials to a national curriculum with generative AI
acts.tool: GPT-3.5; GPT-4o mini; offline large language model

acts.sum: Working in backward-design order, a technical or vocational educator uses structured prompt templates to have a generative AI tool propose learning outcomes aligned to an occupational standard, then contextualized content such as explanations, safety scenarios, and troubleshooting steps, then an aligned assessment such as a scenario-based case study, multiple-choice items, or a reflective task with a rubric. A further template checks that every outcome is addressed by corresponding content and assessment. The educator evaluates each output critically, localizes it for the setting and industry, and iterates prompts until it fits. The complete lesson design then goes to peer review and mentor feedback and is scored by facilitators on alignment, creativity, and pedagogical clarity. The worked example pairs an outcome on proper use of personal protective equipment with a formative case study.

srp: To build educators’ confidence and competence with generative AI while producing contextualized, gender-responsive, and inclusive OER through non-hierarchical mentoring.

Mentors and mentees are paired and prepared, co-create teaching resources with ChatGPT and Canva with feedback, have the OER evaluated for inclusivity, implement them, and then sustain peer mentoring and OER sharing.
Co-created AI-supported OER evaluated for inclusivity, plus a continuing peer-mentoring structure.
acts.sum: The Co-Creative Mentoring Model pairs educators as mentors and mentees and works through four phases. In Preparation, facilitators scaffold readiness for gender-responsive, AI-enhanced teaching. In Co-Creation, each pair uses ChatGPT to generate lesson prompts, assessments, and simplified content and Canva to create accessible visuals, receives feedback, and produces open educational resources that are evaluated for inclusivity and freedom from bias. In Implementation, the resources are used in teaching, and in the Sustainability and Reflection phase, peer mentoring is established and OER sharing promoted. The model was run with 23 participants from Ghanaian colleges of education, basic schools, and regulatory agencies; participants named the hands-on co-creation sessions as the most valuable part, and limited training time and internet connectivity as the main obstacles.
acts.t: Four-phase mentor-mentee pairing that co-creates inclusive open resources with ChatGPT and Canva

acts.sum: For open and distance learning, this design builds an authentic assessment that states in writing exactly which uses of generative AI learners may make. The instructor makes the task as context-specific as possible, provides a rubric of requirements and criteria for each section, and hands learners one of several scope statements, for example that AI may be used for planning, idea development, and research as long as the final submission shows how ideas were developed and refined, or that it may assist with drafting and refining provided learners critically evaluate and modify what it produces. The task is broken into parts sequenced across a semester, learners self-assess and cite the page numbers where evidence of each requirement appears, and reflection, disclosure, and demonstration of process serve as accountability. The booklet cautions that using GenAI to mark student work currently carries more risk than benefit.
acts.t: Authentic assessment designed with an explicit, written scope for permitted student GenAI use

acts.sum: In a distance-learning Java programming course, the course coordinator builds a practice application in which GPT-4, reached through an API, returns immediate feedback on students’ code. Rather than accepting open-ended work, the application offers predefined tasks mapped to the same skill taxonomy and criteria as the graded assignment, and evaluates each submission for correctness, coding style, efficiency, and adherence to good practice, pitching explanations to the learner’s level: foundational explanations and error analysis for beginners, optimization suggestions for more advanced learners. Students use it during self-managed study before attempting the graded assignment and may resubmit as often as they wish without penalty, refining their code each time. The pilot at Open University Malaysia involved 24 volunteers in a Diploma in Information Technology course, evaluated through a focus group.
acts.t: GPT-4 practice environment whose tasks mirror the graded assignment’s skill taxonomy

The team integrated a GPT-4 agent into a bespoke dashboard aggregating module and participation data; students asked it about their feedback, and a small study of 34 students examined weekly reflective writings; extra scaffolding was added for students less able to use the agent.

acts.sum: A teaching team builds a learning-analytics dashboard that aggregates real-time data from students’ module activities and classroom participation and shows it back as visual feedback, then embeds a conversational agent built on the OpenAI API (GPT-4) so each student can ask questions about their own analytics. The agent clarifies the visualizations, answers specific questions with context-aware responses, recommends reflective writing strategies and routines, and prompts goal setting, progress monitoring, and planning of next steps. Students write weekly reflections on what they did with the feedback. At University College London the team found students’ capacity to use an agent varied, so extra scaffolding was added, and students reported that some responses were not specific enough. The authors recommend that institutions regularly evaluate response parameters such as length and temperature settings.

acts.sum: Starting from the claim that poor generative AI results often stem from poor prompts, the authors propose treating quality prompts as open educational resources. Faculty and other experts write prompts for their domain, release them under an open license, and deposit them in a shared online prompt bank built to be sustainable. Experts from various fields enrich the bank, quality assurance procedures check the validity and robustness of prompts, and users rate the prompts they reuse so future users can see quality and administrators can spot low-quality entries and request revisions. Teachers and students both reuse prompts from the bank in their own contexts. The authors add that open frameworks for writing prompts, especially for domain-specific knowledge, could improve results. The article presents this as a proposed scenario rather than a reported implementation.
acts.t: Openly licensed, rated prompt bank maintained as a shared educational resource

acts.sum: Within an open-pedagogy stance that treats students as co-creators of the teaching process, the teacher first gives a thorough introduction to responsible generative AI use, framing the tool as a support for self-directed learning rather than an answer generator, and shares prompting strategies such as supplying context and assigning roles. Teacher and students then write prompts together in the classroom, run them, and assess the different outputs that come back, with the teacher acting as facilitator while students build their own learning pathways individually and collaboratively. The authors cite evidence that students engaged more smoothly once teachers had shared such strategies. The output is a set of class-authored prompts, the model’s responses, and the class’s comparative judgment of those responses.

acts.sum: Before putting generative AI output into an openly licensed resource, a faculty author runs a due-diligence check for infringement of individual protected works. The first step is to read the prompt critically: a prompt aimed at a trademarked character invites infringement, while prompts for an abstract book cover with a beach and a whale or a three-paragraph description of hydrocarbons are unlikely to. For text output, the author searches the web to make sure the exact language does not already exist in copyrighted content; for images, they run a reverse image search with a tool such as TinEye or Google Images. Output with no identical match is treated as likely includable; output that matches a protected work is not used. The guidance notes that US copyright does not protect styles or ideas and points to fair-use codes for OER.
acts.t: Infringement due-diligence check on generative AI output before it goes into an open resource

acts.sum: A faculty author creating new open teaching material with a language model starts from one or more openly licensed resources, checks each license, and writes a prompt that names the specific source by URL and states the transformation wanted, for example a one-paragraph summary of an OpenStax section on type conversion. The new work keeps the source’s open license and attributes the original. When sources are combined, the author applies the most restrictive license among them, so an OpenStax section under CC BY mixed with a CC BY-NC-SA algebra chapter yields a CC BY-NC-SA derivative. ShareAlike sources require the same license on the new work; for assessments that should not be public, the author credits the source, applies the same license, and offers colleagues a way to request the material. AI-generated portions are labeled, with explanatory text in a preface or attributions slide.
acts.t: Prompting a model with a named openly licensed source and carrying that source’s license into the derivative

acts.sum: In the final unit of a visual communication course, the instructor shows students about twenty pictures of students around campus, half taken by the campus photographer and half generated with AI, without saying which are which, and asks how they might authenticate them. Students propose and test techniques. One approach compares inconspicuous background elements with architectural details or landscape features actually present on campus, extending the verifiability principle used for written sources to images. Students also note content anomalies, such as only the generated images showing people carrying books. The model’s output is the thing examined; students generate the authentication methods and the reasoning behind each judgment.

acts.sum: UNESCO’s AI competency framework for students gives a matrix of assessment tasks by competency aspect and three progression levels (Understand, Apply, Create), with a different task type at each level. For the human-centered mindset aspect, the task types are conflict-based opinion taking, critical evaluation, and social interactions; for the ethics of AI they are scenario-based value orientation, ethical behaviors, and rule-making. An instructor picks an aspect and a level, pairs a paper or computer-based test on the main points of that competency block with open questions that put a contested claim to students, and adapts those questions to the local context. Sample items ask whether media reports that artificial general intelligence will arrive by 2030 are correct, whether students still need to learn to draft reports if AI drafts meeting minutes, and whether AI will enhance or threaten inclusion locally. Students answer by stating, evaluating, and analyzing positions; no AI tool is used.
acts.t: Conflict-based and scenario-based assessment tasks built from a competency-by-level matrix

The team fine-tuned LLaMA on the curriculum with vector-database retrieval, deployed it with logging and encryption, gave in-person students instructor and tutor access and remote students the tutor plus weekly facilitator sessions, and evaluated with pre/post tests, assignment metrics, surveys, interviews, and optional journals.

acts.sum: A teaching team curates its course curriculum, here virtualization, cloud architectures, distributed systems, and container technologies, fine-tunes an open-weights LLaMA model on it, and connects the model to a vector database for context retrieval behind a mobile-responsive web front end with interaction logging, end-to-end encryption, and anonymized storage. Students ask the tutor about concepts and assignments, and it explains ideas, helps with debugging, and guides step-by-step problem solving. In the hybrid arrangement, in-person students have both instructors and the tutor, while remote students use the tutor as primary support, supplemented by weekly virtual sessions with human facilitators. Across more than 370 students in rural and semi-urban regions, the authors report gains in assignment accuracy and debugging, measured against past cohorts rather than a control group.

Phase 1 evaluates the simulation prompt before deployment across six domains (clinical/content credibility, alignment with objectives and cognitive level, persona clarity, inclusivity and cultural competence, transparency about AI identity, personalization), each scored by faculty on a 0–2 rubric.

acts.sum: Before any student meets a nursing chatbot simulation, faculty evaluate the prompt that configures it. The first phase of the AIMS framework scores the prompt on six instructional domains using a 0–2 rubric: clinical and content credibility; alignment with the educational objectives and intended cognitive level; persona clarity, meaning whether the bot’s role and tone are defined; inclusivity and cultural competence of the scenario and language; transparency about the AI’s identity to learners; and personalization to learner needs. Domains that score low point to revisions in the prompt before deployment and before Phase 2, which evaluates the chatbot in live interaction. The authors state that prompt design is where inaccurate, biased, or unsafe interactions can be prevented, and they also demonstrated automating the scoring with a GPT-4.0-based Eval-Bot v1.
acts.t: Pre-deployment review of an AI simulation prompt against six instructional domains (AIMS Phase 1)

acts.sum: Once a nursing chatbot simulation has passed prompt review, its behavior in live interaction is scored. Faculty rate eight criteria on the same 0–2 rubric used in the framework’s first phase: credibility and accuracy, user experience, feedback and assessment quality, user agency, equity and accessibility, transparency, learning outcomes, and interactivity quality. In the article, the authors ran an automated evaluator, Eval-Bot v1 built on OpenAI GPT-4.0, and had three experienced nursing faculty score independently for the first phase’s prompt review, so the two sets of scores could be compared; the same pairing can be applied to these eight criteria, which the article defines but does not test, with the automated evaluator as an option. The output is a scored performance evaluation of the deployed simulation with human scores and, where the automated evaluator is used, its scores side by side, used to decide whether the simulation performs acceptably in use and not only on paper.
acts.t: Scoring a live AI nursing simulation on eight criteria, triangulating an automated scorer with faculty review (AIMS Phase 2)

The chatbot, configured by faculty with a documented prompt structure covering roles, escalation phases, and debriefing rules, acts as scenario engine: it presents time-sensitive prompts and raises complexity across defined phases. acts.sum: An instructor and a teaching assistant build a classroom card game on international trade and population health for fifteen sovereign states. They use ChatGPT to compile historical health-affecting events, build economic profiles with GDP, per-capita indicators, and import-export portfolios, decide which resources each state starts with and must obtain, and run repeated simulations to check that the allocations could realistically be met through trade. Adobe Firefly generates deliberately generic imagery for resource and event cards, avoiding identifiable people or places. Every country-specific figure is then cross-checked against authoritative sources, every card is reviewed for biased or stereotyped portrayals, images are screened for appropriateness, and the whole game is playtested by people a month before the pilot. The output is a complete, playable set of state profiles, resource and event cards, and trading rules.

acts.sum: In a 75-minute undergraduate public health class, groups of two or three represent sovereign states, dividing the roles of Trade Representative, Health Minister, and Finance Minister. Each group holds three to ten resource cards according to its nation’s GDP and must meet its health needs through trade. Three ten-minute rounds stand for 2018, 2019, and 2020; trading starts among designated partners and opens more widely at the end of each round, and the 2020 round simulates the COVID-19 pandemic with heavy restrictions. The instructor plays the US Trade Representative, and the teaching assistant plays US aid agencies, introducing event cards and observing against the learning objectives. Reflection runs between rounds, by regional bloc, and as a class debrief, followed by a written reflection within 48 hours. Students are told the background data and graphics were AI-assisted.

acts.sum: Before adding AI and chatbot content to an existing graduate health communication course, the instructors check whether there is demand for it. They email a small group of peer faculty at other institutions who develop health interventions, asking whether they know of courses on digital health intervention development and whether such a course is needed, and record every response. With a need established, they build a logic model that maps inputs, actions, outputs, and short- and long-term outcomes, and design four new lecture topics and a new chatbot lab against it. After delivery they run the standard anonymous course evaluation and a supplemental evaluation, summarizing multiple-choice data descriptively and analyzing free responses for themes, and note which long-term outcomes must wait for graduates in the field. No AI tool is used in this planning work.

The prompt was refined across four versions incorporating the OTIPM and added context; the final prompt required a scenario, assessment results, and clinical questions; five cases were generated in a single ChatGPT session (temperature 0.7, 2048 maximum tokens); ten OT experts rated them on three domains on a five-point scale, with intraclass correlation computed.
