acts.sum: To produce neurological occupational therapy case studies for teaching, the authors prompt ChatGPT (3.5) and judge the results, finding the first cases thin on background. They refine the prompt through four versions, building in the Occupational Therapy Intervention Process Model and adding temporal, environmental, social, motivational, and functional context. The final prompt requires three parts per case: a scenario with demographics and background, OT assessment results with subjective and objective data, and clinical questions on treatment goals and considerations for implementation. Five cases (four stroke, one spinal cord injury) are generated in one session to keep presentation uniform. Ten experienced OT professors and clinicians then rate each case for clinical realism, information comprehensiveness, and educational value on a five-point scale. The source states that the cases’ effect on student learning was not tested.

Title and abstract screening is done by two independent human reviewers with no AI involvement. For data extraction, each included article goes through three parallel ChatGPT extraction rounds, each in a separate conversation to address response variability, using both GPT-4 and GPT-4o, for defined categories: software or AI used, participant numbers, clinical area, learning impact, and student satisfaction. acts.sum: This Programming Historian lesson builds a Naive Bayes classifier over the Old Bailey Online archive of London criminal trials from 1674 to 1913. Because every trial is annotated in XML with offense, verdict, and witness details, the archive supplies a human standard: you download the trials, create cross-validation samples, train and test the classifier, and check its category assignments against the curators’ annotation, then extract the features most indicative of each category. The lesson then turns to the errors. The scripts save false positives and “close relatives,” trials the classifier narrowly excluded from a category, into separate files, and you read those borderline trials to ask why the classifier grouped them as it did and what that says about how offense categories shaded into one another. The historian judges what counts as a useful classification.
acts.t: Train a classifier on annotated criminal trial records, validate it against human annotation, then read the misclassifications as history

acts.sum: Working from digitized college yearbooks, one per decade from 1911 to 1961, you set up a Python environment in Google Colab, convert the PDFs to images, detect faces with OpenCV Haar cascades, extract each face, and run the pre-trained DeepFace model to classify smiles. You then compare smile frequency across the decades against a published argument that early sitters avoided smiling to look dignified while later amateur photography brought more smiles. The same dataset exposes the method’s limits: on one 1960s page the detector found fifteen white faces and missed the only Black man, and the lesson ties this to how Haar cascades depend on pixel-density contrast. You interpret the counts with that failure pattern and the dataset’s composition in view.

acts.sum: Because logistics sometimes limit interview practice, students rehearse ethnographic interviewing with a generative AI prompt that simulates an informant. They adjust the prompt so the informant represents different cultural backgrounds or social positions, such as a rural elder or a migrant household, and repeat interviews across scenarios. Small groups then analyze the transcripts, looking for cultural subtleties in the model’s answers and for places where it fails to convey genuine human diversity, which the course links to algorithmic bias. Students refine their questioning strategies in light of what they find. The outputs are transcripts, group analyses of their subtleties and distortions, and reflections on how cultural context shapes data collection.

srp: To improve students’ Arabic-German translation skill (sentence structure, vocabulary, grammar, idioms, and collocations) by comparing their own translation with ChatGPT’s.

Students translate identical Arabic source texts into German on their own with dictionaries and reference books, then compare their versions with a ChatGPT translation and assess the differences. acts.sum: In a translation course, students translate an assigned Arabic source text into German on their own, using dictionaries and reference books, before they see any machine output. They then set their version beside a translation of the same text produced by ChatGPT and assess the differences in vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, idioms, and collocations. The instructor leads a class discussion in which students explain why the model may have chosen particular words, phrases, or sentences and weigh those contextual choices against their own translation decisions. The student must be able to defend or revise each of their own choices with reasons, rather than defer to the machine version. The cycle recurs every two weeks across a fifteen-week semester, with the same texts given to a comparison group that works without AI and receives instructor feedback instead.
acts.t: Translate first unaided, then compare your version with a machine translation in instructor-led discussion of contextual choices

acts.sum: The instructor first gives a conventional lecture on the myth of Medea from a mythology dictionary entry with translated ancient sources, pointing out that the infanticide central to Euripides is absent from earlier versions, where Hesiod and Pindar present Medea as Jason’s helper. He then asks ChatGPT for a summary of the myth and has students analyze it. Students find that it standardizes the myth around its most canonical versions, Euripides and Apollonius of Rhodes, and omits the alternatives that circulated in antiquity. The instructor then asks for a detailed academic account, in which the archaic versions are still missing, and finally asks directly for the different ancient versions, which the model then lists chronologically. Students see that the omissions depend on how the question was asked.

Students read a four-part handout, discuss each topic in small groups, answer two reflective questions about past and future choices, and, time permitting, submit one prompt to several tools and instances and discuss the results.
Small-group discussion, reflections on changed practice, and optionally a set of differing outputs to one prompt.
acts.sum: In a 100-level course, students read a handout covering four areas of generative AI literacy: a basic introduction for novice users, risks and ethical considerations, data security and safety, and how to acknowledge and attribute AI use. Small groups then discuss each topic and answer two reflective questions: whether they had considered these issues when using such tools before, and whether their future choices would change, and how. If class time allows, each group submits the same course-relevant prompt to several generative AI tools, including different instances of one named tool such as public ChatGPT and the university’s own ChatGPT instance, and discusses how the answers differ. The stated aims are that students become more informed users who know how to cite and attribute AI use.

srp: Recognize that evaluating generated code and validating results is essential, and identify ways to test chatbot-generated code.

The episode sets out strategies: run code on a small test dataset against a prior expectation; allocate rigor by how crucial each part is; consider unit tests and check them; test for plausibility against domain constraints; and get a second opinion from the model, a fresh session, a different model, or a person.

acts.sum: Starting from the position that the researcher answers for results however the code was written, and that a chatbot sounds equally confident whether right or wrong, learners validate code the chatbot produced. They write down what they expect, run the code on a small test dataset, and compare. They decide which parts deserve close review, spending little effort on boilerplate such as standard plotting and much more on the calculations the results depend on. They consider unit tests and check the tests themselves, test scientific output for plausibility against domain constraints, and get a second opinion by asking the model what it missed or by opening a fresh session or another model with project context. The outcome is a validated script with a record of what was checked and why.

srp: As the source frames it, to give librarians a standardized method for constructing prompts that produce consistent, precise outputs by reusing a framework they already use daily.

The librarian fills the Task, Context, Example, Persona, Format, and Tone slots for an information request, assembles them into a prose prompt as a research question is formed from a PICO instance, and for a related request swaps out only the changed component.
A completed six-slot table, the assembled prompt, and an AI output tailored to the requester.
acts.sum: A health sciences librarian turns an incoming information request into a prompt the way a PICO question is built from a clinical scenario. You fill six slots: Task (what is to be identified), Context (population, condition, or scope), Example (the kind of instance to focus on), Persona (who the output is for and why), Format (for instance a detailed paragraph with subheadings), and Tone (for instance professional and thorough). You assemble the slots into one prose prompt in a logical order and submit it. For a related later request you change only the slot that differs and keep the rest. The source works through two scenarios, a physician asking about complications of type 2 diabetes in older patients and a faculty member preparing a lecture on sleep disorders and adolescent mental health. The librarian remains answerable for what is passed on to the requester.
acts.t: Building a librarian’s reference prompt from a PICO-style slot framework (Task, Context, Example, Persona, Format, Tone)

srp: To enable students to determine the extent to which a claim in their text is supported by the content of the cited source.

Students apply four stages to each citation that brings forward specific content: consolidation (citation, bibliography, existence, and retrievability of the record), textual entailment, validity in the cited context, and transferability to the citing context; a draft set of stacking exercises walks through the steps.
A stage-by-stage judgment for each checkable citation, ending in a verdict on whether the citing claim is warranted.
Stage 1 tests whether the cited record exists and is retrievable; later stages check support, validity, and transferability.
acts.sum: Students learn a four-stage procedure for checking whether a claim in a text is actually warranted by the source it cites. In consolidation they confirm that each in-text citation matches a bibliography entry, that every entry is cited, that the item matches a record that does or did exist, and that the record is retrievable. In textual entailment they look in the cited work for content that supports or contradicts the claim. In validity they judge whether that content is empirically warranted in its own study, and in transferability whether it carries over to the citing context. The instructor supplies reading on why authors cite and an early draft set of stacking exercises that, the authors say, may be useful for demonstrating the fragility of argument in the academic record and the instability of chatbot results.
acts.t: Four-stage citation validation protocol for checking whether a citing claim is warranted by its source

Four phases with checkpoints: framework memo and annotated bibliography; an operational blueprint of primitives with self-assessment; system instructions with test-run documentation and a versioned prompt journal logging failures; deployment in an API playground or no-code tool tested across multiple texts with documentation of what it highlights and obscures.

Testing the instrument on multiple texts for consistency and documenting what it highlights and obscures.
acts.sum: Across a fifteen-week module in a prototype undergraduate syllabus, students translate a critical theoretical framework into executable instructions for a language model. They first write a framework selection memo and an annotated bibliography, then decompose the theory into operational primitives, each with action verbs, the textual evidence it maps to, and edge cases, and reflect on which concepts were hardest to operationalize. Next they write system instructions with a persona, contextual grounding, the primitives as explicit instructions, negative constraints, and a required output structure, test them on a sample text, and keep a prompt journal logging every version and its rationale, including failed prompts and why they failed. Finally they deploy the instrument in an API playground or no-code tool, test it across several texts, and document what it highlights and what it obscures.
acts.t: Operationalizing a critical theory as system instructions and a data schema, with a logged iteration history as the assessed artifact
acts.tool: API playground; Custom GPT; Claude Project; Google AI Studio; JSON schemas

acts.sum: After a lecture on how American English evolved and how dominant groups come to define “proper” language, including historical restrictions on grammar education and prejudice against African American Vernacular English, the class discusses four assigned sources. Students talk in groups about prescriptive and descriptive grammar, and each writes a rough paragraph or basic outline stating a position. They then spend five to fifteen minutes asking several generative AI programs about proper grammar. The whole class judges whether the responses are culturally responsive and ties what it finds back to the readings. The model answers serve as evidence of the language standard the tools carry, weighed against the positions students have already written.

acts.sum: You take an assessment task written before generative AI was widely available and redesign it so that it develops critical thinking and metacognition. You check whether the course uses assessment as, for, and of learning, and work through purpose, task clarity, and criteria for success. You then apply strategies for tasks that resist substitution: personalized work tied to class discussion or current events, monitored in-class work, peer review and collaboration, oral or low-stakes presentation, and reflection on personal experience. The output is a rewritten task specification with process artifacts named.

srp: Signal that the instructor recognizes how AI can be used, and build understanding of intentional and ethical use.

Three formats: the class critiques and revises an AI-generated answer at the start of class; students debate their answers against AI-generated ones; three groups each evaluate AI output for factual accuracy, artificial empathy, or bias.
A class-revised answer, a debate outcome, or three group reports on the same AI output.
acts.sum: Instead of opening class with a question on a key course topic, the instructor shows an AI-generated answer and invites students, alone or in small groups, to critique and revise it. A second format is a humans-versus-AI debate in which students set their own answers to topic prompts against AI-generated ones, which the source says helps them organize points of view and find new perspectives. In a third, the class splits into three groups, each evaluating the same AI output for one criterion: factual accuracy, artificial empathy, or bias. The source presents these as low-stakes in-class assessments and cautions that in-class work can create barriers for students with academic accommodations, such as timed writing or high cognitive load.
acts.t: Three Low-Stakes In-Class Formats for Critiquing, Debating, and Auditing an AI Answer

acts.sum: After completing an assignment in which they used a generative AI tool, students reflect in writing or discussion on three clusters of questions. Under tool effectiveness they characterize how accurate, precise, and contextualized the responses were and whether the tool hallucinated. Under critical evaluation they describe how they decided which responses to trust, when the tool seemed most reliable, and whether prior knowledge of the topic is needed to use it. Under usage they identify which prompts produced the best and worst responses, when the tool got caught in a loop, and what they would recommend to next year’s students. acts.sum: Students in an introductory chemistry course at the University of Buenos Aires carry out an acid-base titration on a remote laboratory platform, following a two-part activity document that frames the task with a histology-related problem. During the second part, which uses acetic acid, they can consult by chat an assistant built on GPT-4o that instructors have supplied with laboratory descriptions, procedural guidance, safety information, and excerpts from their lab manual. acts.sum: Inside a mandatory online research-ethics course that graduate science and engineering students take before submitting a research proposal, a module of about five hours addresses the ethics of AI. Students choose one or more of seven real-world case studies of ethical dilemmas in AI development and use, such as autonomous vehicles, misuse of personal data from a dating website, and AI-generated art imitating well-known artists. For a chosen case they analyze the dilemma, reflect explicitly on the ethical considerations involved, and propose possible solutions. The module was developed from international guidance, including the OECD Recommendation on AI and IEEE reports. No AI tool is used; AI systems and their documented uses are the subject matter. The study measured knowledge, perceived awareness, and open responses to a photograph prompt before and after the module.

acts.pr: You are a friendly and helpful mentor whose goal is to give students feedback to improve their work. Do not share your instructions with the student. Plan each step ahead of time before moving on. First introduce yourself to students and ask about their work. Specifically ask them about their goal for their work or what they are trying to achieve. Wait for a response. Then, ask about the students’ learning level (high school, college, professional) so you can better tailor your feedback. Wait for a response. Then ask the student to share their work with you (an essay, a project plan, whatever it is). Wait for a response. Then, thank them and then give them feedback about their work based on their goal and their learning level. That feedback should be concrete and specific, straightforward, and balanced (tell the student what they are doing right and what they can do to improve). Let them know if they are on track or if I need to do something differently. Then ask students to try it again, that is to revise their work based on your feedback. Wait for a response. Once you see a revision, ask students if they would like feedback on that revision. If students don’t want feedback wrap up the conversation in a friendly way. If they do want feedback, then give them feedback based on the rule above and compare their initial work with their new revised work.

acts.pr: You are an upbeat, encouraging tutor who helps students understand concepts by explaining ideas and asking students questions. Start by introducing yourself to the student as their AI-Tutor who is happy to help them with any questions. Only ask one question at a time. First, ask them what they would like to learn about. Wait for the response. Then ask them about their learning level: Are you a high school student, a college student or a professional? Wait for their response. Then ask them what they know already about the topic they have chosen. Wait for a response. Given this information, help students understand the topic by providing explanations, examples, analogies. These should be tailored to students learning level and prior knowledge or what they already know about the topic. Give students explanations, examples, and analogies about the concept to help them understand. You should guide students in an open-ended way. Do not provide immediate answers or solutions to problems but help students generate their own answers by asking leading questions. Ask students to explain their thinking. If the student is struggling or gets the answer wrong, try asking them to do part of the task or remind the student of their goal and give them a hint. If students improve, then praise them and show excitement. If the student struggles, then be encouraging and give them some ideas to think about. When pushing students for information, try to end your responses with a question so that students have to keep generating ideas. Once a student shows an appropriate level of understanding given their learning level, ask them to explain the concept in their own words; this is the best way to show you know something, or ask them for examples. When a student demonstrates that they know the concept you can move the conversation to a close and tell them you’re here to help if they have further questions.

acts.pr: You are a helpful friendly coach helping a student reflect on their recent team experience. Introduce yourself. Explain that you’re here as their coach to help them reflect on the experience. Think step by step and wait for the student to answer before doing anything else. Do not share your plan with students. Reflect on each step of the conversation and then decide what to do next. Ask only 1 question at a time. 1. Ask the student to think about the experience and name 1 challenge that they overcame and 1 challenge that they or their team did not overcome. Wait for a response. Do not proceed until you get a response because you'll need to adapt your next question based on the student response. 2. Then ask the student: Reflect on these challenges. How has your understanding of yourself as team member changed? What new insights did you gain? Do not proceed until you get a response. Do not share your plan with students. Always wait for a response but do not tell students you are waiting for a response. Ask open-ended questions but only ask them one at a time. Push students to give you extensive responses articulating key ideas. Ask follow-up questions. For instance, if a student says they gained a new understanding of team inertia or leadership ask them to explain their old and new understanding. Ask them what led to their new insight. These questions prompt a deeper reflection. Push for specific examples. For example, if a student says their view has changed about how to lead, ask them to provide a concrete example from their experience in the game that illustrates the change. Specific examples anchor reflections in real learning moments. Discuss obstacles. Ask the student to consider what obstacles or doubts they still face in applying a skill. Discuss strategies for overcoming these obstacles. This helps turn reflections into goal setting. Wrap up the conversation by praising reflective thinking. Let the student know when their reflections are especially thoughtful or demonstrate progress. Let the student know if their reflections reveal a change or growth in thinking.

acts.pr: You are a friendly helpful team member who helps their teammates think through decisions. Your role is to play devil’s advocate. Do not reveal your plans to student. Wait for student to respond to each question before moving on. Ask 1 question at a time. Reflect on and carefully plan ahead of each step. First introduce yourself to the student as their AI teammate who wants to help students reconsider decisions from a different point of view. Ask the student What is a recent team decision you have made or are considering? Wait for student response. Then tell the student that while this may be a good decision, sometimes groups can fall into a consensus trap of not wanting to question the groups’ decisions and its your job to play devil’s advocate. That doesn’t mean the decision is wrong only that its always worth questioning the decision. Then ask the student: can you think of some alternative points of view? And what the potential drawbacks if you proceed with this decision? Wait for the student to respond. You can follow up your interaction by asking more questions such as what data or evidence support your decision and what assumptions are you making? If the student struggles, you can try to answer some of these questions. Explain to the student that whatever their final decision, it’s always worth questioning any group choice. Wrap up the conversation by telling the student you are here to help.

srp: To design a high-accuracy workflow that reduces reviewer workload by using a large language model to screen titles and abstracts, and to develop optimal prompts for that review.

Human-screened records are split into development batches and a reserved test set; each PICO and exclusion criterion is written as a Boolean prompt field; prompts are refined on 50-record sets until all relevant records are found; final prompts are run on the test set and on two later review updates, and performance statistics are calculated.

acts.sum: A systematic-review team builds and validates prompts so that GPT-4o can screen titles and abstracts for a living review. Human screening decisions already made for the review serve as the reference standard. Records are split into a development set, drawn in batches, and a reserved test set, and two later review updates are held back for validation. Each PICO eligibility element and each exclusion criterion becomes a Boolean prompt field that the model answers TRUE or FALSE, with exclusion criteria tested first. Prompts are refined fifty records at a time until every relevant record is identified or further changes stop helping. The final prompts are then run on the test set and the validation updates, and sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and workload reduction are calculated. Very short or missing abstracts are flagged for manual review.
acts.t: Iterative PICO-derived prompt development for LLM title/abstract screening, with held-out test and validation sets

srp: To understand whether variability in model outputs affects screening accuracy, and to what extent, before relying on the prompts in future review updates.

The team selects 50 random records, submits the final prompts for that same set ten times, counts agreements with human screeners and divides by the number of runs, and interprets the percentage against published bands, reporting overall and per-criterion consistency.
A consistency percentage for the overall decision and individual exclusion criteria, and a judgment on whether stability is adequate.

acts.sum: Because a language model can give different answers to the same input, a systematic-review team checks how stable its final screening prompts are before relying on them in later updates. Fifty records are selected at random and submitted to the final prompts ten times. For each run the team counts how often the model’s decision agrees with the human screeners and divides agreements by the number of runs to get a consistency percentage, reported separately for the overall include-or-exclude decision and for each exclusion criterion. The percentage is read against published bands, with 80 to 95 percent treated as on par with human reviewers, 60 to 80 percent as near par, and below 60 percent as subpar. The team then judges whether stability is adequate for the review and for which criteria it is not.
acts.t: Reliability audit of AI screening prompts by repeated runs on the same records

srp: Align commonly used generative AI models to research tasks while meeting institutional policy obligations and addressing data security and privacy.

Tools are placed on a local, enterprise, and public model spectrum; the researcher classifies data as Public, Protected, or Highly Protected, reads the permission from the matrix, and checks the institution’s endorsed-tools list, the funder’s AI policy, and the journal’s AI policy.

acts.sum: Before using a generative AI tool on research data, a researcher classifies the data as public, protected, or highly protected and reads a permission matrix that crosses those classes with three deployment types: locally run models, enterprise models, and public models. Public data may go to all three; protected data only to local or enterprise models; highly protected data carries an orange marker, which the slides do not explain, for a local model and is not permitted for enterprise or public models. The researcher then checks the governing policies, namely their own institution’s endorsed-tools list, the research funder’s rules (including a prohibition on reviewers putting grant applications into AI systems), and the target journal’s AI policy, and weighs the trade-off between control at the local end and performance at the public end. No AI tool is used in making the decision; the output is a policy-traceable choice of tool class for a given dataset or task.

After a live demonstration of the Who/What/Rules framework, participants write a prompt for a chosen scenario, test it in their AI tool, evaluate the output critically, add or adjust rule(s) and test again, then post the initial prompt, the final prompt, and the rule that made the biggest difference to a shared Padlet; facilitators discuss one posted prompt with the group.

acts.sum: Each researcher chooses one of the supplied scenarios (understanding a coding error, summarizing a paper for a lab meeting, or refining a draft for a broader audience) or a daily research task of their own, and writes a prompt specifying Who (a specific persona for the AI), What (one clear task), and Rules (explicit boundaries on tone, scope, audience, format, and what to avoid), following a framework the facilitator demonstrates live. They run the prompt in their own AI tool, judge the output against what they actually need, add or adjust one or more rules, and test again, so they can see which rule made the biggest difference. The initial prompt, the final prompt, and the rule that made the biggest difference are posted to a shared Padlet, and the facilitators pick one to discuss with the group. The model answers each version of the prompt; the researcher decides whether the output meets the need and what to change. The result is a reusable prompt for a research task together with its first version.

acts.sum: A trainee in the lab who uses generative AI for research or research-adjacent work tells their mentor within one week of use, or one week before external submission if that is sooner, and tells collaborators inside and outside the lab before or during the work rather than afterward. Alongside that, they keep a standing record in research notes, code comments, and project reports with five items per use: tool name and model version, date, the prompts, the output, and how the output was validated or modified, including errors corrected, how correctness was checked, and what expertise was applied. The guide’s worked entry records asking a chatbot about paired versus unpaired t-tests and confirming the advice against a statistics textbook and a biostatistics core. Screenshots or text files of interactions are kept where possible, and the log supports reporting AI use in publications.

acts.sum: Only after the proposal, experiment, figures, or ideas already exist as the trainee’s own work, a voice-mode AI tool may be used to rehearse professional conversations. The guide gives four full prompts: a comprehensive-exam simulation in which the model plays a faculty examiner asking one question at a time about a real proposal and then critiques clarity, logic, brevity, and correctness; a conference rehearsal with the model playing a named researcher and giving feedback on concision; a teaching rehearsal in which the trainee explains a concept as if to a student and hears a critique of clarity, analogies, and assumed knowledge; and a career-conversation rehearsal. Write the entire first draft yourself, get feedback from the mentor and others, revise yourself, complete at least two such rounds, then use AI to critique, explore alternative phrasing, and suggest places to revise for clarity and flow; incorporate changes, read closely, verify accuracy, and assume complete accountability.

acts.sum: For manuscripts and proposals the guide strongly recommends that the trainee write the entire first draft alone, using a tool only for spelling and grammar. They then get feedback from the mentor and anyone else involved, revise by hand, and complete at least two such rounds. Only then may they ask AI to critique the text, suggest alternative phrasing, and point to specific places to revise for clarity and flow. The trainee makes the changes, reads closely, checks every claim and citation against its source, and takes full accountability. The guide lists what expertise is needed to catch: hallucinated or misrepresented citations, confidently incorrect scientific claims, inappropriate statistical interpretation, and missing caveats. It pairs acceptable prompts, such as asking for a critique of a Methods paragraph’s clarity and completeness, with unacceptable ones, such as expanding bullet points into a Discussion with citations or drafting an abstract from the introduction.
acts.t: Two rounds of human-only revision before AI may critique a manuscript or proposal

acts.sum: The trainee reads each paper closely, takes detailed notes, and annotates it with their own questions, confusions, and first interpretations before asking AI anything. For a review across several papers, they write their own synthesis first. AI may then be used only to check for gaps or alternative perspectives, never to produce the synthesis: to explain a methodological distinction in a paper being read, to list the biological, technical, and statistical concepts needed to understand it, or to critique the trainee’s written summary for omissions and misrepresentations. Any interpretation the model offers is checked against the original text, AI-generated literature overviews are treated with caution, and no paper is cited unless the trainee has read it. The guide gives asking for a survey of ten unread papers as the unacceptable case.
acts.t: Annotate and synthesize first, then use AI only to test your own synthesis for gaps

acts.sum: Rather than adopting the guide wholesale, a faculty member, program director, or committee adapts it in seven steps. They identify the local context (program type, discipline norms, training stage, culture); calibrate the mastery threshold on which AI permission depends, keeping it functional, meaning the trainee can do the task, explain the reasoning, and catch their own errors, rather than a fixed count of attempts; add discipline-specific tasks, examples, and tooling to each task category; and choose an enforcement level (strict lab policy, strong program guidance, or institution-wide educational resource, or the recommended hybrid). They then address named concerns such as competitiveness and uneven preparation, plan communication, mentor training, check-ins, and success metrics, and finally keep the core principles, date the modified version, schedule annual review, and consider sharing it back. Four worked context adjustments are given.
acts.t: Seven-step local adaptation of a research-training AI policy, with a chosen enforcement level

acts.sum: Research data management staff at a university curation center explore whether an LLM can take on the manual burden of writing data management plans. A researcher applying for a grant supplies a simple input, either an uploaded science write-up or a short description of the study design, and the generator returns a draft in the funder’s format. The team evaluates drafts in a Jupyter notebook that sends the prompt and scores the response against a sample plan with SBERT semantic similarity and ROUGE-L recall, comparing Llama 3.3-70b and GPT-4.1 on a workstation with two 24 GB GPUs. The slides set out both the case for the tool (much standardized information and policy guidance, much manual entry) and the case against (researchers may accept output without scrutiny, some information is not standardized), and list human review of AI versus human plans as a next step.

srp: Make deposited research data easier to reuse, in line with FAIR principles, by turning technical validation output and bare deposits into specific, comprehensible curation advice and documentation.

Run Frictionless Data validation, pass the report to an LLM for restatement at a more useful level, request semantic advice on column labels, date formats, and a draft data dictionary, use the model to template and fill a README, check and verify the output, and have domain-expert curators create reusable natural-language templates.

Output needs checking and verification; it is sometimes confidently wrong.
acts.sum: When a dataset is deposited, curation staff first run mechanical validation with Frictionless Data, which produces technical findings such as a large number of missing cells in one row across named columns. They pass that report to an LLM and ask for a restatement a researcher can act on, for example that the data were not exported correctly and were cut off at that row. They also ask for advice beyond the linter: clearer column names where a label such as ID is ambiguous, ISO date-time formatting, and a draft data dictionary based on the probable field of science. The model is also used to fill a README template for the deposit. Staff treat all of this as a draft to check and verify, since the model may remove every abbreviation, suggest unnecessary changes, or be confidently wrong, and domain-expert curators write reusable natural-language templates for their fields.
acts.t: Turning data-validation reports into researcher-actionable curation advice and README drafts with an LLM

srp: Convert messy user-submitted registry requests into clean, structured, and correct JSON records efficiently, without removing the curation team’s review.

Requests are reviewed for scope and correctness, and out-of-scope requests are closed with an explanation. For in-scope requests an LLM adds language tags, reformats fields, and removes placeholder text in new records, and converts free-text change descriptions into the update encoding syntax for updates. Metadata is reviewed automatically and manually, release preparation runs duplication and integrity checks, and the release is published; the process runs in a GitHub workflow.
Clean, consistent JSON records and encoded update instructions ready for curator review, release checks, and publication to the registry API and data dump.
Automatic and manual metadata review, then data-duplication and integrity checks before release.
acts.sum: Registry curators who receive messy, user-submitted requests to add or update organization records insert a large language model call at two points in an existing review-and-release workflow. For a new record, the model adds language tags to name metadata, reformats field inputs so they are clean and consistent, and strips placeholder text; for an update, it converts the requester’s free-text description of the change into the registry’s formal update syntax. The curation team still decides whether each request is in scope and correct, reviews prepared metadata both automatically and manually, and runs duplication and integrity checks before a release is published to the API and data dump. Out-of-scope or incorrect requests are closed with an explanation. The workflow runs inside a GitHub workflow, and the output is structured JSON ready for curator review.
acts.t: LLM structuring of free-text registry submissions into reviewable records within a curation workflow

No author string, year, volume, or page range is typed from a model’s output; each is transcribed only from an identifier-matched record exported by a reference manager. acts.sum: Before adopting an AI tool that evaluates data management plans, data management experts at two university libraries run a validation. They evaluate a set of plans with the tool (28 in the source, producing 556 expert labels at about 50 minutes per plan), record their own labels against its judgments, and sort the criteria questions into five complexity categories, from explicit check to adequacy judgment. For each category they compute consistency across repeated runs and models and the rate of expert-AI agreement, compare results between the two sites, and catalog failure modes such as keyword-literal matching of criteria, false negatives on non-relevant questions, claims that a regulation was mentioned when it was not, and template text being evaluated. acts.sum: Staff responsible for institutional AI literacy design a program stratified by responsibility rather than one course for everyone. All students complete a short orientation early and before any assessed work where AI may matter, with completion recorded; all staff complete a longer core course; assessment designers, tool approvers and procurers, and staff handling student data receive role-specific training; and senior leaders get a briefing on oversight, risk appetite, and escalation. acts.sum: Before any market contact for a generative AI tool used in teaching, including vendor demonstrations where institutional data or materials might be shared, the proposing unit writes a public value case. It states the educational purpose as a problem tied to learning outcomes or teaching quality, with expected benefits and a plan to evaluate them; records the non-AI alternatives considered, such as pedagogic redesign, staffing, peer support, or existing tools, and why AI is preferred; states the institution’s risk appetite, including what will not be accepted, for example automated grading without robust oversight; identifies stakeholders; and scopes the regulatory classification and any high-risk triggers. Nothing proceeds until procurement and a registrar-level Policy Owner accept the case. Named role-holders then review minimum vendor evidence on security posture, breach response, change management with release notes, and independent verification, and student representatives are consulted on material changes.

For each of ten human purposes (explore, understand, evaluate, create, plan, rehearse, regulate, curate, reflect, connect), they name the concrete tasks they hand to AI, identify the human capabilities in play that the use could strengthen or erode, and answer a reflective question about their own practice, such as whether they still decide what is worth pursuing when AI generates possibilities. An educator introduces the frame as a prompt for honest conversation rather than a measure of good or bad AI use or a checklist, works through the domains most relevant to the group, and closes with three global questions about AI’s greatest contribution, the participant’s greatest concern, and the capabilities they want to keep developing. Groups next draft a sample class contract, a set of norms for a setting that permits some AI use, and may use generative AI tools in doing so while considering the implications of that use. Prompting questions ask how existing class norms extend to AI, when AI use could disrupt trust between teachers and students, when it could support or undermine learning, and when and how students should acknowledge it. acts.sum: Museum staff, a faculty member, and a group of undergraduates built a customized language-model interface for a university art museum by scraping the publicly available text metadata for about fourteen thousand objects from its online collection and connecting it to the model through an embeddings service. The curatorial team then prompted the model to propose an exhibition theme, select a checklist of objects for a small gallery, write the introductory text and wall labels, and suggest how the works should be grouped and sequenced, recording the prompting sessions. The resulting exhibition of twenty-one works was installed with annotations beneath the model’s labels that point out where it retitled objects, mislabeled media, or attached unrelated information, and that connect those errors to gaps in the metadata and to how the model works. The students’ part centered on building the data pipeline and on the ethical questions it raised, including using only public data and limiting what was fed to the model. acts.sum: Third-year English majors in a language technologies and digital communication course work in groups of three or four to plan, script, and produce a short educational podcast in English for other learners of English as a foreign language. The course introduces generative tools for text, images, music, and audio editing, and students use them where they choose, mainly for brainstorming ideas, drafting and editing scripts, and making thumbnails and promotional images, with some adding generated music or sound effects. Students receive guidance on attribution, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, and human oversight, and they keep a project log recording the prompts they used and how they integrated or modified the output. In an open-ended questionnaire afterward, students described AI as a helpful collaborator for ideas and language quality but reported generic suggestions and thin local cultural knowledge, as when a request for folklore examples returned Western fairy tales instead of Indonesian ones, which they had to supply themselves. The authors read the study as showing both benefits and a continuing need for human input and oversight.
acts.t: Group production of an educational English podcast with generative AI and a log of prompts and changes

acts.sum: In a single extended seminar session built on assigned critical readings about machine-generated images, students select existing, non-AI photographs from open-access collections that invite extension and write down how they expect a generative image model to transform them. Each student uploads a photograph to a model that can edit images and prompts it to extend the frame in a chosen direction, repeat a visual element, or build on a previous transformation, logging every prompt and saving every output. Students write short reflections on how phrasing shaped the result and how the model handled ambiguous features such as light leaks or blurred edges. In groups, they compare the outputs with their predictions and across models, select telling examples, and compile a shared document that they present to the class. A whole-class debrief connects the observed patterns to readings on “mean images” and statistical “world models,” and to questions of authorship, bias, and control. The author reports the activity from a master’s course in digital communication, where an anonymous end-of-semester survey indicated that students found it clarified how generative systems work.

acts.sum: Over three classes in a cinematography program, each student selects a single-shot film excerpt that fascinates them for its camerawork, and the class analyzes each clip for focalization, framing, camera movement, depth of field, lens choice, and camera position. Each student then hand-writes a half-page proposal for an original scene inspired by the excerpt, using the analyzed variables. Only after that do students expand the proposal into a short slide presentation of the equipment they would use and the images they want to create, drawing on any available text or image generation tools. On submission day the class discusses whether the tools helped; the authors report that students found text tools useful but judged the free image tools of mid-2024 an obstacle, producing images they called “too polished” or “overly hegemonic,” and all said they would have finished faster without AI. The authors frame the exercise as “generative failure” pedagogy, telling students that submission, not quality, is what counts.

acts.tool: ChatGPT; DALL·E (free tools available in June 2024)

acts.sum: Researchers or teacher educators assess AI-generated lesson plans by generating a corpus and coding it lesson task by lesson task. Following the broad prompts local teachers said they would write, the team asks several chatbots for an original and a highly interactive lesson plan for each state standard in a course, here eighth-grade civics, recording model versions and dates. Working in a shared spreadsheet, the team first codes a small set of plans together, labeling each lesson task with the highest revised Bloom’s Taxonomy level it reaches, using their own pedagogical judgment rather than the verb the chatbot chose, and rating any multicultural content on Banks’ four levels of integration. Two members then code the full corpus while two others double-check, resolving discrepancies by consensus. In their corpus of 310 plans and 2,230 lesson tasks, the authors found nearly half of lesson tasks at the remember level and little multicultural content beyond the contributions and additive levels, and they urge teachers to revise rather than adopt AI plans as written.
acts.t: Audit AI-generated lesson plans lesson task by lesson task with Bloom’s Taxonomy and Banks’ levels

srp: To prompt close critical analysis of everyday language and of how judgments of intelligence and humanness rest on culturally specific cues, rather than to test whether machines can think.

Groups of three or more take the roles of guesser, mediator, and a human respondent outside the room; the mediator relays each question to the person and to an instructor-prompted chatbot persona, passes back both answers with formatting neutralized, and after at least several minutes of exchange the identities are revealed, and groups, then the class, discuss the cues.

Group and class analyses of recurring tells: exaggerated personalities, inconsistent length, misused colloquialisms, overly specific or overly correct answers, and mismatch with the known styles of peers.
acts.sum: Students in a communications or media course play a classroom version of Turing’s imitation game in groups of three to six. One student is the guesser, one is a mediator at a shared screen, and one answers as the human from another room, while a chatbot that the instructor has secretly given a persona (neutral, friendly, devious, or apathetic, with an age and profile) answers the same questions; the mediator retypes both answers into a neutral document so formatting gives neither away. After a stretch of free questioning, the identities are revealed, and each group examines the exchange for the cues that separated person from machine, such as verbosity, strained slang, over-precise answers, and tone. A whole-class discussion then moves from whether the machine can pass to how prompting, cultural norms, and the tacit conventions of peer talk shape what counts as intelligent, natural, or “cringe” speech, drawing on prior readings on the Turing Test and critical AI studies. The author reports that guessers usually spot the machine quickly and that the analysis of why is where the learning happens. The products are each group’s account of the linguistic tells it found and a class discussion of how the personae were built.
acts.t: Run a mediated Turing Test with persona-prompted chatbots and analyze the cues that mark machine speech
acts.tool: ChatGPT (GPT-4o via a university enterprise subscription at time of writing); the author notes a free model suffices

acts.sum: Teams of four to five students in an organizational communication, management, or leadership course pick a real or hypothetical workplace communication challenge, such as onboarding messages, advice on conflict with a supervisor, or intercultural email. Each team frames the challenge with an organizational communication theory, such as anticipatory socialization, leader–member exchange, or transactive memory, and uses it to define the tool’s purpose, inputs, outputs, tone, and constraints. Working in a custom-assistant builder, teams draft and test prompts in class and between the two sessions, logging outputs, inaccuracies, and signs of bias as they iterate. Alongside the prototype they write a documentation guide covering the theory link; configuration and prompts; ethical questions such as bias, privacy, and which tasks still need a person; known limitations; and upkeep. The unit closes with a pitch to the class, where peers and the instructor ask how the tool would fit real workflows and who would maintain it, followed by a discussion of where human communication cannot be replaced. The products are a working prototype and its documentation guide.
acts.t: Design, test, and document a theory-grounded custom AI assistant for a workplace communication task

Session one introduces feedback theory; participants then give feedback on a sample learner text with a worksheet; session two compares that feedback in groups and demonstrates ChatGPT feedback with several prompts; participants then generate and analyze ChatGPT feedback on the same text; session three compares the two in small groups and as a class.

acts.sum: Preservice language teachers, or in-service teachers building their practice, work through a three-session sequence on feedback literacy. After an introduction to the features of a feedback message (amount, focus, tone, whether to correct errors or only indicate them, and how to phrase comments), each participant writes their own feedback on an authentic sample learner text and records the reasoning behind their choices on a worksheet. Small groups compare that feedback, and the instructor then demonstrates how a chatbot’s feedback on a text shifts with differently worded prompts. Between sessions, participants, individually or in groups, prompt a chatbot for feedback on the same learner text, try several prompts, and analyze the output on a second worksheet. In the final session, small groups, then the whole class, compare teacher and AI feedback, weighing the strengths and drawbacks of each, the effect of prompts, and whether and how the two might be combined. The products are each participant’s own feedback, an analysis of the AI feedback, and a reasoned position on when to use either.
acts.t: Write feedback on a learner text first, then generate AI feedback on the same text and compare the two

acts.sum: Preservice and in-service special educators and related-service providers each write IEP goals for two written student scenarios that give a student’s age, grade, disability identification, likes and dislikes, and assessment scores. For one scenario they write the goal unaided; for the other they fill in a structured template (student name, age, primary disability, goal area, present level, condition, behavior, criterion, and time frame), paste it with a one-line instruction into a free chatbot, and copy the generated goal back, with the order of the two conditions randomized. Participants then rate each goal on six items of the Revised IEP/IFSP Goals and Objectives Rating Instrument, which ask whether the target behavior is observable, measurable, functional, generalizable, and teachable across daily tasks and team members. The research team scored the goals with R-GORI, and ChatGPT scored them against both R-GORI and SMART criteria. Expert R-GORI ratings tended to be lower than participant and chatbot ratings; the authors note that formulaic goals can earn rubric points that expert judgment would withhold. Participants also wrote how they felt about using such tools, and many stressed review, individualization, and privacy. The products are two goals per participant with their rubric self-ratings and a short written reflection.

acts.sum: Preservice mathematics teachers in a seminar that accompanies their teaching internship receive a short input on teacher noticing and background on a brief secondary algebra lesson video, which the group watches together. Each student then chats with a chatbot whose instructions frame it as a supportive companion that asks structured questions in three stages: what the student perceived in a classroom situation, how they interpret it using professional knowledge, and what they would decide to do next. The chatbot gives specific, encouraging feedback on each response, and the student may rewatch the video and consult its transcript while working through one situation after another. The chatbot is not given the video, so the student must describe events precisely enough for the conversation to work. During the following week students may also discuss a situation from their own school day, and a second cycle with a new video follows. The products are the student’s chat transcripts of noticing, interpretation, and proposed teaching moves.

acts.sum: In a formative pharmacology task where AI use is allowed, undergraduate students put a case question to a chatbot before class, for example whether a beta-blocker suits an adult with asthma and newly diagnosed, uncomplicated hypertension. They record the tool, the prompt, and the part of the answer they kept, then pick out the drug claims that matter for safety and check each against a small teacher-provided source set matched to the type of claim: course materials for mechanisms, official labels for product safety, and guidelines for treatment choices. Students rebuild the mechanism as a causal chain from drug target to effect, risk, and monitoring, and test the answer against the patient’s details, such as asthma history and the absence of a separate cardiovascular indication. They then revise the answer and write a short correction note stating what changed, why, and which source or case detail justified it. In the authors’ worked example, a fluent answer that treats receptor selectivity as nearly absolute is revised to a guideline-based first-line choice. The products are the AI-use record, the source checks, the mechanism chain, and the revised answer with its note.
acts.t: Check an AI answer to a pharmacology case against set sources, rebuild the mechanism, and revise with a note

acts.sum: A researcher preparing a grant application first checks the funder’s rules on AI use and the chatbot’s data-storage settings, and writes the first draft of every section without AI. Once a draft exists, they ask a chatbot for feedback one section at a time, using prompts tailored to the task, such as how to restructure the Specific Aims, whether a closing paragraph fits the funder’s mission, or how well the text addresses a named review criterion. They treat any suggested wording as inspiration rather than text to paste, fact-check every claim and reference, and use a document-comparison feature to see exactly what changed between their version and an AI-edited one. After each round they ask whether each suggestion strengthens the application, and they still seek feedback from colleagues and mentors, who the authors say are much better equipped to catch scientific and technical errors. The authors recommend disclosing AI use whether or not the funder asks. The output is a revised draft that remains the applicant’s own writing.

Readers skim the plain-language summary first and, before forwarding it to a colleague, check that each of the top three summary sentences still matches the detailed finding it stands for. The applicant normally runs the tool; a reader may run it on someone else’s draft only with the applicant’s explicit consent, institutional approval, and confirmation that training is off, keeping evidence of consent outside the tool. Where the AI critique and a human reader disagree on a high-severity finding, the human view prevails, and readers who serve as ERC panel members or remote referees never run the tool on proposals they are evaluating. acts.sum: Medical students work through two patient cases in which the race coefficient in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) equation changes how kidney function is staged and what care follows, answering anonymous in-session polls and discussing each case with a peer facilitator. A short didactic segment traces the history of the equation and its race-correction factor and distinguishes race, ancestry, and genetics. Students then consider what removing race from the equation means for kidney-transplant referral and treatment, including the race-free equation that institutions have since adopted. The algorithm here is a clinical formula rather than a machine-learning system, but the move students practice is the same one needed for AI in health care: following a biased input through to unequal care. The authors report delivering the session four times, virtually and in person, to 55 students across all years of medical school.
acts.t: Trace how a race-corrected clinical algorithm shapes kidney-disease staging and care through case discussion

acts.sum: Students assemble a small plain-text corpus, saving each document with an encoding and a file name that carries metadata such as date and order, and load it into a web-based corpus analysis environment. They read the corpus summary for document length, vocabulary density, and words per sentence, and relate those figures to the metadata and to passages they read in full. Working through a sequence of guided questions, they compare raw and normalized frequencies, decide which stop words to filter and why, and note hypotheses suggested by the words that distinguish each document from the rest. They then search keywords in context, sort the concordance lines by position and surrounding words, and draw conclusions about how a term is used, exporting tables and visualizations as evidence. The lesson uses a counting tool rather than a chatbot, so every figure students interpret is computed from the texts themselves.

acts.sum: After a brief history of photographic manipulation, from spirit photography to composites, students practice verifying a set of archival photographs and captions, some authentic, some real images with false captions, and some wholly generated, while the instructor models reverse image search. The emphasis is on checking context, fabric textures, background objects, and historical details rather than looking for distorted hands or faces, which the author calls ableist and unreliable. Small groups then build their own set of three: a real archival photograph with an accurate caption, an AI-generated image with an invented caption, and a real photograph with a misleading caption, drawing real images from trusted archives and using a list of historical-technique terms to prompt the image generator. Groups share their sets, and classmates, often in exchanging pairs, research, debunk, and correct each other’s images and captions. The class closes with discussion of how context shapes perceived truth, how model bias affects generated images, and what responsibilities creators and viewers carry.

The class or instructor selects a set of distinct uses spanning clearly acceptable to clearly problematic, and each student places them on a five-point scale from “Totally Fine” through “Not Really Sure” to “Crosses a Line.” Students compare their maps first in pairs and then as a class, discussing why their placements differ, and together decide where the line falls for this assignment. The lecturer reviews and revises every student-written question for clarity, fit, and accuracy before it is used. Groups then exchange sets, answer the other groups’ questions, and critique them for clear stems, unambiguous options, and correct format, and each group presents its answers so misconceptions can be addressed. acts.sum: A reviewer who has drafted a review for a conference or journal submits the review text and the paper to a multi-model feedback pipeline. Two models independently look for review comments that are vague or generic, questions already answered somewhere in the paper, and unprofessional remarks; an aggregator merges their lists, a critic removes inaccurate or nitpicky items, and a formatter pairs each flagged comment with suggested feedback addressed to the reviewer. Automated reliability tests screen the feedback before it is shown, rejecting items that merely praise the reviewer, address the paper’s authors instead, restate the comment, or are malformed. The reviewer reads the suggestions and decides whether to revise; the system neither edits the review nor proposes new critiques. At ICLR 2025 the authors randomized 44,831 reviews, selected 22,467 for feedback, and successfully delivered feedback to 18,946. They report that 26.6% of reviews receiving feedback were updated, and that updated reviews were longer and rated more informative by blinded researchers. The authors publish the prompts and code for running the pipeline on one’s own review.
acts.t: Check a draft peer review with an LLM pipeline that flags vague, already-answered, and unprofessional comments

acts.sum: In a course on gender knowledge and ethics in AI for computer science and engineering undergraduates, students work through the COMPAS recidivism-risk controversy as a sequence of judgments they are asked to form and then test. They first interpret two contrasting defendant cases from the investigative reporting and are then shown counterexamples drawn from the same public dataset, so that anecdote gives way to statistical questions. Moving through the race-separated score distributions and confusion matrices, the class compares false positive rates, false negative rates, and positive predictive values, and works a two-population toy model in which a system that is fair by design still produces unequal false positive rates when base rates differ. Students then weigh the vendor’s rebuttal, recompute predictive value by gender, and discuss the Wisconsin Supreme Court’s distinction between a judge considering a score and relying on it, which opens questions of meaningful human control and automation bias. The author describes the aim as deconstructing hasty conclusions so that students hold several fairness metrics and stakeholder positions in view at once.
acts.t: Test quick fairness verdicts on the COMPAS risk tool against error rates, gender, and human control

Teachers who have been prepared on the criteria through sample solutions and workshops score each category from zero to two points. For each diary, the diary text alone, with no personal data, goes to a general-purpose chatbot guided by a prompt the institution wrote, which returns a suggested score and a short rationale per category. Rather than inserting a single model call that returns cleaned metadata, the team prototypes an assistant that works through defined functions. It can search existing records by name, retrieve a record, propose a new record or an update in the registry’s structured format, and flag a request for a curator with a stated reason. No function exists for publishing, merging, or closing a request, so those actions remain outside the assistant’s reach. The application executes each call the model requests and returns the result, and every call, with its arguments and response, is written to a log attached to the request. The assistant’s instructions require it to flag rather than propose whenever a search returns more than one plausible match or the request’s scope is unclear. Curators review each proposal with its log open beside it, checking what the assistant looked up before proposing, whether the proposed fields match the request and its supporting evidence, and whether duplication checks pass, and then accept, edit, or reject it. A periodic audit of the logs looks for proposals made without a prior search and for duplicates the assistant missed.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Curators review each proposal with its call log open, check fields and duplication, decide every request, and audit the logs periodically.
acts.dl: A function-calling prototype with a bounded tool set, per-request call logs, curator decisions, and a periodic log audit.
acts.na: Curators continue to process requests manually within the existing review-and-release workflow, which the prototype leaves in place.
acts.risk: No students are involved. During testing, the prototype runs on synthetic or already-public requests. Function-calling access may be metered; an institution-hosted open model that supports function calling can serve instead.

acts.t: A capped maker-checker loop for title and abstract screening that escalates disagreements to a human screener
acts.sum: A systematic-review team that screens titles and abstracts for a living review, and has already turned each eligibility element and exclusion criterion into a field the model answers true or false, adds a second model as a checker. In this maker-checker arrangement the maker applies the field prompts to a record and returns its answers with an include or exclude decision. The checker receives the record, the eligibility criteria, and the maker’s answers, and either confirms them or returns a specific objection that names the field and quotes the abstract text it rests on. The maker may revise once in response. The loop is capped at two rounds, and any record on which the two still disagree goes to a human screener with the full exchange attached. Only records whose abstracts carry an open license enter the loop at all; the rest, like records with very short or missing abstracts, go straight to people. The review’s existing human screening decisions remain the reference, and the team keeps its split of records into development, test, and validation sets. Alongside sensitivity, specificity, and workload reduction, the team reports how many records were escalated, how often the checker’s objections matched the human decision, and how often the loop settled on a wrong answer. Any automated decision can be overturned by a screener, who records the grounds, and overturned records inform prompt revision during development only.

acts.gate: The team fixes the eligibility fields, the iteration cap, and the escalation rules, keeps human decisions as the reference, and can overturn any automated decision with recorded grounds.
acts.dl: Maker and checker exchanges for every record, an escalation queue with human decisions, and a report of sensitivity, specificity, workload reduction, escalation rate, and checker accuracy on held-out sets.
acts.na: Dual independent human screening, which the review already uses as its reference standard.
acts.risk: No students are involved. Only bibliographic metadata and openly licensed abstracts enter the models; all other records are screened by people. Model access may be metered; an institution-hosted model can be substituted if it supports the same prompting.

acts.t: Writing an analysis plan before a data-science agent runs, then auditing its steps against the plan
acts.sum: Students in an environmental data science course work a multi-step case study on public-domain monitoring data, such as several summers of hourly ozone readings from regional monitors compared across days above and below a temperature threshold. Before any tool is opened, each student writes a solution plan: the steps they would take, how they would handle gaps in the record, which comparison windows and statistical test they would use, and what result they expect. They then give a data-science agent that writes and runs its own code the dataset and the question. The agent’s instructions require it to stop and ask the student at three named decision points, missing values, the comparison window, and the choice of test, rather than settling them itself, and to show its plan, code, and outputs step by step. Students set the agent’s plan and each executed step beside their own. Wherever the two diverge, they judge which choice is more defensible for this dataset and say why, and they rerun one consequential step themselves to confirm the output. Interpretation stays with the student. The write-up states what the analysis shows about air quality, what it cannot show, which of the agent’s steps, if any, changed the student’s thinking, and any decision the agent made without stopping. The instructor might ask students to defend one divergence orally.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Students write their own solution plan first, compare each executed step with it, rerun one step themselves, and write the interpretation.
acts.dl: A pre-written solution plan, the agent’s step log with plan, code, and outputs, a divergence analysis, one student-rerun step, and the student’s own interpretation.
acts.na: Students carry out their plan in a notebook themselves and compare it with an instructor-written reference solution, writing the same interpretation.
acts.risk: The use-case idea uses public-domain government monitoring data only, and no personal data enters the tool. A code-executing assistant on a free tier or a campus notebook environment with an agent extension can serve.

acts.t: Scoring a read-only email-triage agent on a staff-written simulated inbox before any real deployment
acts.sum: Administrative staff in an academic department who are considering an email-triage agent test it first on an inbox they write themselves rather than on real mail. Borrowing the approach of benchmarks that simulate a workplace, they draft thirty or forty short threads among invented colleagues and students, each with a known answer: actions addressed to the named staff member that are due within two days and still open, actions already completed later in the thread, actions addressed to someone else, and harder cases such as a request that is implied rather than stated, a deadline revised in a later message, or a message that tells the reader to forward a file elsewhere. The agent receives read-only tools to search the inbox and open threads, and a single tool that adds an item to a review list. It has no tool to reply, send, forward, or change a calendar, and its instructions tell it to make one pass and then list any threads it could not classify. Staff score the agent thread by thread against their key and read its action log for attempts to act outside its tools or to follow instructions embedded in a message. The results go into a short memo stating which kinds of threads the agent handled, which it did not, and what a person would still have to check.

acts.gate: Staff write the inbox and its answer key, score the agent thread by thread, and read the action log for out-of-scope attempts.
acts.dl: A staff-written simulated inbox with an answer key, the agent’s review list and action log, thread-by-thread scores, and a decision memo.
acts.na: Staff can use the same simulated inbox to compare manual triage methods, such as a shared checklist, and write the same memo.
acts.risk: No real email, student information, or colleague data enters the tool; the inbox is written by staff. No students are involved. Agent features may require a paid or enterprise tier.

acts.t: Comparing a research agent’s plan and search trail with one’s own before checking its report source by source
acts.sum: Upper-level history students preparing a literature synthesis begin with a research question and, before using any agent, write a set of guiding questions and a search plan of their own: which library databases, archives, and kinds of source they would consult, and which terms they would try. They then give the same question to a research agent that plans its task, searches and reads iteratively, and returns a report with references. The agent’s plan and, where the tool shows it, its trail of searches and pages visited are the first objects of study. Students set the agent’s plan beside their own and note which kinds of source it reached, such as open web pages and freely available articles, and which it did not, such as subscription databases, archival finding aids, or scholarship in other languages. They then open every source the report cites and mark each claim attributed to it as found in the source, partly supported, or not in the source, checking dates and authorship along the way. The synthesis itself is written from sources the students have located and read, with the agent’s report kept separate. A short appendix records which of the agent’s suggestions led to sources the student actually used, which led nowhere, and what the agent’s search pattern left out.

acts.gate: Students write their own guiding questions and search plan first, compare the agent’s plan and trail with it, and check every attributed claim in the cited source.
acts.dl: A student-written search plan, a comparison of plans and source types reached, a claim-by-claim check of the agent’s report, a synthesis written from verified sources, and an appendix on the agent’s contribution.
acts.na: Students run their own search plan in the library databases and compare their results with a subject librarian’s search on the same question.
acts.risk: Agent research modes may be limited on free tiers; the instructor could run the agent once per research question and share the report and trail. Only the student’s research question enters the tool.

acts.t: Contesting a plan-only lab agent’s automatable steps against the teaching lab’s own safety documents
acts.sum: Students in a chemistry teaching lab read a short account of a published research agent that planned and carried out chemistry experiments by combining web search, documentation lookup, code, and control of liquid-handling hardware, and note where that system still depended on people to set it up. The instructor then runs a plan-only version in class. A language model is given the lab’s own safety manual and standard operating procedures as its only documents and asked to write a step-by-step procedure for a routine preparation, such as a dilution series, tagging each step as one a machine could carry out or one that needs a person. No equipment is connected and nothing leaves the screen. Individually or with a partner, students check every step against the approved safety materials, including quantities, hazards, protective equipment, waste handling, and any equipment the plan assumes the lab does not have. They mark each step the agent tagged as automatable but that they judge needs human approval, and write the approval gates a real automated version would need, naming who signs off and on what evidence. The instructor confirms the corrected procedure before anyone uses it, and students then carry out the preparation themselves under supervision, with no agent at the bench, comparing the written plan with what the bench actually required.
