acts.t: Predicting hyperparameter effects in an age-prediction model
acts.sum: Learners following the Galaxy Training Network tutorial on age prediction treat the regression models they build as the AI under study. Having reproduced the tutorial’s two analyses, an ElasticNet pipeline with feature selection on RNA-seq data and a gradient boosting regressor on DNA methylation data, each learner changes one element of a hyperparameter grid and writes down, before rerunning, what they expect to happen to the R2 score and why. The workflow is then rerun in Galaxy, and the new score table, parallel coordinates plot, and predicted-against-true-age plot are set beside the prediction. Where the outcome differs from the expectation, the learner drafts an explanation in terms of the model: the regularization setting, the number of features kept, the number of estimators. A class session is given over to taking these discrepancies apart, with learners presenting their change, their prediction, and their result. Parameter choices and scores go into a shared table, so the class can see how far results move across the grid and how they compare with the published work the tutorial refers to.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Learners produce a written prediction of how one hyperparameter change will move the score, made before rerunning, and their own explanation, in terms of the model, of any gap between prediction and result.
acts.dl: A prediction-and-result record for one hyperparameter change, with an explanation of the discrepancy, entered in a shared class table and presented in the debrief.
acts.risk: Galaxy runs in a browser on public servers that typically require a free account; the tutorial is CC BY 4.0 and its datasets are openly hosted, and reruns may queue at busy times.

acts.t: Checking AI search briefings on the South Napa earthquake
acts.sum: In the GETSI unit on the 2014 South Napa earthquake, each student researches one aspect of the event (seismology, faulting, or damage) before a jigsaw. In this version the pre-class research is done twice: once with a search-oriented AI tool that returns a briefing with citations, and once by going to the sources the briefing cites and to agency and survey reports found independently. Students list the guiding questions for their aspect, record the tool’s answer to each, and mark every claim as confirmed in the cited source, present in the source but altered, or not traceable. Magnitudes, dates, fault names, and damage figures receive particular attention. In the jigsaw, each expert reports both the content of the briefing and how reliable it proved for their aspect. Groups then go on to the unit’s GPS strain calculation for stations P198, P200, and SVIN, and compare their computed coseismic strain and recurrence estimate with any figures the briefings asserted.

acts.gate: Each student marks every briefing claim as confirmed, altered, or not traceable in its cited source and reports its reliability in the jigsaw; groups compute the coseismic strain and recurrence estimate that the briefings’ figures are compared against.
acts.dl: A claim-by-claim source check of an AI search briefing on one aspect of the earthquake, reported in the jigsaw, followed by the unit’s written strain calculations.

acts.t: Ranking AI explanations of enzyme inhibition against a simulation
acts.sum: Students receive three short AI-written explanations of how competitive, uncompetitive, and noncompetitive inhibition change a Lineweaver-Burk plot, and use the LearnChemE enzyme inhibition simulation, as published, to decide which statements hold. The instructor generates the explanations beforehand from a prompt of their own on standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics, keeping a set in which at least one explanation confuses two mechanisms or misstates which intercept moves. One explanation gives only the final pattern, while another reasons through which complex the inhibitor binds, so the set contrasts a bare result with a worked rationale. Students move the inhibitor concentration slider under each mechanism, switch between the direct and reciprocal plots, and note for every claim whether the slope and intercepts behave as described. Each explanation is ranked, the failing sentences are quoted and corrected, and every correction is tied to an observation in the simulation. No student uses an AI tool, and nothing from the simulation site is entered into one.

acts.gate: Students produce a ranking of the three explanations, quote and correct each failing sentence, and tie every correction to an observation they made in the simulation.
acts.dl: A ranked set of three AI explanations with failing sentences quoted, corrected, and tied to specific simulation observations.
acts.risk: The simulation runs free in a browser and is linked unmodified, as no reuse license is stated on its page; students need no AI account, and plot-reading tasks call for a described or tabular alternative for students who use screen readers.

acts.t: Comparing AI-simulated survey answers with a community’s own
acts.sum: Students in the InTeGrate unit collect natural hazard survey responses from their own social networks. Before opening the results, they ask a conversational assistant to answer the same survey questions as it expects residents of their community to answer, repeating the request several times to obtain a small set of synthetic respondents. The two sets are tabulated side by side: perceived likelihood of each hazard, self-rated knowledge, preparedness steps taken. Students look for patterned differences. The synthetic answers may cluster around a textbook view of risk, may favor hazards prominent in national coverage, or may flatten variation that the real responses show. Each difference is written up with a proposed source, such as training data that under-represent the region or a default toward generic advice, and with what the real data say instead. The comparison feeds the unit’s second pass, in which students frame a research question from the full dataset. Only the survey questions, never respondents’ answers, are entered into the tool.

acts.gate: Students tabulate synthetic and real responses side by side, write up each patterned difference with a proposed source and what the real data say instead, and then frame their own research question from the full dataset.

acts.risk: Real respondents’ answers stay out of the AI tool; collecting survey data from personal networks may call for a check with the institution’s review office, and adapted materials carry CC BY-NC-SA attribution.

acts.t: Testing AI-proposed modeling assumptions against rocket video data
acts.sum: Students track a rocket’s launch frame by frame in the Tracker file from the Open Source Physics activity and obtain position-time data for the phase in which it speeds up. Before computing anything, each student writes down the assumptions they would make to turn a measured acceleration into a force. They then ask a conversational assistant what assumptions a simple model of the launch needs; it commonly proposes constant thrust, constant mass, and negligible air resistance. Every proposed assumption is treated as a claim to test. A constant-thrust, constant-mass model predicts constant acceleration, so students check whether their velocity-time graph is linear over the tracked interval and how the fitted acceleration changes when the interval is shortened. Each assumption is accepted, amended, or rejected with a reference to the data, and the student’s own list is compared with the assistant’s to see which considerations each had missed. The force calculation is then reported with the surviving assumptions stated and an uncertainty drawn from the scatter in the tracking.

acts.gate: Each student writes their own assumptions first, accepts, amends, or rejects each proposed assumption with reference to their tracked velocity-time data, and reports the force with the surviving assumptions and an uncertainty drawn from the tracking scatter.
acts.dl: A lab report giving the measured acceleration and inferred force, with a table of accepted, amended, and rejected assumptions and the data supporting each decision.
acts.risk: Tracker and the activity file are free, and the handout is offered in English and Chinese; a free-tier assistant suffices, only general physics questions are entered, and adapted handouts carry CC BY-NC-SA attribution.

acts.t: Translating a galaxy research question into SQL with an assistant
acts.sum: In the SDSS Voyages Galaxy Color investigation, used as published, students frame their own question about galaxy color and draw a sample from the survey database with a query. Here the query is drafted by a coding assistant from the student’s plain-language criteria: the student states the task, the region of sky, the kind of object, the brightness limits, and the columns wanted, and explains what the sample is for. None of the activity’s text is given to the assistant. The student runs the returned SQL in SkyServer and inspects what comes back, looking for stars admitted because no object-type condition was set, missing magnitude limits, or objects outside the intended region. Each defect is traced either to a gap in the plain-language request or to an error by the assistant; the request is revised, and the cycle is logged. When the sample matches the criteria, the student proceeds with the investigation as its page describes. The log of requests, queries, and returned samples is submitted with the investigation’s results.

acts.gate: Students produce their own question and plain-language sampling criteria, a log tracing each defect in the returned sample to their request or to the assistant, and the completed investigation.
acts.dl: A log of successive plain-language requests, the SQL each produced, and the defects found in each returned sample, submitted with the completed investigation.
acts.risk: SkyServer tools are free in a browser; the investigation is reached by link since no reuse license is stated, and the student’s own criteria (not graded prose) are what enter the assistant, which may require an account.

acts.t: Questioning an AI-played stakeholder in a polio trial deliberation
acts.sum: While groups deliberate in the STEW lesson on choosing a study design for the 1954 polio vaccine field trial, taught as published, a conversational assistant plays one additional stakeholder who is not among the lesson’s assigned roles. The instructor writes the persona brief from public historical accounts, for instance a county health officer anxious about enrollment, and runs the assistant on a projected screen; no lesson material is entered into the tool. Each group puts spoken questions to the persona about which design it prefers and why, and records the statistical claims it makes about randomization, comparison groups, consent, and the number of children needed. Back in their own roles, groups sort those claims into sound, unsound, and unverifiable, and decide whether any of them changes their recommendation. Because the persona argues fluently for its position, groups face a live opponent whose reasoning has to be examined on its merits before the lesson reaches its own conclusion. The sorted claims accompany each group’s presented recommendation.

acts.gate: Each group sorts the persona’s statistical claims into sound, unsound, and unverifiable, decides whether any of them changes its recommendation, and presents the sorted claims with its own study-design recommendation.
acts.dl: A sorted list of the persona’s statistical claims (sound, unsound, unverifiable) presented with the group’s design recommendation.
acts.risk: One instructor-run session on a shared screen means students need no account and enter nothing themselves; the lesson is used by link because its author retains copyright, and spoken exchanges call for captioning or a typed channel where needed.

acts.t: Fine-Tuning a Small Model as a Corpus Lens
acts.sum: A humanities researcher with a bounded text corpus of their own, such as a run of digitized newspaper articles or a periodical’s back file, fine-tunes a small, openly released language model on it and reads the generated text as evidence about the corpus, following the procedure of an openly licensed Programming Historian lesson. Before any training run, the researcher writes down their own reading of the corpus: the themes, recurring word associations, and framings they expect, from close reading of a sample. The fine-tuned model is then prompted with short questions about the corpus’s topic, and its outputs are read for recurring phrases and framings. Each interpretive observation is entered in a run log together with the prompt, the hyperparameters, and the output file, and the log sits in the project’s shared notes, visible to collaborators. Every pattern the model appears to surface is traced back to the corpus by keyword and concordance search; generated quotations and attributions are treated as model output, not as statements from the sources. Differences between the prior reading and the model-prompted reading are written up as questions for further archival work.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The researcher decides which patterns the model appears to surface actually hold in the corpus, tracing each by keyword and concordance search, and treats generated quotations and attributions as model output, not as statements from the sources.
acts.dl: A reproducible run log pairing each interpretive observation with its prompt, settings, and output, plus a memo of research questions arising from differences between the researcher’s prior reading and the model-prompted reading.
acts.risk: Fine-tuning needs GPU access, usually through a cloud notebook account with usage limits or fees, and a corpus of copyrighted or sensitive material may not be suitable for upload to a hosted environment.

acts.t: Two Text Generators, One Public-Domain Source
acts.sum: Students choose a public-domain literary text, such as a poet’s collected verse or a novel’s opening chapters, and build two generators from it in a notebook: a Markov chain whose transition table they can inspect, and a small neural language model whose internal workings they cannot. A coding assistant drafts the scripts for both from each student’s plain-language description. Students check the Markov script by hand-computing the transition counts for a ten-line sample and comparing them with the table the script produces, and they record any correction they had to request. With both generators running, they produce short passages at varied settings and write a stylistic commentary identifying which features of the source’s voice (diction, meter, syntax, recurring images) each procedure retains or loses, quoting the source text for every claim. Passages worth keeping are assembled into a short piece with a note stating which lines came from which generator and which were edited by hand. The design takes only the general idea of comparing a statistical and a neural generator from a published creative-computing course; none of that course’s assignment text is entered into a tool.
acts.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
acts.gate: Each student hand-computes transition counts to check the Markov script, writes a commentary on which features of the source’s voice each procedure retains or loses with a quotation for every claim, and attributes each line of the assembled piece.
acts.dl: A notebook with two working generators, a stylistic commentary quoting the source text, and a short assembled piece with a line-by-line note on what came from which generator or from the student’s hand.
acts.risk: A browser-based notebook avoids local installation, though hosted notebooks and coding assistants commonly require accounts, and students without programming background may need paired work or a starter notebook.

acts.t: Correcting a Vision Model’s Document Analysis
acts.sum: Students work with a scanned document from the National Archives catalog and the National Archives’ Document Analysis worksheet for its type, whether written document, photograph, map, poster, or cartoon. The worksheet’s four-part progression (meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, use it as historical evidence) is put twice: once to a multimodal model that is given the scan and the worksheet questions, and once to the students themselves, who complete their own worksheet before seeing the model’s. Pairs then go through the model’s answers line by line against the scan and the catalog record. In the observation section they mark anything the model reports that is not visible on the document, and any misread date, name, stamp, or handwriting. In the later sections they mark inferences the model has stated as observations and claims about context that the catalog record does not support. Each correction is recorded with the grounds for it, and each answer is labeled accepted, amended, or rejected. The corrected worksheet and the list of grounds are the submitted work.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students produce their own completed worksheet before seeing the model’s, then a line-by-line correction of its answers against the scan and catalog record, labeling each accepted, amended, or rejected with the grounds.
acts.dl: A corrected Document Analysis worksheet in which each of the model’s answers is labeled accepted, amended, or rejected, with the grounds for every correction.
acts.risk: The worksheets are public domain and free to copy, while individual archival documents may carry their own rights, so the scan chosen for upload is one the catalog marks as unrestricted; the instructor can run the model and distribute its answers so students need no account.

acts.t: Sorting the Claims in an AI-Written History
acts.sum: Students who have completed OER Project’s Claim Testing lesson as published receive a one-page narrative of a historical episode from their course, such as the Columbian Exchange or the collapse of a particular empire, that the instructor has generated beforehand with a conversational model from an instructor-written prompt. No student uses an AI tool, and no part of the lesson’s materials is entered into one. Working in small groups, students break the narrative into its separate claims and decide, for each, what kind of support it would need and whether the narrative supplies any. They then check a selection of the claims against the course textbook and assigned primary sources, recording where the narrative is supported, where it states something not found in the sources, and where it leaves out actors, regions, or causes that the sources treat as significant. Groups compare their tables and discuss claims they classified differently. The product is a claim table with the evidence consulted and a short list of omissions, each tied to a source that documents what is missing.

acts.gate: Groups produce a claim table setting out the support each claim would need, what the textbook and primary sources show, and a list of omitted actors, regions, or causes, each tied to a source.
acts.dl: A group claim table listing each claim in the narrative, the support it has or lacks, the evidence consulted, and a list of omissions tied to course sources.
acts.risk: Students need no account, device, or payment because the narrative is distributed on paper or as a file, and only the instructor’s own prompt enters a tool.

acts.t: Verifying Assistant-Proposed Sources for Letter Annotations
acts.sum: Students annotate a transcribed nineteenth-century letter from a public-domain digital collection chosen by the instructor, writing short researched notes on the people, places, and terms it mentions. The design takes from a published archives exercise only the general idea of dividing research into small, separately checkable annotations; that exercise’s letters and handouts are not used. For each annotation a student works two routes. A search-enabled assistant is asked what a named place, regiment, or term refers to and returns an answer with linked sources; the student also searches library databases and newspaper archives for the same item. The student opens every source the assistant links, records whether it exists, whether it says what the assistant reports, and what kind of source it is, and then compares it with what the library search turned up. An annotation enters the final set only when its claims rest on a source the student has read. Alongside the annotated letter and bibliography, each student submits a verification log showing, per annotation, which assistant-supplied claims held, which could not be traced, and which the library sources corrected.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Each student writes annotations whose claims rest on sources the student has read, with a bibliography and a log showing which assistant-supplied claims held, could not be traced, or were corrected by library sources.
acts.dl: An annotated letter with bibliography and a verification log recording, for each annotation, which assistant-supplied claims held, could not be traced, or were corrected by library sources.
acts.risk: Search-enabled assistants generally require an account and may limit free use, and some linked sources sit behind paywalls that library access can or cannot resolve; the letter is drawn from a public-domain collection so that no restricted archival image enters a tool.

acts.t: Testing a Chatbot’s Grammar Rules Against the Data
acts.sum: Students first solve a published NACLO translation puzzle on their own, working from the competition PDF by link, so that they have the experience of deriving word order and word forms from a handful of translated sentences. The AI component then uses a different data set: six sentences in a constructed language written by the instructor, each with an English gloss. Because the language is invented, a model cannot draw on outside knowledge of it, and every rule has to come from the six sentences. Students paste this instructor-written set into a conversational model and ask it to state the word-order and affix rules and to show its reasoning. They treat each stated rule as a hypothesis, test it against all six sentences, and mark it confirmed, falsified, or untestable on the data given. Where the model’s reasoning names a step, students check whether the step follows from the sentences or from an assumption imported from English or another language. The write-up lists the rules that survived, the counterexample for each that did not, and the students’ own corrected rule set, compared with the instructor’s key.
acts.f: Arguing With and Against AI
acts.gate: Students produce a write-up of the rules that held against all six sentences, a counterexample for each rule that did not, and their own corrected rule set.
acts.dl: A write-up listing each rule the model proposed, its status against the data with counterexamples, and the student’s own corrected rule set.
acts.risk: The published puzzle stays on the competition site and is not pasted into any tool; the constructed-language set can be run once by the instructor and the output shared, so students need no account.

acts.t: Generating an Image from a Couplet
acts.sum: After a class has read a poem through the Academy of American Poets’ Teach This Poem lesson, used as published, students turn to a poem in the public domain and work with an image generator. Each student chooses one couplet, writes down what the lines literally name and what they leave unstated, and then enters only the couplet’s words as the prompt. The generator returns several images. Students annotate one of them against the lines: which named things appear, what the generator added that the poem does not mention (figures, a season, a quality of light), and what in the couplet has no visual counterpart, such as sound, rhyme, negation, or a shift in tense. Small groups place images from different couplets in the poem’s order and discuss what a sequence of pictures does to the poem’s argument. The lesson’s own painting and song are not uploaded to any tool; the comparison is between generated image and poem text. Each student writes a paragraph of close reading that uses a specific mismatch between image and couplet as evidence for a claim about how the poem’s language works.
acts.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
acts.gate: Each student writes what the couplet names and leaves unstated, annotates a generated image for what appears, what was added, and what has no visual counterpart, and writes a close reading that argues from one specific mismatch.
acts.dl: An annotated generated image and a paragraph of close reading that argues from one specific mismatch between the image and the couplet.
acts.risk: Image generators often require accounts and limit free generations, so one shared classroom account or instructor-run generation is an alternative; students who are blind or have low vision need written descriptions of the generated images to take part in the comparison.

acts.t: Pressing a Chatbot on Responsibility for AI Harm
acts.sum: Students read the Ethics Unwrapped case on accountability for a fatal autonomous-vehicle crash as published and discuss it in class. For the written assignment they work with a conversational model on a different, instructor-written scenario, a hypothetical hospital triage system that misranks a patient, so that no case text is entered into a tool. Each student asks the model who bears responsibility and then presses it over several turns with objections drawn from the course readings on moral responsibility: that the operator lacked control, that the developer could not foresee the failure, that the system itself cannot be blamed. Students annotate the transcript, marking each point where the model’s allocation of responsibility shifts and whether the shift followed from an argument or from the wording of the challenge. They sort the model’s statements by the level they address: the underlying technology, the specific product, or its deployment in a setting. Claims the model attributes to philosophers are checked against the assigned texts. The submitted paper sets out the student’s own allocation of responsibility and uses the annotated transcript as a foil.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Students press the model with objections from the course readings, mark where its allocation of responsibility shifts and whether argument or wording caused it, and argue their own allocation in a paper that uses the transcript as a foil.
acts.dl: An argumentative paper allocating responsibility in the instructor-written scenario, submitted with an annotated transcript of the exchange.
acts.risk: Students submit their own typed objections to a conversational tool, so an institutionally provided or free tier with clear data terms matters, and the hypothetical scenario keeps real persons and the published case text out of the tool.

acts.t: Annotating an AI Overview of Hindu Worship
acts.sum: Students read Harvard Divinity School’s Religion in Context case study on online pujas as published, along with the sources it links. They then receive a printed overview of “Hindu worship” that the instructor generated beforehand with a conversational model from a one-line prompt of the instructor’s own; the case text is not entered into the tool, and students use no AI. Working in pairs, students annotate the overview sentence by sentence. For each sentence they note whether the case complicates it, citing the passage or linked source that supplies the missing setting, and whether it speaks of the tradition as a single uniform thing where the case shows variation by place, community, or medium. They also note whose perspective the overview defaults to and which practitioners it leaves out. Pairs rate the overview against criteria the class has drafted for an adequate description of a living tradition, and compare ratings with another pair and with the instructor’s. The product is the annotated overview and a rewritten paragraph in which each general statement is either tied to a specific context or removed.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: Students produce sentence-by-sentence annotations citing the case and its linked sources, a rating against the class’s own criteria, and a rewritten paragraph in which each general statement is tied to a specific context or removed.
acts.dl: An annotated AI-generated overview with case citations, a criteria-based rating, and one rewritten paragraph in which general statements are tied to specific contexts.
acts.risk: Students need no account or device because the overview is printed, and the case is read on the publisher’s site so that no copyrighted case text is copied or entered into a tool.

acts.t: Auditing an Agent’s Report on a Religious Community
acts.sum: Students delegate a bounded research task to an agentic deep-research tool: compile a sourced profile of one religious community in the region around the campus, such as a gurdwara, mosque association, or Orthodox parish. The agent searches the web and returns a report with linked sources. Students then audit the report instead of using it. They reconstruct the agent’s steps from its action log, open each source, and classify it by who is speaking: the community itself, another religious body, journalists, scholars, or a commercial directory. Using questions about whose voice is heard, whose is missing, and who decides, they identify members of the community (by generation, gender, language, or lay and clerical standing) who do not appear in any source the agent chose. They mark sentences that describe a whole tradition where the source describes one congregation, and sentences that state a belief in the community’s own voice without attribution. The AAR Religious Literacy Guidelines are assigned as background reading as published and are not entered into the tool. The audit memo ends with a list of sources a researcher would need to add.

acts.gate: Students produce an audit memo classifying each source by who is speaking, naming community members who appear in no source the agent chose, flagging overgeneralized and unattributed sentences, and listing sources a researcher would need to add.
acts.dl: An audit memo that classifies each source the agent used by speaker, flags overgeneralized and unattributed sentences, and lists the sources and voices a researcher would need to add.
acts.risk: Deep-research and agentic features are often limited to paid tiers, so one instructor-run report per community shared with the class is an alternative; the profile draws only on public web pages and names no private individuals.

acts.t: Voice Rehearsal Before a Language Exchange
acts.sum: Learners of French complete The Mixxer’s lesson on meals as published and, before meeting their human exchange partner, rehearse the conversation aloud with a voice-mode conversational model. The model is given an instructor-written instruction to speak as a French-speaking peer and to talk about everyday meals; no lesson text is entered. Before the rehearsal each learner writes down what they expect to be able to say and what they expect a French speaker to say about meals. During the rehearsal they note expressions they lacked and any description of “typical” French meals the model offers. They then hold the live exchange with their partner and afterward compare the two conversations: which expressions and corrections came only from the partner, which of the model’s generalizations the partner’s own account confirmed, qualified, or contradicted, and how each interlocutor handled the learner’s errors. Vocabulary and constructions taken from the rehearsal are checked against the course textbook or a dictionary before reuse. The written reflection closes with what the learner would prepare differently for the next exchange.

acts.gate: Each learner writes expectations before the rehearsal, compares it with the live exchange to find which of the model’s generalizations the partner confirmed, qualified, or contradicted, checks borrowed expressions against the textbook or a dictionary, and plans the next exchange.

acts.risk: Voice mode records the learner’s speech, so the tool’s audio retention terms and a text-chat alternative matter for learners who decline voice recording or have speech or hearing disabilities; voice features may require an account or app.

acts.t: Listening to a Position You Reject
acts.sum: Each student names a position on a public controversy that they reject and asks a conversational model to argue it in the voice of someone who sincerely holds it. Writing Commons’ article on rhetorical listening is assigned reading in its published form; none of it is entered into the tool, and the analysis students write is in their own terms. Students read the model’s argument and write an account of the reasoning and commitments from which the position makes sense to its holders, without rebutting it. They then tell the model their own view and record what happens: whether it holds the position, softens it, or moves toward agreement with the student. Pairs who rejected opposite positions next exchange their own first-person statements and write the same kind of account of each other, then discuss the two experiences. The comparison centers on friction: what the model’s readiness to accommodate made easier or left unpracticed, and what the classmate’s presence required. Students check their account of the opposing reasoning against two published pieces by actual advocates of the position, noting what the model’s version omitted.
acts.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
acts.gate: Students write accounts of the opposing reasoning from both the model’s argument and a classmate’s statement without rebutting either, compare the two listening experiences, and check their account against published advocates for what the model omitted.
acts.dl: Two written accounts of an opposing position’s reasoning (one from the model’s argument, one from a classmate’s statement) and a comparison of the two listening experiences.
acts.risk: Students type their own views on a controversy into a tool, so topic choice stays with the student, and a tool with clear data-retention terms or an institutional deployment matters; a printed model argument supplied by the instructor is an alternative for students who opt out.

acts.t: Predictions from Text or from Memory
acts.sum: Students read two nineteenth-century short stories in the public domain in installments: one widely anthologized, one obscure. At pauses the instructor has set, each student writes a prediction of what happens next, the textual clue it rests on, and a confidence rating, before reading on. The same excerpts, up to the same pause, are given to a conversational model with a request for its prediction and its grounds. Afterward, students lay their predictions beside the model’s and beside what each story actually does. For every model prediction they judge whether its stated grounds are present in the excerpt it was given or whether it refers to events, names, or an ending the excerpt had not yet reached. The contrast between the famous story and the obscure one centers the discussion: where the model appears to recall a text it encountered in training, and where it reasons, as the students did, from foreshadowing, narration, and genre. Students write a short note on what distinguishes inferring from a text and recalling it. The published lesson plan that suggested the format is not reproduced or entered into a tool.

acts.gate: Students write their own predictions with a clue and a confidence rating before reading on, judge whether each of the model’s grounds appears in the excerpt it was given, and write a note on inferring from a text versus recalling it.
acts.dl: A prediction sheet with clues and confidence ratings for both stories, annotated against the model’s predictions, and a short note on inferring versus recalling.
acts.risk: Only public-domain story excerpts enter the tool, and the instructor can collect the model’s predictions in advance and distribute them, so students need no account or device.

acts.t: Checking an AI-Written Label Against a Latin Epitaph
acts.sum: Students in a Latin or Roman history course receive a short museum-style label for a Roman funerary inscription, written by a general-purpose AI model, together with the inscription itself: a photograph, a transcription with expanded abbreviations, and a translation from an open-access epigraphic database. The instructor produces the label beforehand by giving a model only the database text, so no student uses an AI tool and no museum’s teaching notes enter one. Pairs take the label apart sentence by sentence and sort each statement about the deceased into three groups: what the stone says outright (names, age at death, the dedicator), what follows from epigraphic convention (filiation or its absence, a freed person’s formula, tribe, an opening such as Dis Manibus), and what the label supplies without support, which may include an occupation, an emotional bond, or a social rank. Pairs then rewrite the label so that every inference is marked as one. The Ashmolean’s teacher notes on death and burial inscriptions are linked as background reading on status, family, and commemoration.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Each pair sorts every statement in the label into what the stone says, what epigraphic convention implies, and what the label supplies without support, then rewrites the label so every inference is marked as one.
acts.dl: A sentence-by-sentence sorting sheet for the label and a rewritten label in which each inference is marked.
acts.risk: Students need no account or device beyond a way to view the photograph and database entry; a transcription and translation accompany the image for learners who cannot work from the photograph.

acts.t: Drafting and Testing Correction Rules After Text Recognition
acts.sum: A faculty member preparing a corpus of digitized sources works with a coding assistant to draft the correction scripts that follow automatic text recognition, and tests every rule before it touches the corpus. The researcher begins by hand-correcting a sample of pages to serve as ground truth and by listing the recurring recognition errors in the output: a long s read as f, broken ligatures, words split at line ends, confusions such as rn and m. For each error type the coding assistant drafts a regular expression or a short Python routine. Each rule is run on a second, held-out sample, and a log records every substitution with its surrounding line. The researcher reads the log and marks false corrections, which often include period spellings normalized away and proper names altered. Rules are kept, narrowed, or dropped on that evidence, and the character error rate is computed before and after against the ground truth. The surviving rules, the log, and the error rates go into the project’s documentation of its correction method.

acts.gate: The researcher hand-corrects the ground-truth sample, reads every logged substitution to mark false corrections, and decides which rules are kept, narrowed, or dropped on that evidence.
acts.dl: A tested set of correction rules with a substitution log, before-and-after error rates, and a documented decision about the correction method for the corpus.
acts.risk: Recognition output from unpublished or rights-restricted archival material is subject to the holding institution’s terms, so the error examples given to the assistant can be limited to short strings or to public-domain pages.

acts.t: Sourcing a Generated “Period Photograph”
acts.sum: Students in a history methods course use an image generator to produce a plausible “photograph” of a late nineteenth-century classroom and then treat the result as a candidate historical source. Beside it they place a public-domain photograph of a comparable scene, chosen by the instructor from a national library’s online collection, with its catalog record. For both images students fill in the same sourcing sheet: maker, date, place, who commissioned it and why, physical format, and how it reached the collection. For the library photograph each line is answered from the catalog record. For the generated image the lines stay empty or can be answered only with the student’s own prompt and the date of generation. Students then look at what the generated image does contain, which often includes dress, furniture, or poses drawn from different decades, and note what it suggests about the pictures the model was built from. No real, named person is depicted. A short written comparison states what makes a photograph usable as evidence. The Digital Inquiry Group’s lesson on evaluating photographs is linked as a published companion.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Students complete the same sourcing sheet for both images, note details in the generated image drawn from different decades, and write a comparison stating what makes a photograph usable as evidence.
acts.dl: Two completed sourcing sheets and a short written comparison of what each image can and cannot serve as evidence for.
acts.risk: Image generators often require an account and may limit free use, so generation can be done once by the instructor or in groups; both images need text descriptions for students who cannot view them.

acts.t: Structured Academic Controversy with a Source-Bound Paraphrase Check
acts.sum: Students work in teams of four, split into two pairs, on a contested historical question, each pair holding a set of public-domain documents that supports one assigned position. One pair presents; the other restates what it heard without rebutting, and the presenters confirm the restatement. At that point the listening pair types its restatement into a document-grounded assistant that has been loaded only with the team’s document set. The assistant marks any statement it cannot locate in the presenting side’s documents and quotes the nearest passage. Both pairs go to the documents and accept or contest each mark, recording their grounds; the assistant may miss a fair paraphrase or treat a reasonable inference as an addition, and those cases are part of what the team settles. Roles then reverse. In the last phase the pairs set aside their assigned positions and write either a consensus statement or a statement of where they still disagree, with each sentence keyed to a document.

acts.gate: The team produces the restatements, a decision with recorded grounds to accept or contest each mark against the documents, and a consensus or disagreement statement with every sentence keyed to a document.
acts.dl: A log of accepted and contested flags with reasons, and a team consensus or disagreement statement keyed to the documents.
acts.risk: A short typed restatement by students enters the tool, so a campus-licensed or no-login grounded assistant on one shared device per team limits account and privacy demands.

acts.t: Three Transcriptions of One Civil War Letter
acts.sum: Students transcribe a passage from the facsimile of one of the three letters that Lot Sabine Willard, a first lieutenant in the 11th Illinois Cavalry, wrote to his family in March and April 1862, working from the handwriting alone. A vision-capable model is then given the same facsimile image and returns its own transcription. Students set three versions side by side: their own, the model’s, and the typeset transcription published by the Newberry. Every point of disagreement goes into a table with a proposed explanation, which may be a letterform, an abbreviation, a line break, or the model’s tendency to modernize spelling or supply a word that makes the sentence read smoothly. Students then return to the central question of the Newberry activity, how Willard’s attitude toward battle changes across the three letters, and note whether any disputed word bears on that reading. The handwritten original remains the reference; the typeset text is treated as an expert reading that can itself be questioned.

acts.gate: Students transcribe the passage from the handwriting alone, explain every disagreement among the three versions, and note whether any disputed word bears on how the writer’s attitude toward battle changes across the letters.
acts.dl: A three-column transcription table with an explanation for each disagreement and a short note on whether any disputed reading affects the interpretation of the letters.
acts.risk: The site states that digitized images may be used for any lawful purpose subject to the Newberry’s Rights and Reproductions Policy; image upload usually requires an account, and students who cannot read the facsimile can work from the two typed versions.

acts.t: Mapping Current AI Commentary onto a 1929 Radio Debate
acts.sum: Students who have worked through the National Humanities Center’s lesson on the 1929 magazine debate over commercial radio, used as published, turn to present-day commentary on generative AI and ask which arguments return with each new medium. No AI tool is used; AI is the subject. The instructor supplies two recent, openly readable opinion pieces, one welcoming generative AI and one objecting to it. Students name the kinds of argument they found in the 1929 essays in their own words and build a chart that sets those against the claims in the two current pieces, quoting a line for each cell. Some cells fill easily and others stay empty, and the class discusses both. A last column asks a question drawn from the idea that a technique fades from view once it is routine: which worries about radio are no longer noticed because radio became ordinary, and which claims about AI concern things that may become similarly unnoticed. Students write a paragraph on one argument with no counterpart in the other period.

acts.gate: Students name the 1929 argument types in their own words, set them against the two current pieces with a quoted line for each cell, and write a paragraph on one argument with no counterpart in the other period.

acts.t: Rehearsing Judges’ Questions Before an Ethics Bowl
acts.sum: In the week before an in-class ethics bowl, each team rehearses its position with a chatbot that plays a judge and may only ask questions. The team works on an instructor-written case and drafts its own outline: the stakeholders, its answer to the case question, and its reasons. The outline goes to a general-purpose chatbot with an instruction to respond only with questions about assumptions, consistency, and overlooked parties, and to offer no position or verdict of its own. The team answers aloud or in writing and keeps the transcript. Afterward members sort each question into one of three groups: it exposed a real gap in the position, it was already answered in the outline, or it rested on a misreading of the case. The team revises its outline in response to the first group only and says why the other questions were set aside. The bowl itself runs with human presenters, respondents, and judges, and the PLATO lesson plan for an in-class ethics bowl is linked as the published guide to that format.

acts.gate: The team produces its own outline of stakeholders, answer, and reasons, sorts each question by whether it exposed a real gap, was already answered, or misread the case, and revises only for real gaps, saying why the rest were set aside.
acts.dl: An annotated transcript sorting the chatbot’s questions into three groups, and a revised position outline.
acts.risk: A team’s outline enters the tool, so one shared login or a campus-licensed chatbot per team limits individual account requirements, and a human questioner can stand in for teams that opt out.

acts.t: Writing Consent Terms for a Synthetic Voice
acts.sum: Students listen to a short synthetic voice clip of a consenting speaker, placed beside a real recording of the same person, and write the consent and disclosure terms they would require before such a clip could be made or shared. The instructor prepares the clip in advance with a voice-generation tool, using the instructor’s own voice or that of a colleague who has agreed in writing, so students use no AI tool. Groups first map the people with a stake in a cloned voice: the speaker, family or an estate, listeners, the tool’s provider, and performers whose work depends on their voice. They then look at the clip at three levels: the underlying technology, this particular artifact, and the settings in which it might be used, from a course announcement to a performance released after a speaker’s death. Each group drafts terms covering scope, duration, labeling, withdrawal of consent, and use after death. The Markkula Center’s case on an AI-generated comedy special is read by link as the real event against which the terms are tried.

acts.t: Question-Only Assistant for a Scripture Analysis Draft
acts.sum: Students in an introductory course on Judaism, Christianity, and Islam draft a short analysis of one assigned scripture passage and revise it in response to an assistant that may only ask questions. The passage comes from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, or the Qur’an in a public-domain or openly licensed translation. The student gives a document-grounded assistant the passage and the draft; the assistant is configured to ask, for each interpretive claim, where in the passage it is anchored, and to offer no interpretation or rewriting. Students answer by quoting a verse or phrase, or by recognizing that a claim rests on later tradition, a commentary, or the textbook instead of the passage. They revise and attach a note on which questions led to a change, which they set aside, and any point at which the assistant drifted into supplying a reading of its own. The exchange is ungraded and comes before instructor feedback; grading stays with the instructor. Later papers in the course are written with fewer rounds of questions or none.

acts.t: Ordering in French with a Voice Assistant as Server
acts.sum: First-year French learners who have studied the food chapter of Français interactif hold a spoken role-play in which a voice-capable assistant plays a server in a French restaurant. The instructor writes a short menu and a role card that tells the assistant to stay in character, speak at a beginner’s pace, and avoid correcting the learner. Each learner orders for two people, asks about one dish, and changes one item, and the session transcript is saved. In pairs, learners go through their own lines in the transcript and check partitive articles, expressions of quantity, forms of prendre and boire, and questions with inversion against the chapter’s grammar pages. They also compare the assistant’s lines with how servers and customers speak in the chapter’s restaurant and interview videos, noting phrasing that sounds scripted or unlike those speakers, and places where the assistant let an error pass without comment. A class debrief collects the most frequent errors and the points where the simulated server and the filmed speakers differed.

acts.t: One Request, Three Ways: Testing a Chatbot’s Uptake
acts.sum: Language learners write the same request in the target language three ways (blunt, hedged, and indirect or ironic) and send each version to a chatbot in a separate conversation to see how it is taken. The situation is one the instructor sets, such as asking a neighbor to turn down music or asking a professor for an extension. For each version the learner records the wording, what was meant, and what the chatbot’s reply shows it understood: whether it treated the hint as a request, registered the irony, or answered the literal words. Learners then put the same three versions to the instructor or another proficient speaker and record how that person says each would land in the setting described. The two sets of responses are compared. Discussion turns on where the chatbot’s sense of politeness and directness follows target-language convention and where it appears to follow a different default, often that of English. The CASLS InterCom issue on pragmatics is linked as background reading on the gap between what is said, meant, and understood.
acts.f: Style, Genre and Language Through AI Imitation
acts.gate: Each learner writes one request bluntly, with hedging, and indirectly or ironically, records what each version meant, and sets the chatbot’s uptake beside a proficient speaker’s account of how each would land in the stated setting.
acts.dl: A three-row record of wording, intent, and uptake for the chatbot and for a proficient speaker, with a short comparison.
acts.risk: Chatbots vary in quality across languages, and free versions may be weaker in less widely supported ones, so one shared demonstration account can replace individual accounts.

acts.t: Following an AI Search Tool’s Citations to Their Origin
acts.sum: Students in a college writing course pick one factual claim from a recent opinion piece and ask an AI search tool whether the claim is accurate, then follow every source the tool cites back toward its origin. Only the claim, restated as a question in the student’s words, goes into the tool. For each citation the student opens the page and keeps going until reaching the report, dataset, or statement the information began with, entering one of four results in a trace log: the source says what the tool reported, it says something narrower or different, it does not mention the claim, or it cannot be opened. Students then look for the same claim once more through the library’s databases and news indexes without the tool, and add what that search finds. The finished log supports two verdicts written in a short memo: one on the claim in the opinion piece, and one on how closely the tool’s answer matched its own cited sources. The Writing Spaces activity on moving through information networks is linked as a published companion.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Each student follows every cited source to the report, dataset, or statement where the information began, records one of four results for each, searches the library without the tool, and writes verdicts on the claim and on the tool’s answer.
acts.dl: A citation trace log and a short memo giving a verdict on the claim and on the search tool’s report of its sources.
acts.risk: Some cited sources sit behind paywalls, so library database access and a log category for sources that cannot be opened are part of the design; free tiers of AI search tools may limit the number of queries.

acts.t: Reading the Campus Assistant’s Terms Beside the Course Policy
acts.sum: First-year writing students read the data and use terms of the assistant their campus licenses alongside the course AI policy, and then check what they read against the tool’s behavior. Each group produces a one-page sheet with two columns, what the course policy permits a student to do and what the tool does with what a student gives it, and lists questions the two documents leave open. Those questions go to the instructor and, where relevant, to the campus office that manages the license. The Writing Spaces activity comparing AI and human summaries is linked as a published companion.

acts.t: Accepting or Rejecting an AI’s Cuts to One’s Own Paragraph
acts.sum: Students take a paragraph from their own draft that they judge to be wordy, ask a chatbot to revise it for concision, and then decide on every cut the chatbot made. The original and the revision are set side by side, and each change is numbered. For each one the student records a decision (accept, amend, or reject) and a reason, with attention to what the cut did besides shorten the sentence: a qualification removed, an emphasis moved, a term replaced by a near-synonym, or a sentence rhythm flattened into something that no longer sounds like the writer. The student then assembles a final version from the accepted and amended changes. Before working on their own paragraphs, the class rates two revisions of a sample paragraph written by the instructor and compares its ratings with the instructor’s, since concision allows more than one acceptable result. The Purdue OWL’s exercises on eliminating wordiness are linked for further practice with their own answer pages and are not entered into any tool.

acts.t: Testing an AI Cultural Generalization Against eHRAF Evidence
acts.sum: Students in a cross-cultural methods course receive a short AI-written claim that two cultural traits tend to occur together, for example that societies with a given marriage practice also show a given residence pattern, and treat it as a hypothesis to be tested against ethnographic evidence. The instructor produces the claim in advance with a conversational model and distributes it on paper together with the prompt that generated it; students use no AI tool. Working from the published Cross-Cultural Correlation Study assignment, used as it stands by link, they restate the claim in testable form, assemble their comparison sample in eHRAF World Cultures, and judge the strength of support in the way that assignment specifies. A closing section of the paper returns to the AI claim: which societies fit it, which do not, and whether its wording reflects a default vantage point, such as English-language sources or one region standing in for humanity. The claim is checked against primary ethnographic passages cited by page, not against the model’s own elaboration.

acts.gate: Students produce a testable restatement of the claim, their own comparison sample of societies, and a paper judging where the claim holds, fails, or overgeneralizes, citing primary ethnographic passages by page.
acts.dl: A research paper that tests the AI-written claim against a sample of societies and closes with an assessment of where the claim holds, fails, or overgeneralizes.

acts.t: Second-Coding an AI’s Codes for Afterlife Beliefs
acts.sum: Students act as second coders alongside a document-grounded assistant that proposes codes for beliefs about the afterlife in ethnographic passages. They begin with HRAF’s published Religion exercise, completed by hand as it stands, which gives practice in reading an ethnographic excerpt for a specific trait. The AI stage uses different material: the instructor loads a set of public-domain ethnographic accounts into a grounded assistant along with an instructor-written codebook, and no text from the HRAF exercise or the eHRAF database enters the tool. Each student codes the same passages independently and records those codes before seeing the assistant’s. The class then computes simple percent agreement between human and machine coding, and pairs resolve each disagreement by quoting the sentence in the account that supports one code over the other. The assistant may assign a code that the quoted passage does not support, or may read a moral judgment into a plain description; such cases are logged with the passage as the deciding reference. The log of resolved disagreements feeds a short memo on what the codebook left ambiguous.

acts.t: Adding a Local Judicial Independence Decision with AI Search
acts.sum: Students use an AI search tool to locate a recent court decision on the independence of judges or prosecutors from their own jurisdiction, then verify it before it joins class discussion. The UNODC exercise on judicial decisions and documents is used as published for the shared discussion; this design adds a locally sourced case beside it. Each pair writes its guiding questions before searching: which court, which period, what kind of interference is alleged. The search tool returns candidate decisions with summaries and links, and it may cite a case that does not exist, misstate a holding, or attach a real citation to the wrong court. Pairs trace each candidate to the official reporter or the court’s own website, read the decision itself, and keep a log showing which details in the AI summary matched the text and which did not. The verified decision is presented with a one-page brief and two discussion questions written by the pair. Nothing from the UNODC page is entered into the tool; the queries are the students’ own.

acts.gate: Pairs produce their own guiding questions, a log of which details in each AI summary matched the decision text, and a one-page brief with two discussion questions on a decision they have read themselves.
acts.dl: A one-page brief of a verified local decision with two discussion questions and a log comparing the AI summary with the decision text.
acts.risk: Access to official reporters varies by jurisdiction; free court websites or a library-licensed legal database can stand in, and queries contain no student personal data.

acts.t: Questioning an AI Stakeholder in an AI Governance Simulation
acts.sum: During CFR Education’s Regulating AI simulation, run as published, the student council questions a conversational assistant that plays one outside stakeholder, such as an AI developer’s policy director or an allied government’s envoy. The stakeholder brief is written by the instructor; no text from the simulation is entered into the tool, and the instructor operates the assistant on a shared screen while council members pose questions aloud. The assistant answers in role, and its replies are treated as one voice in the room whose contributions are open to challenge, not as a source of record. A student recorder enters each substantive claim on a stakeholder map with one column for interests and one for evidence. After the session, small groups sort the recorded claims: supported by the case’s background materials, supported by another citable source, or unsupported. The council then deliberates and advises on the policy options the case presents, noting which stakeholder claims influenced the recommendation and on what evidence. Because the simulation concerns AI governance, the debrief can also take up what it meant to consult an AI system about its own regulation.

acts.gate: Students record each stakeholder claim on a map of interests and evidence, sort the claims by whether the case materials or another citable source supports them, and the council advises on the policy options, naming the claims that shaped its recommendation.
acts.dl: A stakeholder map of the assistant’s claims sorted by evidentiary support, and the council’s oral recommendation with the claims it relied on.

acts.t: Correcting an AI Reading of a 1917 Political Cartoon
acts.sum: Students ask a vision-capable model to interpret a political cartoon from early 1917 and then correct its reading using period documents. The use-case idea sits beside CFR Education’s Zimmermann Telegram simulation, which is used as published; the cartoon given to the model is a public-domain image the instructor draws from a library or archive collection, so that no file from the simulation is uploaded. Before prompting, each student writes a brief interpretation of their own: figures, symbols, caption, likely target. The model’s reading is then set beside it. The model may misidentify a figure, miss a visual convention of the period, or explain the image with events that had not yet happened when it was drawn. Students mark each statement in the output as supported by the image, supported by a dated primary source, anachronistic, or unsupported, citing the documents they read for the simulation and the archive’s catalog record. The corrected reading is brought into the cabinet deliberation as evidence of how the question of neutrality looked to the public at that moment.

acts.gate: Each student writes an interpretation before prompting, classifies every statement in the model’s reading as supported by the image, supported by a dated source, anachronistic, or unsupported, and brings a corrected reading to the cabinet deliberation.

acts.t: Checking Voting Barriers Against a Current State Election Code
acts.sum: After completing David Price’s three voting simulations, students ask whether the barriers their character met would apply in their own state today. Each student carries a voting profile through the electoral settings in the published resource, ending with the Jim Crow-era election. The sequence then moves from that distant case to a near one. Students load the current text of their state’s election code, a public legal document, into a document-grounded assistant and ask which provisions bear on a voter in their profile’s circumstances: registration deadlines, identification, absentee eligibility, polling hours. The assistant answers with references to sections of the uploaded code. It may cite a section that says something narrower than its summary, or overlook a relevant provision. Students open each cited section, read it in full, and record whether the answer holds, noting the statute’s effective date and any matters the code leaves to county practice. The product is an annotated profile listing each barrier, then and now, with the statutory section that governs it or a note that the assistant’s claim was not found in the source.

acts.gate: Each student reads in full every section the assistant cites, records whether its answer holds, the statute’s effective date, and what the code leaves to county practice, and pairs each barrier, then and now, with its governing section.
acts.dl: An annotated voting profile that pairs each barrier from the simulations with the current statutory section governing it, or with a note that no support was found.

acts.t: Comparing a Simulated Coalition with the Actual Agreement
acts.sum: After negotiating a governing coalition in Colin Brown’s Germany simulation, run as published, students use an AI search tool to find out what an actual coalition agreed. The simulation supplies the experience of bargaining under constraint; the search stage supplies a real case to set beside it. Working in their negotiating teams, students ask a search-oriented assistant for the coalition agreement that followed a recent German federal election, the parties’ pre-election positions in two or three policy areas, and which party received which ministries. The queries are the students’ own, and the simulation’s character sheets are not entered into the tool. The assistant returns summaries with links; it may blur manifesto pledges with agreed text or attribute a concession to the wrong party. Teams follow each link to the agreement itself, to party documents, or to reporting from established outlets, and correct the summary where needed. The debrief sets two tables side by side, the class’s negotiated trades and the verified real ones, and considers what a simplified model of bargaining includes and what it leaves out.

acts.t: Auditing an AI Argument About Korematsu
acts.sum: Students audit an AI-written argument about Korematsu v. United States, separating what it reports from what it asserts. The instructor generates the argument beforehand by asking a conversational model whether the ruling was justified and distributes the printed output; students use no AI tool. The session sits beside Annenberg Classroom’s wartime civil liberties lesson, which is used as published. Each student reads the argument once and notes an initial reaction, agreement or unease, before any checking. Pairs then mark every sentence as description of the ruling, opinion about it, or a blend, and check each descriptive sentence against Executive Order 9066 and the majority and dissenting opinions, all public-domain texts. Findings may include a quotation that does not appear in the opinion, a dissent’s reasoning attributed to the majority, or a confident claim about later legal history that the documents cannot settle. Pairs compare their sentence-level judgments with another pair’s and with the instructor’s marked copy, discussing where a first reaction and a checked judgment came apart. The audited copy, with page references, is the product.

acts.gate: Each pair produces an audited copy of the argument with every sentence marked as description, opinion, or blend, and each descriptive sentence referenced by page to the executive order and the opinions.

acts.t: Ranking an AI Theory of Change Among Student Drafts
acts.sum: An AI-drafted theory of change is placed, unlabeled, among students’ own drafts, and the class ranks them before learning which is which. The program being modeled is a short fictional description written by the instructor, for instance a campus peer-mentoring scheme; J-PAL’s Chicago summer employment case is used afterward as published, and none of its text is entered into a tool. Each group drafts a table linking the program’s actions to the changes it is expected to produce. One further table comes from a conversational assistant given the same description and operated by the instructor. All tables are anonymized and ranked against criteria the class has agreed: whether each link states an assumption, whether each outcome could be measured, and with what data. After the reveal, students put questions to the assistant about why it chose particular links. Its table arrives as a finished product; the reasoning behind it has to be drawn out and may not hold up under questioning. The class then turns to the published case and works through it by hand, without AI, carrying the same criteria forward.

acts.gate: Students draft their own theory-of-change tables, rank every table blind against the class’s agreed criteria with written justifications, and question the assistant’s stated reasoning before working the published case by hand.
acts.dl: A ranked set of theory-of-change tables with written justifications, and notes on the assistant’s stated reasoning for its links.

acts.t: Simulating Selection Bias with a Coding Assistant
acts.sum: Students use a coding assistant to build a simulated dataset in which the true effect of a program is known, then watch two evaluation methods disagree about it. The idea of estimating one program several ways comes from J-PAL’s Happiness on Tap case, which is read as published; its data and text are not entered into the tool. Students describe in their own words a hypothetical program that households choose to join, and ask the assistant for R or Python code that generates household records in which better-off households are more likely to enroll. They set the true effect themselves. The assistant then writes code for a simple comparison of participants with non-participants and for a comparison under random assignment. Because the data are synthetic, runs can be repeated, reset, and altered: stronger selection, smaller samples, a different effect. Students read every line of generated code, confirm that the simulated selection mechanism is the one they specified, and check that the randomized estimate recovers the effect they set. A short report explains the gap between the two estimates in terms of comparison groups and assumptions.

acts.t: Cross-Checking a Grant’s Power Analysis by Simulation
acts.sum: A faculty researcher preparing a grant proposal for a cluster-randomized study uses a coding assistant to write a simulation-based power analysis and reconciles it with an independent calculation. The researcher first settles the design inputs from pilot data and the literature: expected effect size, outcome variance, number and size of clusters, intracluster correlation, anticipated take-up. A formula-based calculator or hand calculation gives a first answer, recorded before the assistant is consulted. The assistant is then asked for commented R code that simulates the design many times and reports the share of runs that detect the effect. The two answers may differ, because the code may ignore clustering, mis-specify the variance, or treat take-up differently from the formula. The researcher traces each discrepancy to a line of code or an assumption and documents the resolution. J-PAL’s power calculations exercise informs the choice of design features to vary; none of its text or parameters is used. The reconciled figure, the code, and a note on how it was checked go into the proposal’s methods section and data-management record. No participant data enter the tool.

acts.risk: Only design parameters are entered, never participant data; funders and institutions differ on disclosure of AI assistance in proposals, so the note on how the code was produced and checked is kept with the application.

acts.t: Voice Practice Intake with an AI Client
acts.sum: Students conduct a spoken practice intake interview with a voice-enabled AI model playing a client, then code their own transcript for interviewing behaviors. The client is a fictional profile written by the instructor, with a presenting concern, a reason for reluctance, and details the client offers only if asked in an open way. Georgia State’s intake interview case study video is viewed as published before the session; nothing from it is entered into the tool. Each student speaks with the AI client for about ten minutes and exports the transcript. Working from the course’s interviewing text, students mark each of their own turns as open question, closed question, reflection, or interruption, and note where the client’s answers narrowed or widened in response. The AI client may be more forthcoming and more patient than a person at a first agency contact, and the debrief names those differences. The rehearsal is positioned as preparation for a later interview with a trained human role-player or field supervisor, where human assessment takes place. A coded transcript and a paragraph on two exchanges the student would handle differently are submitted.

acts.t: Hand-Checking an AI-Coded Population Pyramid
acts.sum: Students build one population pyramid by hand and a second with a coding assistant, then verify the coded one against their own arithmetic. The hand stage uses public age-and-sex counts for one country from United Nations population estimates or a national statistical office: students work out cohort shares and draw the pyramid on graph paper. Population pyramids are a general demographic technique; Population Education’s Power of the Pyramids lesson, which also teaches them, informs this design at the level of the idea only. For a second country, students download current counts and ask a coding assistant for a script that computes cohort percentages and draws the pyramid. The script may use the wrong denominator, such as each sex’s total in place of the whole population, reverse an axis, or merge the oldest age groups. Students recompute three cohorts by hand, compare them with the plotted values, and read the code to locate any discrepancy. With both pyramids verified, they write a comparison of the two shapes and what each suggests about past fertility, mortality, and migration, stating which inferences the counts support and which would need other data.

acts.dl: Two population pyramids, one hand-plotted and one coded, with a verification table for three cohorts and a written comparison of the two shapes.
acts.risk: The census data and a browser-based notebook are free; the hand-plotted stage needs only graph paper, and the coded figure carries alt text or a data table for readers who cannot use the image.

acts.t: Checking AI-Written Hominin Narratives Against Cranial Measurements
acts.sum: Students in a biological anthropology lab test AI-written accounts of human evolution against the cranial measurements they have taken themselves. The measuring is done first, using the Smithsonian-listed skulls lab as published, with casts or photographs of ape, modern human, and fossil hominin crania. Before class the instructor asks a conversational model for short evolutionary narratives about the same species, working from an instructor-written prompt that names the taxa only; nothing from the lesson is entered into the tool. Each student pair receives a printed narrative and marks every sentence as supported by their tabulated values, contradicted by them, or beyond what cranial features can show, such as claims about behavior, diet, or direct ancestry. Pairs then compare markings and trace disagreements back to the measurement table. Model output of this kind often states inferences with the same confidence as observations, and the sentence-level sorting makes that difference visible. A closing discussion gathers the sentences placed in the third category and considers what further evidence, such as postcranial remains or dated strata, would bear on them.

acts.gate: Student pairs produce their own cranial measurements and a sentence-by-sentence marking of the narrative as supported, contradicted, or beyond what cranial features can show.
acts.dl: An annotated AI-written narrative in which every sentence is marked as supported, contradicted, or beyond what the measured cranial features can show.
acts.risk: Students use no AI tool or account; the narrative is distributed on paper or as a file, and photographs can stand in for casts where a cast collection is not available.

acts.t: Auditing an Assistant-Written Script for Earthquake Data Preparation
acts.sum: Students in an introductory GIS or geoscience course map recent earthquakes from public USGS records, and a coding assistant writes the script that prepares the download for import. The source exercise has students clean and reformat the catalog by hand in a spreadsheet; here that stage becomes an audit. Students describe the needed transformation to the assistant, run the script it returns, and then inspect the result before any mapping: the record count is compared with the original download, latitude and longitude columns are checked for order and sign, and the handling of missing magnitudes or depths is traced in the code. They ask the assistant to explain its reasoning for each operation and annotate where the explanation and the code diverge. Only the audited file goes into the GIS software, where students map the distribution, overlay plate boundaries, and commit to a prediction about where earthquakes occur relative to those boundaries. The report includes the script, the audit notes, the maps with scale and orientation, and the tectonic interpretation.

acts.dl: A report containing the assistant-written script, the audit notes, the processed data file, maps with scale and orientation, and a tectonic interpretation with predictions.
acts.risk: The earthquake records are public and contain no personal data; the design needs access to a coding assistant and GIS software, and the source material’s noncommercial share-alike terms apply to any adapted handout.
