acts.t: Interviewing a Simulated Bystander in a Fictional Dilemma
acts.sum: Learners in an international humanitarian law or human rights course question a chatbot that plays a bystander at the moment of decision in a fictional incident the instructor has written. The scenario, set in an invented town during an armed conflict, stops where the character has to choose whether to help a stranger at personal risk. In small groups, learners interview the character about what it fears, what options it sees, and whom it believes responsible, then record the reasons it gives. Each learner privately ranks those reasons from most to least credible before the group works toward a shared ranking, and the gaps in the story surface where people and the model filled in details differently. The class then turns to the documented bystander accounts in the ICRC exploration, read as published and never entered into the tool, and compares the simulated reasoning with what real people in those accounts faced and did. Discussion considers which obstacles and risks the simulation left out, softened, or resolved too easily.

acts.dl: A group ranking of the simulated bystander’s stated reasons with a short written comparison to one documented account.
acts.risk: One shared instructor or group account is enough, since the interview can be run from a single screen; the scenario is fictional, so no real person’s story is entered into a tool.

acts.t: Questioning a Treaty-Grounded Assistant on Minimum Recruitment Ages
acts.sum: Learners studying the law on child soldiers put questions to a document-grounded assistant that holds only the treaty texts the instructor has loaded, such as the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions and the Convention on the Rights of the Child with its Optional Protocol on armed conflict. The assistant answers questions about minimum ages for recruitment and participation in hostilities and cites the article it relies on. Before asking, each pair writes its own guiding questions and its own reading of one provision, so that there is a prior position to compare. Every cited article is then opened in the official text and checked: whether the wording matches, whether the obligation is framed as taking all feasible measures or as a prohibition, and whether the instrument applies to states, to armed groups, or to both. Pairs chart where the instruments set different ages and where the assistant merged them. The ICRC exploration on child soldiers is used alongside as published; its materials are not loaded into the tool.

acts.dl: A comparison chart of minimum-age provisions across instruments, with each assistant answer marked as matching or departing from the cited article.
acts.risk: Treaty texts are public documents; a document-grounded tool may require an institutional license or accounts, and a single instructor-run instance can serve the whole class.

acts.t: Critiquing an Assistant’s Estimate of Relational Contact Effects
acts.sum: Students in a political behavior or research methods course ask a data-analysis assistant to estimate whether relational voter contact raised turnout, using a synthetic contact-and-turnout table the instructor has built. The table is constructed so that volunteers chose whom to contact, which means contacted and uncontacted voters differ before any contact occurs. Each student first writes a short analysis plan naming the comparison group and the threats to inference they expect. The assistant is then asked for an estimate and for the code behind it, and students compare its approach with their plan: which voters it compared, whether it adjusted for prior turnout, and whether its written summary claims a causal effect that the design cannot support. Because the instructor knows the effect built into the data, the class can see how far each estimate lands from it. The topic follows a Harvard Kennedy School case on relational organizing in Ohio, which is cited as background; no case text or data is used or entered into the tool.

acts.risk: The dataset is synthetic, so no voter records or personal data are involved, and the design does not require students to buy the case.

acts.t: Updating a Published Case Timeline with AI Search
acts.sum: Students who have read a published Harvard Kennedy School case on flood protection at New York City’s East River Park use an AI search tool to assemble the public record of the project since the case was written. The case is read as purchased, by each student, and none of its text is entered into the tool; queries are written from the students’ own knowledge of the project’s name and location. Each team asks the tool for developments in a stated period and receives a summary with linked sources. Every link is opened, and an item enters the shared timeline only when the team has found the claim in a city agency document, court filing, council record, or dated news report and has recorded a working link to it. Claims the team cannot trace are logged separately with the wording the tool used. The finished timeline is set beside the case’s account of participation and transparency, and teams note which later events bear on the questions the case raises.

acts.t: Debating Deference to a Moderation Classifier in Role
acts.sum: Students playing The Oversight Board microgame, used as published under the Reacting Consortium’s membership and permission terms, take on one added question: how much weight the Board gives to an automated classifier. Before the session the instructor writes a small set of sample political posts, some in more than one language or dialect, and runs them through an openly available toxicity classifier, recording the score for each. The game’s own case materials are not entered into any tool. Factions receive the posts and scores on paper and argue in role for accepting, amending, or overriding each automated call, giving grounds a Board member could record. The set is built to include near-identical posts that receive different scores, so players meet the question of patterned error directly. The Board then votes on a short rule for when human review is required. In the debrief, students step out of role and compare the reasons they gave with public documentation of how such classifiers are trained and where their scores have been reported to vary across groups of speakers.

acts.gate: Students produce in-role arguments for accepting, amending, or overriding each automated score, and the Board’s own rule for when a classifier decision requires human review.
acts.dl: An in-role argument on each automated call and a Board-adopted rule stating when human review of a classifier decision is required.
acts.risk: Students use no AI tool or account. The game materials are available to Reacting Consortium members, or to non-members for a $10 purchase, and every user is asked to file a permissions request before classroom use.

acts.t: Coding a Multi-Agent Deliberation for Group Decision Phenomena
acts.sum: After reading the open Noba module on the psychology of groups, student teams watch a multi-agent AI system deliberate and code the transcript with the module’s concepts. Each team starts a run from an instructor-written brief in which several agents, each given different pieces of information, have to agree on a decision such as choosing among three candidates for a grant. The agents exchange messages, and the system returns the full transcript with its final choice. Teams code each turn using the module’s definitions: whether shared information is repeated while unshared information goes unmentioned, whether positions move toward a more extreme version of the initial lean, and whether signs associated with groupthink, such as pressure toward agreement, appear. Class time is spent taking the transcripts apart instead of rerunning them. Teams compare codings and consider where the vocabulary of human groups fits the agents’ behavior and where it does not, since the agents have no need to belong and no status to protect. The module’s discussion questions on groups students have belonged to supply the human comparison.

acts.gate: Teams produce a turn-by-turn coding of the transcript against the module’s definitions and an account of where the vocabulary of human groups fits the agents’ behavior and where it does not.
acts.dl: A turn-by-turn coded transcript of the agents’ deliberation with a short account of where group-process concepts did and did not apply.
acts.risk: Multi-agent runs can consume paid usage, so a single instructor-run transcript shared with all teams is a lower-cost variant; the brief contains no student data.

acts.t: Screening Study Designs During a Literature Review
acts.sum: A faculty researcher sorting articles for a literature review uses a document-grounded tool to extract, for each study, the four things the Noba Statistical Thinking module asks of any article: the research question, how participants were selected, the summary results, and the strength of the evidence. The module’s closing task is written for students critiquing one article; here it becomes a screening protocol applied across a set of open-access or licensed PDFs that the researcher is permitted to upload. For a subset of articles the researcher reads the methods section and fills in the four fields before querying the tool, which gives a baseline for judging its extractions. Each tool answer is then checked against the methods section, with particular attention to whether random sampling and random assignment have been conflated, since that distinction governs whether a study supports generalization, causal conclusions, both, or neither. Disagreements are logged by type. The resulting evidence table records, for every article, the extracted fields, the page checked, and whether the entry was corrected.

acts.gate: The researcher fills in the four fields by hand for a subset first, checks every extraction against the methods section, especially for conflated random sampling and random assignment, and logs each disagreement by type.
acts.dl: An evidence table for the review listing each article’s research question, selection method, summary results, and strength of evidence, with the page checked and any correction noted.

acts.t: Rehearsing a Co-Facilitation Dilemma with Simulated Group Members
acts.sum: Social work students practicing group facilitation rehearse a response to a critical incident with a chatbot that plays several members of a youth group, in a scenario the instructor has written. The scenario is original, with its own group, setting, and incident, and is built around a moment when a member’s culturally grounded action meets a group norm and the co-facilitators read it differently. The IASWG case Somali Boys Group is read as published and is not entered into the tool. Students type their intervention, the simulated members react, and the exchange continues for a few turns. The debrief has two parts. Students review their facilitation choices against group-work concepts such as norms, inclusion, and co-leader communication. They then read the transcript for what the simulation assumed about the young people it voiced, marking flattened or stereotyped responses and noting whose knowledge would be needed to judge them. The published case is the comparison for how a practitioner with cultural knowledge read a moment of this kind.

acts.gate: Students produce their own typed interventions and a transcript annotated for their facilitation choices and for the flattened or stereotyped responses the simulation gave, with a note on whose knowledge would be needed to judge them.
acts.dl: A role-play transcript annotated for facilitation choices and for the cultural assumptions the simulation made, with a short reflective commentary.
acts.risk: The scenario is invented and no client or case material is entered; students who share the background of the simulated members may find the portrayal uncomfortable, so an observer role or a different scenario can be offered.

acts.t: Testing an AI Explanation of Shooting Hotspots Against Maps
acts.sum: Sociology students compare an AI-written explanation of why fatal shootings cluster in certain urban neighborhoods with the evidence in public interactive maps. Students first complete the TRAILS mapping activity as published, locating areas of concentrated fatal shootings and viewing the same areas on maps of inequality, segregation, and criminal justice disparities. The instructor separately obtains a one-page explanation from a conversational model, using a general question that contains nothing from the activity, and distributes it on paper. Students begin by writing down their first reaction to the text and whether it sounds right. They then go through it claim by claim, marking statements the maps can support, statements about individual motives or character that area-level data cannot support, and statements that move from spatial overlap to cause. Legends, units, and data years are checked wherever the text cites a pattern. In discussion the explanation is treated as one more reading open to challenge, and students compare their first reactions with what the checking showed.

acts.gate: Each student marks which claims in the explanation the maps can support, which assert individual motives the area-level data cannot carry, and which move from spatial overlap to cause, and notes how that checking compared with their first reaction.
acts.dl: A claim-by-claim annotation of the AI-written explanation with a short note comparing the student’s first reaction to the result of checking.

acts.t: Comparing Human and Vision-Model Accessibility Audits of a Route
acts.sum: Students studying the social model of disability compare their own audit of a travel route with one produced by a vision-capable model. The TRAILS virtual field activity, used as published, has students travel a route from the position of a wheelchair user and record barriers and supports. For the AI component, students work with a different route documented in their own photographs of campus or in openly licensed street-level imagery, so that no part of the published activity or its mapped imagery is uploaded. The model is asked to list barriers and supports visible in each image. Students set its list beside their own and classify the differences: features both found, features only one found, and things a still image cannot show, such as a door’s weight, a curb ramp blocked at certain hours, or how staff respond to a request for help. The last category carries the discussion toward nonmaterial factors. Students also consider whose experience would be needed to settle disagreements and what the exercise itself, done by people imagining a wheelchair user’s position, cannot convey.

acts.gate: Students audit the route themselves, classify each difference from the model’s list as found by both, found by only one, or not visible in a still image, and consider whose experience would be needed to settle disagreements.
acts.dl: A side-by-side comparison of the student’s and the model’s barrier lists for one route, with a classified account of the differences and of what images cannot show.

acts.t: Modeling a fishery from a team’s own catch records
acts.sum: After playing the Fishbanks simulation as published, each team works with the log it kept during play: fleet size, where its ships fished, and catch in every round. A coding assistant in a shared notebook helps the team write a small stock-and-flow model of a fishery, with one stock, a regrowth term, and a catch that depends on fleet size. The model is kept deliberately plain, a few lines the team can read aloud, because the aim is to see the feedback structure, not to reproduce the simulation’s internals, which the team has no access to. Teams adjust two or three parameters until the model’s catch curve roughly follows their own record, then use it to test a rule they propose themselves, such as a fleet cap or a per-round quota, and observe whether the stock recovers. Each line of generated code is annotated with what it represents in the fishery. In the debrief, teams set their plots side by side and discuss where the simple model departs from what happened in play, and what the delay between overfishing and falling catch did to their decisions.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Each team annotates every line of the model with what it represents in the fishery, proposes and tests its own policy rule, and accounts for where the simple model departs from what happened in play.
acts.dl: Each team submits an annotated notebook with its fitted model, one tested policy rule, and a short account of where model and play diverge.
acts.risk: Only the team’s own play log and student-written prompts enter the coding tool; a free notebook environment suffices, though access to the simulation itself follows the publisher’s terms.

acts.t: Auditing an AI-drafted due diligence memo on FTX
acts.sum: Students in a financial accounting or ethics course receive a two-page due diligence memo, written by a conversational AI tool at the instructor’s request, that recommends a private investment in FTX as of early 2022. The instructor produces the memo from a short prompt of their own, without giving the tool any part of the MIT Sloan case, and labels it as AI-drafted. Students read the case as published and annotate the memo sentence by sentence with four marks: supported by the case, contradicted by the case, not addressed by the case, and knowable only in hindsight. A second pass looks at what the memo leaves out, working through the incentives of employees, regulators, investors, and customers and noting which of them the memo never questions. Before discussion, each student rates the memo against the course’s criteria for a due diligence document, covering evidence, governance, related-party exposure, and audit quality, and then compares that rating with the instructor’s. Discussion centers on the gaps between ratings and on what a reader in early 2022 could have asked for.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Each student produces the four-mark annotation of the memo against the case, a list of the stakeholders and questions the memo never raised, and a rating against the course’s due diligence criteria.
acts.dl: Each student submits the annotated memo with a criteria-based rating and a list of the questions the memo did not ask.
acts.risk: Students need no AI account; the case is read from the publisher’s page, and the memo is distributed as a labeled handout in an accessible format.

acts.t: Testing a single-cause answer against a causal loop diagram
acts.sum: Before opening the Boeing 737 MAX 8 case, each team asks a general conversational assistant, in the team’s own words, for the single root cause of the two crashes and saves the reply. The assistant answers from its general training; nothing from the case document is pasted into it. Teams then read the case as published and sort candidate causes on a fishbone diagram under headings they choose, such as design, schedule, cost, oversight, and communication. The fishbone is redrawn as a causal loop diagram, with each arrow tied to a page of the case, so that reinforcing pressures become visible. The saved answer is placed on the diagram: teams mark which loop it sits in and which loops it leaves out. In a second exchange, a team describes one omitted loop in its own summary and asks the assistant to defend or revise its answer, then judges whether the revision rests on reasons or simply agrees. Teams present the diagram alongside both exchanges and state where their account and the assistant’s still differ.
acts.f: Arguing With and Against AI
acts.gate: Teams produce a fishbone sort under headings they choose, a causal loop diagram with every arrow tied to a page of the case, and a statement of where their account and the assistant’s still differ.
acts.dl: Each team presents a page-referenced causal loop diagram with the two saved AI exchanges located on it.
acts.risk: A free general assistant is sufficient; the case is read from the publisher’s page and is not uploaded, and teams can share one account so that no individual sign-up is needed.

acts.t: Pitching an innovation measurement plan to a skeptical physician
acts.sum: Students who have read Yale’s Design at Mayo raw case rehearse a pitch with an AI assistant playing a senior physician who doubts that a design lab’s results can be measured. The persona brief is written by the instructor from general knowledge of physician-led organizations; no page, video, or document from the case site is given to the tool. Each student drafts, in their own words, a one-page plan for how an in-house innovation center might show clinicians what its work has achieved, then pitches it in a text or voice exchange. The simulated physician raises objections about clinical time, patient outcomes, and what counts as evidence, and the student revises the plan after each one. The topic is bounded and the student does the talking. Afterward, students sort the objections in their transcript into those that match something they found in the case materials and those that are generic, and note any objection a physician in the case would likely raise that the simulation never did. Class debrief compares the sorted lists and the revisions they prompted.

acts.t: Checking a scaling model against one new region’s evidence
acts.sum: After reading Yale’s SELCO Foundation raw case, teams test its scaling question on a region the case does not treat. Each team picks a region and writes guiding questions about what a decentralized energy program there would depend on: who lends to rural households, who repairs equipment, which agencies and local organizations are active. An AI search tool is used to answer those questions from current public sources, working only from the team’s own queries; nothing from the case site is entered. For every answer, the team opens each cited source and logs who published it, when, in what language, and whether it says what the tool’s summary reports. The log has a column for where a source sits: local organization, national agency, international funder, or press. Teams then look at the balance, since results may lean toward English-language and funder-published material, and where a member reads a regional language, one query is repeated in it for comparison. The closing memo states which of the foundation’s building blocks would likely transfer and which evidence is thin.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Each team writes its own guiding questions, logs who published each cited source and whether it says what the summary reports, and writes a memo on which building blocks would likely transfer and where the evidence is thin.
acts.dl: Each team submits a source log and a transfer memo that separates sourced findings from gaps in the available evidence.

acts.t: Classifying a second industry from AI-gathered market shares
acts.sum: This follow-on to Ezra Pugh’s team-based exercise on fast food market structure moves teams to a second industry whose data they assemble themselves. Teams first complete the original task: from one set of market shares, each commits to an answer pairing a market-structure classification with a position on antitrust action, and defends it. Each team is then assigned another industry, such as domestic airlines or ride-hailing, and writes down the classification it expects before searching. An AI search tool is asked for current market-share figures. Every figure goes into a table with its source, date, unit (revenue, units, or users), and market definition, and the team opens each source to confirm the number appears there. A figure is accepted, amended, or rejected, with the reason recorded; figures that cannot be traced are dropped. With the verified table, the team makes the same kind of paired choice and defends it to the class, explaining where its prior expectation changed and how the market definition it adopted affects the classification.

acts.gate: Teams produce their expected classification before searching, a market-share table with a recorded reason for accepting, amending, or rejecting each figure, and a defended classification and antitrust position built on the figures they confirmed.
acts.dl: Each team submits a verified market-share table with accept, amend, or reject decisions and a defended classification and antitrust position.

acts.t: Two labor-market models rank the mall’s stakeholders
acts.sum: Teams first complete Michael Levine’s team-based activity on a shopping mall split between two cities with different minimum wages, ranking six stakeholders from most negatively to most positively affected in the short run and the long run. A conversational assistant is then given the openly licensed scenario and asked for two rankings of the same stakeholders, one reasoned from a competitive labor-market model and one from a monopsony model, with the assumptions behind each stated. Teams lay the three rankings side by side. Where the orderings differ, they name the assumption doing the work: how responsive employment is to the wage, whether an employer sets wages, whether shoppers and workers cross the city line. The scenario leaves details open, so teams also list what the assistant filled in without being told and what they filled in themselves. Each assumption is tested against the facts the scenario actually gives and against the textbook’s two models. Whole-class discussion moves from the rankings to which assumptions the class finds better supported and why.

acts.t: Plotting average against marginal driver recruitment cost
acts.sum: Students begin with Louis Vayo’s short exercise on driver-recruitment advertising, choosing by hand among four strategies from two small samples of per-driver cost, and write one sentence on why. That choice is made without any tool, since deciding between average and marginal reasoning is the thinking the exercise is about. Students then ask a coding assistant for a short script that simulates two advertising platforms whose cost per additional driver rises as more drivers are recruited, and that plots average cost and marginal cost for each. The script arrives as a finished product. Students turn it into a reasoned one by annotating each line with what it means economically: which variable is the last driver’s cost, where the running average is computed, what the rising-cost assumption is. They change the rate at which costs rise and find the point at which a choice based on averages picks the more expensive platform at the margin. Each student returns to the original four options and states whether the plot changes or confirms the first answer.

acts.t: Comparing an AI price forecast with a classroom pit market
acts.sum: A class runs the Economics Network’s hand-run pit market as published, with one addition: a forecast made by a conversational assistant before trading and kept sealed until afterward. The instructor writes the buyer values and seller costs for the session’s card decks, gives that list to the assistant, and asks it to predict the price range, the number of trades, and how prices will move from round to round, with reasons. Students trade without seeing the forecast, since a prediction shown in advance could steer the prices they ask for. After the last round, the forecast is displayed beside the transaction prices the class recorded. Students separate the forecast into two kinds of statement: those that follow from the deck by arithmetic, which they recompute by drawing the supply and demand steps, and those that are claims about how people behave, which only the class data can test. Discussion turns to which behavioral claims held, which did not, and what would differ had traders read the forecast first. A second session with a new deck lets students write their own forecast.

acts.gate: Students separate the forecast’s arithmetic claims from its behavioral claims, recompute the arithmetic from supply and demand steps, test the behavioral claims against the class’s own transaction prices, and later write their own forecast.
acts.dl: Students produce a marked-up forecast separating arithmetic from behavioral claims, with each claim compared to the class’s transaction record.
acts.risk: Only the instructor uses the AI tool, and only instructor-written card values are entered; the experiment needs open floor space, so seated trading is an option for students with limited mobility.

acts.t: Testing an AI account of a bank failure
acts.sum: After a class has run the Economics Network’s computerized bank-run experiment as published, students receive a one-page explanation of a recent bank failure written by a conversational AI tool from the instructor’s own prompt. The handout is labeled as AI-written, and no handbook material was given to the tool. Students already hold two things to test it with: the conditions under which the Diamond-Dybvig model produces a run, and their own session’s record of when patient depositors withdrew early. They mark each claim in the explanation as one the model accounts for, one their class data illustrates, one that lies outside the model (interest-rate losses, uninsured deposit concentration, social media speed), or one with no support they can find. Factual statements about the bank are looked up in the public post-failure review issued by the relevant regulator. The class meeting is spent taking the experiment apart alongside the handout: where the explanation uses the language of panic, students ask whether their own early withdrawals were panic or a reasonable response to what others were doing.

acts.gate: Each student marks every claim as accounted for by the model, illustrated by the class data, outside the model, or unsupported, and writes a paragraph on what the model and the class data each explain about the failure.
acts.dl: Each student submits the marked explanation with a short paragraph on what the model and the class data each explain about the failure.
acts.risk: Students use no AI tool; the experiment itself requires networked computers or a lab as described on its page, and the handout and regulator review are provided in accessible formats.

acts.t: A vision model’s reading of a customer setting
acts.sum: Students working on a venture idea photograph a place where their intended customer meets the product or service, such as a counter, a shelf, or a waiting area, framed without identifiable people. Following Glenn Fajardo’s d.school exercise, each uploads the photo to a vision-capable assistant and asks what makes the scene interesting, then what story the objects in it might belong to. The replies are saved as a numbered list of observations. Students then go back to the same place with a notebook and no device in hand. For a set period they check each observation against what is in front of them, marking it confirmed, refuted, or not visible from where they stand, and add what the photograph could not carry: sound, waiting time, who speaks to whom, what people do with their hands. The written comparison names one detail the assistant drew attention to that the student had missed and one thing only being there supplied. In class, students state which observations changed their sense of the customer’s situation.

acts.gate: Students produce a return visit’s direct observation, marking each saved observation confirmed, refuted, or not visible, and their own record of what the photograph could not carry, such as sound, waiting time, and who speaks to whom.
acts.dl: Each student submits the photo, the saved AI observations marked confirmed, refuted, or not visible, and a list of what only direct observation supplied.
acts.risk: Photos exclude identifiable people, and private premises need the owner’s consent; a free multimodal assistant is sufficient, and students without a nearby site can use a campus service point.

acts.t: Scripting and voicing an observation walk for a venture
acts.sum: Students who have taken the d.school’s Inspiration Walk, an audio-guided solo walk, write and voice one of their own for a venture challenge they are working on. Each student plans a short route with a few stopping points and scripts spoken prompts that direct a listener’s attention at each one, tying what can be seen there to the challenge. A text-to-speech tool turns the script into an audio track with pauses long enough to look and write. The author listens through first, checking pacing, pronunciation of place names, and whether any instruction is unclear when heard instead of read. A classmate then takes the walk with earbuds and a notebook. The author reads the classmate’s notebook and marks which prompts produced an observation and which produced nothing or confusion. Weak prompts are rewritten and the track is voiced again, which takes minutes, so a second classmate can test the revision in the same week. The group debrief compares prompts that worked across different routes and what each listener noticed that the author had not expected.

acts.dl: Each student submits two versions of the script and audio track with the test listeners’ notebooks and a note on what was revised and why.
acts.risk: Listeners need a phone and earbuds; a transcript, an indoor or step-free route, and a seated version keep the walk open to students with hearing or mobility constraints, and free speech tools may cap track length.

acts.t: Auditing a research agent’s map of a problem space
acts.sum: Teams choosing a venture problem first build the d.school’s six-layer map by hand, posting notes for how their topic shows up as data, technologies, products, experiences, systems, and implications. The same topic is then handed to a research agent, a tool that plans and runs a multistep web investigation from one instruction, with a request to populate the six layers and cite a source for every entry. The agent’s report comes back as a second map. Teams audit it before using any of it. Where the tool exposes its plan and the pages it visited, the team reads that trail and notes what it searched for and what it skipped. For each entry in the data and systems layers, and a sample from the others, a team member opens the cited source and tags the note verified, plausible, or unsupported. Verified notes are merged into the hand-built map in a second color; unsupported ones are set aside with the reason. The team then words its own challenge from the merged map and marks which layer, and whose notes, that choice rests on.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Teams build their own six-layer map by hand, tag each audited entry as verified, plausible, or unsupported against its cited source, merge only verified notes, and word their own challenge, marking which layer and whose notes it rests on.
acts.dl: Each team submits a merged two-color map, an audit table of the agent’s entries and steps, and a worded challenge statement.
acts.risk: Multistep research modes are often limited or unavailable on free tiers, so an institutional license or one instructor-run report per team may be needed; only the team’s topic statement is entered.

acts.t: Checking an AI budget memo against a campaign table
acts.sum: Students first work Geoff Fripp’s Marketing ROI Made Simple exercise by hand from the publisher’s worksheet, as published. The AI component uses a different table that the instructor writes for the class: a fictional retailer, its own product and margin, and a quarter of campaign results with spend, units, and revenue. That instructor-written table is loaded into a document-grounded assistant, which is asked for a one-page memo recommending where next quarter’s budget goes, with return on marketing investment shown for each campaign. Students receive the table and the memo together. They recompute every return figure by hand and check whether the memo’s numbers were calculated on gross margin or on revenue, since the two give different rankings. Each sentence of the memo is then marked as traceable to a cell in the table, as an inference the table permits, or as a statement with no basis in it, such as a claim about audience or seasonality. The course rubric announces that unsupported statements carried into a student’s own final recommendation lose marks, and students write that recommendation last.

acts.gate: Each student recomputes every return figure by hand, marks each memo sentence as traceable to a cell, an inference the table permits, or without basis, and writes their own budget recommendation last.
acts.dl: Each student submits the recomputed table, the sentence-by-sentence marked memo, and a short budget recommendation of their own.
acts.risk: Only the instructor-written table enters the tool, and the instructor can run it once for the class; the published worksheet is used by link, not uploaded, and its solutions are members-only.

acts.t: Auditing chatbot borrowing advice against hand-computed costs
acts.sum: Small groups in a personal finance or introductory accounting course audit a printed piece of chatbot advice about how to pay for a purchase. The instructor writes a short scenario of their own, a fictional renter facing a car repair bill with three ways to finance it, each with a stated rate, fee, and term, and beforehand collects a conversational assistant’s recommendation on that scenario. Groups begin without the printout: they compute the monthly payment and total cost of each route by hand or in a spreadsheet and settle on their own ranking. The printout is then handed out. Each sentence of the advice is labeled as informing the borrower of a consequence, steering toward one choice, or narrowing the options, and every figure in it is recomputed from the scenario’s terms. Groups mark where the advice ignores a stated constraint, such as the renter’s monthly budget, or supplies a number the scenario does not contain. The FDIC module’s own borrowing-comparison activity is run as published, on paper, earlier in the session; none of its text goes into an AI tool.

acts.gate: Groups produce their own cost comparison and ranking before seeing the advice, then an annotated copy in which every sentence is labeled and every figure is recomputed from the scenario’s terms.
acts.dl: Each group produces an annotated copy of the advice with every sentence classified and every figure recomputed, beside its own cost comparison table.
acts.risk: Learners need only paper or a spreadsheet; no accounts are required, no personal financial information is used, and the scenario is fictional.

acts.t: Loan interview role-play mapped to lender criteria
acts.sum: Learners in a consumer finance or financial counseling course sit on the applicant’s side of a loan interview conducted by a conversational assistant. The instructor writes a one-page file for a fictional applicant with a mixed record: steady income, little savings, one old collection account. The assistant is set up as a loan officer and asks whatever it judges relevant; each learner answers in character from the file for about ten minutes and saves the transcript. In the debrief that follows, pairs tag every question the assistant asked with the lender criterion it serves (capacity, capital, or credit history and character) and list what a human underwriter would have asked that the assistant did not. They also mark any place where the assistant stated a lending rule or approval threshold, and check those statements against the course text and current regulator guidance. The FDIC module’s application-review activity and its self-assessment worksheet are used as published, on paper, before the role-play, so learners have already applied the criteria from the lender’s chair. No module text and no personal financial information enters the tool.

acts.gate: Each pair tags every question the simulated loan officer asked with the lender criterion it serves, lists what a human underwriter would have asked that it did not, and checks any lending rule it stated against the course text.
acts.dl: Each pair submits an annotated interview transcript with questions tagged by lender criterion and a list of gaps and checked rule statements.
acts.risk: Learners answer from a fictional applicant file and are told to enter nothing about their own finances; a voice mode or a paired typist can serve learners who prefer not to type.

acts.t: Sorting one’s own negotiation moves after a role-play
acts.sum: After a two-party contract negotiation role-play, students write up their own moves from memory: opening offer, concessions, questions asked, information shared or held back, and the terms agreed. Those notes, and nothing from the licensed role materials, are loaded into a document-grounded assistant limited to the uploaded text. The assistant sorts each recorded move into positional or interest-based bargaining and quotes the line of the notes it relied on. Negotiating pairs then go through the sorted list together and accept, amend, or reject each label, writing a one-line reason whenever they overrule the tool. A move the assistant reads as positional may, in the pair’s account, have been a test of the other side’s alternatives, and that disagreement becomes material for the class debrief. The instructor’s debrief handouts and the published teaching themes remain the reference for what the categories mean. The simulation itself (Sally Soprano I, from the Program on Negotiation) is purchased and run as published, with one licensed copy per participant; students are told to keep confidential role instructions and figures out of their notes.
acts.f: Arguing With and Against AI
acts.gate: Each negotiating pair accepts, amends, or rejects every label the assistant gave its moves, writing a one-line reason for each overrule grounded in what the move was meant to do.
acts.dl: Each negotiating pair produces a sorted list of its own moves with every label accepted, amended, or rejected and a reason for each overrule.
acts.risk: Only student-written notes are uploaded, and the simulation’s per-participant license means its role materials stay out of any tool; a restricted or institutionally provided document assistant keeps the notes from wider reuse.

acts.t: Enumerating multi-party deal packages with a coding assistant
acts.sum: Students in a negotiation or public policy management course test claims about a multi-party deal by having a coding assistant enumerate every possible agreement. The instructor writes an original scoring scheme for a fictional siting dispute: five issues, a handful of options on each, a private point value for every party, and a supermajority rule for approval. After the class has negotiated a scored multi-party simulation, each team asks the assistant for a commented script that lists all packages in the instructor’s scheme, computes each party’s score, and flags which packages clear the approval rule and which are Pareto-efficient. Before trusting the output, teams score three packages by hand from the scheme and compare. They then use the enumeration to examine statements made in debrief, such as “no better deal existed” or “one party could block anything,” and write what the script cannot show: why a party that gains on paper may still hold out. Harborco is run as published under its per-participant license; its role sheets and point values are never typed into the assistant.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Teams hand-score three packages to check the script, test two debrief claims against the enumeration, and write what the script cannot show, such as why a party that gains on paper may still hold out.
acts.dl: Each team submits the commented script, its three hand-scored packages, and a short memo testing two debrief claims against the enumeration.
acts.risk: A free coding assistant and a browser-based notebook suffice; the scoring scheme is instructor-written, so no licensed simulation content enters the tool. The simulation itself is licensed per participant: the instructor orders a copy for every student who takes part.

acts.t: Coding a transcribed video negotiation for process moves
acts.sum: Pairs negotiate a short cross-border licensing deal over video conference, record it with both parties’ consent, and run the recording through a speech-to-text tool that labels speakers. The scenario is two pages written by the instructor, so nothing proprietary is spoken into the recording. Each student corrects the machine transcript against the audio, noting where overlapping talk, accents, or product names were misheard or assigned to the wrong speaker. On the corrected transcript, pairs code a small set of process moves: who proposed the agenda, when the first number was put on the table, interruptions, and questions about the other side’s interests. Counts and time stamps go into a one-page profile of the session. Students then re-record only the first three minutes with a changed opening and compare the two transcripts. The exercise is preparation for Ren the Robot, a Program on Negotiation simulation designed for video conference, which is licensed per participant and run as published, without recording or transcription. Its listed themes of agenda-setting and the effect of the video medium indicate what the practice round attends to.
acts.f: Workplace Communication and Career Readiness
acts.gate: Each student corrects the machine transcript against the audio; each pair codes its own process moves into a one-page profile with counts and time stamps and compares the original opening with a re-recorded one.
acts.dl: Each pair submits a corrected, coded transcript, a one-page process profile, and a comparison of the original and re-recorded openings.
acts.risk: Recording requires each partner’s consent and a stated retention period; transcription accuracy often varies by accent and audio quality, which the correction pass records, and a conferencing platform’s built-in or institutionally licensed transcriber avoids sending recordings to a third party. The simulation itself is licensed per participant: the instructor orders a copy for every student who takes part.

acts.t: Reconciling assistant-written difference-in-differences code with a spreadsheet result
acts.sum: Students complete a published policy-evaluation project twice: once unaided in a spreadsheet, following the project’s own walk-through, and once with code written by a coding assistant. The project is CORE’s Doing Economics Empirical Project 3, used as published by link; its text and data file are not given to the assistant. Instead, each student describes the calculation in their own words (group means before and after a policy, and the difference between the two changes) and asks for a short R or Python function. The function is first run on a twelve-row table the student invents, where the answer can be worked out by hand. Only then is it run locally on the project data. Students place the two sets of results side by side and trace every mismatch to its cause: a filter applied differently, missing values dropped silently, groups defined another way. A short memo records what matched, what did not, which version was right, and how the student knows. The spreadsheet result, built step by step, is the reference throughout.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Each student describes the calculation in their own words, tests the function on an invented table worked by hand, traces every mismatch against their own spreadsheet result, and records which version was right and how they know.
acts.dl: Each student submits the function, its test on an invented table, a side-by-side results table, and a reconciliation memo.
acts.risk: Free coding assistants and free R or Python environments suffice; the project’s text and data are not uploaded, in keeping with its NoDerivatives license, and code runs on the student’s own machine or a campus notebook service.

acts.t: Testing a vision model’s reading of Lorenz curves
acts.sum: Students who have drawn Lorenz curves and calculated Gini coefficients by hand or in a spreadsheet give their finished chart to a vision-capable model and ask it to read the chart back. The curves come from Doing Economics Empirical Project 5, completed as published; only the student’s own chart image is uploaded, with the coefficient values left off. The model is asked which country or year is most unequal, to rank the rest, and to estimate each Gini coefficient from the picture. Students compare those answers with their calculated values and sort the discrepancies: curves that cross and so cannot be ranked by eye, a legend misread, an estimate given to two decimals from a chart that cannot support it. They then redraw the chart once (different colors, direct labels, or a table beneath) and repeat the request to see whether the reading changes. A half-page note states what the chart conveys that the single coefficient does not, and the reverse. The calculation precedes the upload in every case, so the model’s reading is tested and never used as the answer.

acts.gate: Each student calculates the Gini coefficients before uploading, sorts the model’s misreadings against those values, redraws the chart once to see whether the reading changes, and writes what the chart conveys that the single coefficient does not, and the reverse.
acts.dl: Each student submits the original and redrawn charts, a table of the model’s readings beside calculated coefficients, and a half-page note on chart versus coefficient.
acts.risk: A free vision-capable chat tool suffices; only the student’s own chart is uploaded, and a text table beneath the redrawn chart also serves readers who use screen readers or have color vision differences.

acts.t: Comparing language-model agents with class public goods data
acts.sum: After a class has played a public goods game and analyzed its own contributions beside published experimental data, the instructor shows what a group of language-model agents did under the same kind of rules. Before the session, the instructor writes a plain statement of a standard public goods game (endowment, multiplier, group size, ten rounds, with and without a punishment option) and has a small agent workflow play it several times, saving each agent’s stated reasoning and contribution per round. Students receive the run logs and a chart of average contributions. They plot the agents’ path against their class data and against the published cross-country results they worked with in Doing Economics Empirical Project 2, which is used as published. Working from the logs, groups classify the agents’ stated reasons, note whether contributions decay as they did among people, and write down what the agents’ behavior appears to assume about other players. The discussion treats the agent run as a simplified model: where it departs from human data, and what in its setup or training text might account for that. Students use no AI tool themselves.
acts.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
acts.gate: Groups produce a chart setting the agents’ contributions beside their class’s and the published data, a classification of the agents’ stated reasons, and an account of where the agent run departs from human data and why.
acts.dl: Each group produces a three-series chart of agent, class, and published contributions with a one-page account of where the agent run departs from human data and why that might be.
acts.risk: The instructor runs the agents and distributes logs, so students need no accounts or paid tools; the cost of repeated agent runs falls on the instructor or department, and class contribution data are shared only in anonymized form.

acts.t: Checking a model’s backward induction on a hand-drawn game tree
acts.sum: Students draw the extensive form of a two-stage leader and follower quantity game on paper, photograph it, and ask a vision-capable model to solve it by backward induction while explaining each step. The payoffs are ones the instructor sets for the course, written on the board; the tree is the student’s own drawing. The model’s reply is treated as a worked example under examination. Students check that it has read each payoff from the photo correctly, that it starts from the follower’s decision nodes, that each comparison uses the right player’s payoff, and that the path it names follows from those comparisons. Errors are annotated on a printout. Pairs then put a second question to the model: why might a real follower choose the lower-payoff response after an aggressive leader move? They compare its answer with what their classmates did when the class played such a game. EconPort’s Stackelberg classroom experiment is run as published beforehand; its instructions and screens are not uploaded. The hand solution each student completes first is the key the model is checked against.
acts.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
acts.gate: Students draw their own game tree, solve it by hand first, and mark every misread payoff, misplaced comparison, or unsupported step in the model’s solution; pairs then weigh its account of follower behavior against what classmates did.
acts.dl: Each pair hands in its game tree, its own hand solution, and an annotated printout of the model’s step-by-step solution with errors marked.
acts.risk: A phone camera and a free vision-capable chat tool are enough, and pairs can share one device; students with handwriting or motor differences can draw the tree in any diagram tool and upload that image.

acts.t: Adding chatbot alternatives to a whole-system map
acts.sum: Design or entrepreneurship teams build a whole-system map of a product on a wall with sticky notes (components, life-cycle stages, people, connected systems), set priorities from an estimated life-cycle assessment and business needs, and brainstorm at every node, following VentureWell’s Whole System Mapping exercise. This version adds a second round of ideas from a conversational assistant after the team’s own. Once the unaided brainstorm is on the map, one member reads the node list to the assistant and asks for one alternative design decision per node, plus one proposal for removing a part of the system altogether. The assistant’s ideas go up on notes of a different color. Teams compare the two colors: which nodes only the humans touched, which assumptions the assistant reversed that the team had taken for granted, and which of its proposals rest on claims about materials or processes that nobody has checked. Every idea, from either source, is then scored in the team’s decision matrix against the priorities set earlier, and the team records the trade-off that rules each shortlisted idea in or out.
acts.f: Arguing With and Against AI
acts.gate: The team produces its own brainstorm at every node before the assistant’s round, scores every idea from either source against the priorities it set earlier, and records the trade-off that rules each shortlisted idea in or out.

acts.t: Sourcing salary and rent assumptions for a cash-flow projection
acts.sum: Students build a multi-year personal budget projection for an early-career scenario of their choosing, and the work centers on where each input number comes from. A search-oriented assistant is asked for an entry-level wage, typical rent, and a tax estimate for that occupation and place, with links. Students open every link. Each figure goes into an assumptions register with four columns: the value the assistant gave, the value found at the cited page, the publishing body and date, and a decision to keep, replace, or drop. Figures the cited page does not contain are replaced from a government wage or housing series located through the library. The projection is then built in a spreadsheet from the register alone, with rows labeled in the income-statement terms the course later applies to a venture. Students may use a fictional graduate instead of their own plans. The approach of meeting business finance terms first through a personal projection follows a published lesson on TeachingEntrepreneurship.org, which faculty can consult directly; its materials are not reproduced or uploaded here.

acts.t: Prompt and change log for an app-builder assignment
acts.sum: Entrepreneurship students who are building a small web application with an AI app builder keep a structured log of the build and use it to compare two ways of working. The surrounding assignment can be the one published on TeachingEntrepreneurship.org, used as written by link; this use-case idea describes only the log and the comparison. Every prompt is entered with what the builder changed, what stopped working, and what the student did next. Midway, each student builds the same feature twice: once from a single long request that leaves the builder to plan and act, and once in small requests with a check after each. Both versions go to a classmate for a ten-minute user test with three set tasks. The log then records, for each version, which tasks the tester completed, which defects appeared, and how many corrections the student had to make by hand or by further prompting. A closing page, shared with the class as work in progress, states which claims about the app the student has confirmed by testing and which rest only on the builder’s own description of what it made.

acts.gate: Each student keeps the prompt-and-change log, compares two builds of one feature through a classmate’s user test, and states which claims about the app testing confirmed and which rest only on the builder’s own description.
acts.dl: Each student submits a prompt-and-change log, user-test results for the two builds of one feature, and a one-page statement of confirmed and unconfirmed claims about the app.
acts.risk: App builders often cap free use and require accounts, so build quotas, an institutionally provided option, or shared team accounts need settling in advance; students are advised to keep personal data out of test applications.

acts.t: Interviewing a simulated non-reader stakeholder before drafting
acts.sum: Before drafting a workplace recommendation report, each student identifies people who will be affected by the decision without ever reading the document, and interviews one of them in simulation. The student writes a short brief in their own words: the organization, the decision under consideration, and the chosen stakeholder’s position, for example a night-shift employee affected by a scheduling change. A conversational assistant plays that person, and the student asks about concerns, constraints, and what a fair outcome would look like. Afterward the student sorts the assistant’s statements into three groups: concerns that match what the student knows of the actual setting, concerns that sound plausible but would need confirming with a real person, and generic remarks that could apply anywhere. Only the first two groups feed the draft, and the second is listed as open questions for the report’s author to pursue. A revision memo names each change made because of a non-reader stakeholder. Purdue OWL’s stakeholder worksheet is completed as published, on paper, before the interview; the worksheet itself is not uploaded or reproduced.

acts.t: Drafting a committee postmortem from its own records
acts.sum: A department committee that has finished a project, such as a curriculum revision or a new internship program, writes its postmortem report with an institutionally hosted, document-grounded assistant working over the committee’s own records. Agendas, minutes, the project timeline, and the shared message thread are loaded into the hosted environment. The assistant drafts the factual sections (what was decided when, who was assigned what, which deadlines moved), citing the document and date behind each statement. Members read the draft against the records and against their own recollection, correcting entries and adding what was never written down: the hallway agreement, the objection nobody minuted. Those additions are marked as member-supplied. Judgments about what worked, what did not, and what to do differently are written by the members themselves in a meeting, and the assistant is not asked for lessons learned. The report ends with action items, each with an owner. Purdue OWL’s guide page on postmortem reports is consulted as published for the genre’s purpose and its question areas; the page is read by members and is not loaded into the tool.

acts.gate: The committee writes its own judgments of what worked, what did not, and what to do differently, adds the agreements and objections the records never captured, and assigns an owner to each action item.
acts.dl: The committee produces a postmortem report with a cited chronology, member-supplied additions marked as such, member-written judgments, and owned action items.
acts.risk: Committee records can include personnel matters and student names, so they stay in an institutionally hosted environment under campus data rules, and members agree beforehand on which threads are loaded.

acts.t: Testing Peer-Evaluation Weighting Rules on Synthetic Ratings
acts.sum: A program committee responsible for project courses decides how peer ratings will adjust individual grades drawn from a shared team grade, and uses a code-capable assistant to see what each candidate rule does before adopting one. Following Karen Moore’s account of weighted peer evaluation, in which a rating counts for more when the rater worked directly with the person rated, committee members write two or three weighting rules in plain language. They also write a synthetic rating set for an invented twelve-person team with shifting subgroups, so no student data is involved. The assistant turns each rule into a short script, runs it on the synthetic set, and tabulates whose share of the grade rises or falls under each scheme, with a plain average included for comparison. Members recompute a sample of the adjustments by hand in a spreadsheet and read the script against the written rule. The discussion that follows concerns the tension between group and individual grading and how much weight novice raters’ judgments can carry.

acts.gate: The committee writes the candidate weighting rules and the synthetic team, checks a sample of the script’s adjustments by hand and the script against each written rule, and chooses the rule, stated in plain language, that will adjust individual grades.

acts.risk: Only committee-written synthetic ratings enter the tool, so no student records are exposed; reuse of the source’s structure carries its attribution, noncommercial, and share-alike conditions.

acts.t: First-Pass Grouping of Statistics Journals for a Teaching Inquiry
acts.sum: An instructor of a first-year statistics seminar studies a semester of weekly student journals as evidence of how the class reasons about quantitative concepts, with a document-restricted assistant doing a first pass over the full set. The course follows the cycle Michele DiPietro describes: students write a weekly entry in response to a structured prompt, the instructor comments and returns it, and the set is read together for class-wide misunderstandings. At the end of term, with the approvals and student permissions the institution requires, the instructor de-identifies the entries and loads them into an institutionally hosted assistant limited to that corpus. The assistant proposes groupings of recurring misconceptions, for example treating a sample proportion as a population value or reading correlation as cause, and quotes the entries it assigns to each. The instructor opens every quoted entry, rejects groupings the wording does not support, recodes a sample unaided, and records where the two passes differ. The checked groupings inform the next cycle of prompts and a write-up of the inquiry.

acts.dl: The instructor produces a verified codebook of recurring statistical misconceptions with quoted journal evidence and a short methods note on where the assistant’s pass and the unaided pass differed.
acts.risk: Student writing enters a tool, so the design assumes an institutionally hosted environment, de-identified entries, student permission, and whatever ethics review the institution requires for studying course work.

acts.t: Comparing a Hand-Drawn Argument Map With an AI Map
acts.sum: Students in an introductory philosophy course map a short argument by hand, then compare their map with one a conversational assistant produces for the same passage. The task borrows the structure of Mara Harrell’s paired tests: questions about the components of a brief argument, ending in a student-drawn argument map, with parallel versions built on different content. Here the passages are public-domain texts, such as a paragraph from Hume’s Enquiry, and each student commits to a map on paper before opening the tool. The assistant is asked to identify the conclusion, the premises, and the inferential links, and its output is redrawn in the same format. Students mark every node or arrow where the two maps differ and, for each, either defend their own reading or revise it, citing the sentence in the passage that settles the matter. A later round with a new passage of parallel structure repeats the comparison. The assistant’s map is treated as one participant’s reading, open to challenge, and both maps answer to the text.

acts.gate: Each student commits to a hand-drawn argument map before opening the tool, then defends or revises their reading at every point where the two maps differ, citing the sentence in the passage that settles it.

acts.risk: Only public-domain passages are entered, a free conversational tool is sufficient, and an instructor-run demonstration on a shared screen can stand in where students lack accounts.

acts.t: Logging Image-Generator Use in a Design Process Book
acts.sum: Design students who use an image generator during ideation record each use in the process book they keep across a project. The process book, as Dan Boyarski’s account describes it, is a semester-long record of how a project developed, read by faculty alongside the finished work and used in progress conversations. In this version every generated image that enters the project gets an entry: the prompt as typed, a print or thumbnail of the output, the decision to keep, alter, or discard it, and a caption of a sentence or two stating what the image contributed and what the student changed. Hand sketches, references, and material tests sit on the same spreads, so the book shows where generated imagery entered the sequence and where it did not. At progress conversations student and instructor read the entries against the project brief and against the tool’s saved history. Students who decline the generator keep the same book without those entries. The book is read alongside the final piece, not in place of it.

acts.t: A Group Reading of Dewey Beside an Assistant’s Selections
acts.sum: Teacher candidates read a one-page excerpt from John Dewey’s 1897 essay “My Pedagogic Creed,” a public-domain text, using the NSRF Text Rendering protocol as published, and then compare the group’s charted selections with selections made by an assistant limited to the same page. The protocol is followed from the linked document without modification; nothing from it is entered into the tool. Once the group’s chart is on the wall and its discussion has closed, the facilitator gives the assistant only the Dewey excerpt and asks it to choose the passages it finds most significant and to say why. The assistant’s choices are posted beside the group’s. Participants discuss what each set foregrounds, which lines both chose, and which of the group’s choices came from classroom experience the assistant had no access to. Each assistant selection is checked against the page to confirm it is quoted exactly. The unaided reading comes first by design, so the comparison shows what the tool selected and passed over, and its reading stays open to challenge like any participant’s.

acts.dl: A paired wall display of the group’s selections and the assistant’s, with a short written note from each participant on what the two sets foreground differently.

acts.t: Setting a Committee’s Root-Cause Analysis Beside an AI’s
acts.sum: A program assessment committee works through a shared problem, for instance that few sections submit student work samples for the annual program review, using the NSRF Hidden Issues protocol as published, and afterward sets its own analysis beside one from a conversational assistant. The protocol is run from the linked document, unmodified, and none of its text goes into the tool. When the committee’s charts are complete, a member gives the assistant only the one-sentence problem statement the group wrote and asks for its own account of underlying causes. The reply is printed and posted. Members mark which of the assistant’s causes also appear on their charts, which are generic to any institution, and which of their own depend on local knowledge the assistant did not have: staffing patterns, the submission system, a past decision. Each cause the committee keeps, from either source, is tied to evidence someone in the room can name. The committee accepts, amends, or sets aside the assistant’s suggestions and records its grounds before deciding next steps.

acts.gate: The committee completes its own root-cause analysis first, ties each cause it keeps to evidence a member can name, and records its grounds for accepting, amending, or setting aside each of the assistant’s suggestions.
acts.dl: The committee produces an annotated comparison of its own causes and the assistant’s, with a recorded decision and grounds for each suggestion kept, amended, or set aside.

acts.t: Diagnosing Handwritten Math Errors Before an AI Does
acts.sum: Teacher candidates diagnose error patterns in handwritten arithmetic and then compare their diagnoses with a multimodal assistant’s reading of the same pages. The work samples are written by the instructor: multi-digit subtraction and fraction addition completed by hand with consistent errors built in, such as subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in every column or adding numerators and denominators straight across. Candidates first record, for each sample, the error pattern and what it suggests the student understands. A photograph of each page then goes to the assistant with a request to identify the errors and their likely cause. Candidates tabulate where the assistant misread the handwriting, named a slip where there was a pattern, or matched their diagnosis, and check both against the instructor’s key. The exercise precedes the IRIS case study on identifying and addressing student errors and its linked resources, which are used as published by link; no IRIS material is given to the tool. Discussion turns on what a diagnosis requires beyond a correct answer: knowledge of how learners arrive at a procedure.

acts.t: Weighing AI Function Hypotheses Against A-B-C Records
acts.sum: After completing the IRIS A-B-C analysis activity as published, teacher candidates ask a conversational assistant for alternative hypotheses about the function of the behavior and test each against their own observation records. The IRIS handout and video are used unchanged by link and are not given to the tool; what candidates enter is a typed version of the antecedent, behavior, and consequence notes they wrote themselves, with no names. The assistant is asked what functions those records could be consistent with and what further observation would distinguish among them. Candidates sort the replies: hypotheses their recorded entries support, hypotheses that would need data they did not collect, and hypotheses that rest on details not found in their notes. For each they cite the entries that bear on it. They then keep, amend, or reject their original hypothesis and write a paragraph giving the grounds. In debrief the class compares which suggestions were declined and why, and what a single short observation can and cannot establish.

acts.t: Rehearsing a Difficult Parent Conference by Voice
acts.sum: Teacher candidates rehearse a parent conference aloud with a voice-capable assistant playing a parent who disagrees with the school about how to respond to his child’s classroom behavior. The conference follows the class’s reading of the IRIS case “He Just Needs a Little Discipline,” used as published by link. The persona is not taken from that case: the instructor writes an original role brief, with a different family, grade, and history, in which the parent holds a firm view that the child needs stricter consequences and is wary of the school’s recommendations. Each candidate speaks with the assistant for about ten minutes while a peer observes and takes notes. The transcript is saved. Afterward the candidate marks the turns where they acknowledged the parent’s position, where they explained the school’s concern, and where the conversation stalled, and the observer says how the exchange came across to a listener. A second attempt follows the debrief. The assistant’s replies are treated as rehearsal material, and statements made about behavior support are checked against course readings.

acts.t: Claim, Support, Question on an AI Answer About Learning Styles
acts.sum: Students in an educational psychology course examine a printed AI answer to the question of whether matching instruction to students’ learning styles improves achievement, using Project Zero’s Claim, Support, Question routine exactly as published. The instructor generates the answer beforehand with a conversational model and distributes it on paper with the prompt that produced it; students use no AI tool. Working in small groups with the routine open by link, they take the answer one assertion at a time and document on chart paper what the routine asks for, keeping to the support the answer itself supplies and not what they already believe about the topic. Assertions the answer leaves unsupported are flagged. Groups then turn to the assigned research reviews and mark each flagged assertion as supported, contradicted, or not addressed by that literature, with page references. The closing discussion compares charts across groups: where the answer’s confident wording ran ahead of its support, and which of the groups’ questions the readings could not settle either.

acts.t: A Disassembled Device Read by Students and by AI
acts.sum: First-year engineering students take apart a small mechanical device, such as a retractable pen or a hand-crank flashlight, and compare their own account of its parts and purposes with a multimodal assistant’s labeling of a photograph of the pieces. Teams first work through Project Zero’s Parts, Purposes, Complexities routine as published, by link, with the object in hand, and commit their map to paper. They then lay the components out, photograph them, and ask the assistant to name each part and state what it does. The routine’s text is not entered into the tool; the assistant sees only the students’ photograph. Teams annotate the reply against the physical object: parts misidentified, parts merged or missed, and purposes the assistant could not infer from an image, such as a spring’s preload or the feel of a detent. Where the team and the assistant disagree, the object is reassembled and operated to settle it, and a manufacturer’s diagram is consulted where one exists. The comparison shows what handling a mechanism supplies that a description of its picture does not.

acts.t: Predicting and Testing an AI-Drafted 5E Science Unit
acts.sum: Science teaching candidates write down what they expect a conversational assistant can and cannot do when asked to draft a unit on the 5E model, then test that expectation and reflect with Project Zero’s I Used to Think... Now I Think... routine as published. The prediction is written before any tool is opened and names specifics: whether the draft will sequence the five phases correctly, get the science right, and fit a named performance expectation from the standards. Each candidate then prompts the assistant for a unit on a topic they know well, such as phase changes, and annotates the draft against the five phases, against the standard’s wording, and against their own subject knowledge, noting activities placed in the wrong phase, content errors, and places where the draft is usable. With the annotated draft and the earlier prediction side by side, candidates complete the routine from the linked page, unchanged; the routine’s text is not given to the tool. The reflection is about the tool’s performance on a task from their own field.
acts.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
acts.gate: Each candidate writes a specific prediction before opening the tool, annotates the draft for misplaced activities, content errors, fit to the named standard, and usable passages, and reflects on how their view of the tool’s capability changed.

acts.t: Sourcing Both Sides of a Headline Claim With AI Search
acts.sum: Journalism students weigh a contested headline claim, for example that later school start times raise student achievement, using the Tug for Truth routine as published on the Project Zero site, with a search-enabled assistant used to locate candidate evidence on each side. The routine is followed from the linked page, and its text is not entered into the tool. Students pose their own questions to the assistant, asking separately for studies and reporting that support the claim and that cut against it, and collect the sources it returns. A source earns a place in the class display only after a student has opened it, confirmed that it exists and says what the assistant reported, and applied the program’s source-validation checklist to it: who produced it, what kind of evidence it offers, how recent it is. Items the assistant cited that cannot be found, or that say something different, go on a separate list with a note on the discrepancy. The closing discussion considers where the confirmed evidence leaves the claim and what further reporting would be needed.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students pose their own questions, open each returned source to confirm it exists and says what was reported, apply the source-validation checklist before placing it, and list every cited item that cannot be found or says something different.
acts.dl: A class display of confirmed evidence on each side of the claim, plus a discrepancy list of sources the assistant cited that could not be found or did not say what was reported.
acts.risk: Search-enabled assistants vary in free access, and some linked studies sit behind paywalls, so library database access is assumed for opening the sources.
